L16: ## 1 Recommendations/Risk Benefit Assessment
L17: ## 1.1 Recommendation on Regulatory Action
L18: The clinical reviewer recommends approval of raxibacumab for the treatment of inhalational anthrax. The BLA submission under review has fulfilled all four criteria for approval under 21 CFR §601.90-95 “*New Drug and Biological Drug Products; Evidence Needed to Demonstrate Effectiveness of New Drugs When Human Efficacy Studies Are Not Ethical or Feasible*,”1 for Biologics, also referred to as “*The Animal Rule*”:
L19: - There is a reasonably well-understood pathophysiological mechanism of the toxicity of the substance and its prevention or substantial reduction by the product;
The pathophysiology of inhalational anthrax is reasonably well understood and is similar between humans and animal species selected by the applicant for efficacy studies: New Zealand White (NZW) rabbits and cynomolgus macaques, manifesting as a life-threatening infection with multiorgan failure and a cardinal feature of hemorrhagic mediastinitis. *B. anthracis* toxins [Lethal toxin (LT) and Edema toxin (ET)] are thought to be responsible for the morbidity and high mortality characteristic of systemic anthrax infection. Raxibacumab is a recombinant, human IgG1\lambda monoclonal antibody directed at neutralizing the protective antigen (PA) of *B. anthracis*, binding component of the anthrax toxins, thereby preventing downstream toxic effects of LT and ET: cell death, loss of endothelial barrier function, immune suppression/dysregulation, and edema.
- The effect is demonstrated in more than one animal species expected to react with a response predictive for humans, unless the effect is demonstrated in a single animal species that represents a sufficiently well-characterized animal model for predicting the response in humans;
Two animal models of inhalational anthrax were evaluated in adequate and well controlled studies: NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaques. Inhalational anthrax in these models closely resembles inhalational anthrax in humans with respect to susceptibility, disease pathophysiology, clinical presentation, outcome, gross and microscopic pathology findings. Treatment effect of raxibacumab on reducing the risk of mortality was demonstrated in these animal models.
- The animal study endpoint is clearly related to the desired benefit in humans, generally the enhancement of survival or prevention of major morbidity; and mortality
Untreated inhalational anthrax is a highly fatal disease (&gt;95%), therefore, a relevant endpoint for the animal efficacy study, survival, was selected.
L20: 1 Final Rule published in the Federal Register, Vol. 67, No. 105, May 31, 2002, pages 37988-37998; Regulations: 21 CFR § 314.600-650 (New Drugs), 21 CFR § 601.90-95 (Biologics)
L21: - The data or information on the kinetics and pharmacodynamics of the product or other relevant data or information, in animals and humans, allows selection of an effective dose in humans.
L22: The human dose of 40 mg/kg IV over 2 hours resulted in exposures that are similar or greater than those achieved in animals given 40 mg/kg in a single dose (the dose found to be efficacious in NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaque models of inhalational anthrax).
L23: Raxibacumab, when administered as a single intravenous dose of 40 mg/kg dose is found to be safe for the treatment of inhalational anthrax. This safety conclusion is based on the pooled safety analyses of 326 adult subjects treated with the recommended dose of raxibacumab of 40 mg/kg. The database included 303 subjects who received a single dose, 23 subjects who received a 2nd dose 2 weeks after their first dose, and 20 subjects who received a 2nd dose more than 4 months after their initial dose (study HGS1021-C1069). No serious, fatal or life-threatening events attributed to raxibacumab were observed in clinical studies. The most common adverse reaction reported in raxibacumab treated subjects were headache, upper respiratory infections and rash. In study HGS1021-C1064, 6/27 (22%) of volunteers without prior administration of diphenhydramine developed rash and urticaria after infusion of raxibacumab. As a result of this finding, patients are to receive diphenhydramine pretreatment before raxibacumab infusion.
L24: Nonclinical findings of exaggerated CNS pathology (bacteria, inflammation, and hemorrhage) in the raxibacumab-treated non-survivors as compared to placebo-treated non-survivors were observed in monotherapy animal studies in both species. However, when taken together with a survival benefit offered by raxibacumab, negative brain tissue cross-reactivity study results, absence of exposure/response for the CNS findings as well as greater pathologic changes in the organs other than CNS in placebo-treated animals, the CNS findings in raxibacumab-treated non-survivors do not appear to be a direct toxic effect of raxibacumab.
L25: ## 1.2 Risk Benefit Assessment
L26: Untreated inhalational anthrax is a highly fatal (&gt;95%) disease in humans. The reviewer finds that the potential survival benefit of raxibacumab treatment in human inhalational anthrax as evidenced by its reproducible findings of efficacy of 40 mg/kg single dose in three monotherapy studies in two representative animal models of inhalational anthrax in NZW rabbits (35-44% survival) and cynomolgus macaques (69% survival) when treatment was initiated postexposure at the time when all animals were toxicemic/febrile, as well as a trend of improved survival of 17% (not statistically significant, p=0.089) over antimicrobial alone when the treatment is delayed to 84 hours postexposure, outweighs the risk of any known or potential adverse reactions associated with raxibacumab treatment.
L27: Safety of raxibacumab 40 mg/kg single intravenous infusion was established in a database of 326 healthy human volunteers, allowing for exclusion with 95% confidence of serious adverse reactions related to raxibacumab that occur at frequency of 1% or greater.

L29: There are no recommendations for postmarketing risk evaluation and mitigation strategies.
L30: ## 1.4 Recommendations for Postmarketing Requirements and Commitments
L31: Approval under the Animal Rule is subject to a requirement for a postmarketing field study(s) to be conducted with due diligence, to verify and describe the drug's clinical benefit and to assess its safety when used as indicated when such study (ies) is feasible and ethical. The applicant was asked to design a protocol to collect and evaluate efficacy, pharmacokinetics, and safety of raxibacumab for the treatment inhalational anthrax. The protocol was included in the current BLA re-submission and was found adequate. The proposed field study should be ready for implementation in the event of an intentional release of *B. anthracis* in the US population. Coordination of the field study with the government agencies (BARDA, CDC) is recommended.
L32: ## 2 Introduction and Regulatory Background
L33: ## The “Animal Rule”
L34: Products for the treatment or prevention of human disease are generally studied in adequate and well-controlled clinical trials that enroll patients with the disease, and these clinical trials, along with other investigations, serve as the basis for approving or licensing the product. However, inhalational anthrax is extremely rare and human trials are not feasible. The efficacy studies in this BLA submission for raxibacumab for the treatment of inhalational anthrax will be assessed for approval under the “Animal Rule”. The “Animal Rule” is a regulatory mechanism to review efficacy studies in animal models for diseases that cannot be studied in humans. FDA published a Final Rule in 2002 entitled “*New Drug and Biological Drug Products; Evidence Needed to Demonstrate Effectiveness of New Drugs When Human Efficacy Studies Are Not Ethical or Feasible*,”2 that is also referred to as “*The Animal Rule*.” Under the Animal Rule, products intended to reduce or prevent serious or life-threatening conditions in humans may be approved by the FDA based on evidence of effectiveness derived from controlled studies in animal models of the disease with additional supporting safety and pharmacokinetic data. This rule is summarized in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR), in Title 21 CFR 314.600 (Subpart I) for New Drugs and in Title 21 CFR 601.90 for Biologic Products. Raxibacumab is a monoclonal antibody, a biologic product; and therefore, the provisions of 21 CFR 601.90 (Subpart H) apply.
L35: ## *Criteria for Submission*
L36: All animal studies subject to the Animal Rule regulations must be conducted in accordance with good laboratory practices. Products evaluated for effectiveness under Subpart I are expected to be evaluated for safety under preexisting requirements for establishing the safety of new drugs.
L37: 2 Final Rule published in the Federal Register, Vol. 67, No. 105, May 31, 2002, pages 37988-37998; Regulations: 21 CFR § 601.90-601.95 (Biologic Products)
L38: ## *Criteria for Approval of a Drug under the Animal Rule*
L39: The Animal Rule states that a drug can be approved on the basis of adequate and well-controlled animal studies when the results of those animal studies establish that the biological product is reasonably likely to produce clinical benefit in humans.
L40: To ensure applicability of animal data to human disease the following would need to be established:
L41: - **Pathophysiology of the disease and product's mechanism of action** are reasonably well understood;
- The product efficacy is demonstrated in more than one animal species, unless the model in a single animal species is sufficiently well characterized for predicting the response in humans;
- The animal study endpoint is clearly related to the desired benefit in humans; and
- Data on product pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics in animals and humans allow selection of an effective human dose.
L42: In assessing the sufficiency of animal data, the FDA may take into account other data, including human data in other indications. For example, product efficacy in diseases of similar pathophysiology might provide supportive information for the indication being sought. Therefore, data from appropriate studies to address each of the above bullet points would need to be provided to support the conclusion that the product is effective.
L43: In addition, approval under this regulation will be subject to three requirements:
L44: - **Postmarketing studies – The applicant must conduct postmarket studies, such as field studies, to verify and describe the drug's clinical benefit and to assess its safety when used as indicated when such studies are feasible and ethical (for example during or following a bioterrorism event).**
- **Approval with restrictions to ensure safe use – If FDA concludes that a drug product shown to be effective under this regulation can be safely used only if distribution or use is restricted, FDA will require such postmarket restrictions as are needed to ensure safe use of the drug product.**
- **Information to be provided to patients – For drug products or specific indications approved under this subpart, applicants must prepare, as part of their proposed labeling, an information sheet to be provided to patients that includes the following: a disclaimer that the drug's approval was based on solely animal efficacy studies, the indication, directions for use, foreseeable risks and benefits, and any other relevant information required by FDA at the time of approval.**
L45: FDA may withdraw approval if:
L46: - A postmarket clinical study fails to verify clinical benefit;
- The applicant fails to perform the postmarket study with due diligence;
- Use after marketing demonstrates that postmarket restrictions are inadequate to ensure safe use of the drug product;
L47: - The applicant fails to adhere to the postmarket restrictions applied at the time of approval under this subpart;
- The promotional materials are false or misleading; or
- Other evidence demonstrates that the product is not shown to be safe or effective under its conditions of use.
L48: ## 2.1 Product Information
L49: Inhalational anthrax is caused by the exotoxin-producing Gram-positive bacterium, *Bacillus anthracis*. In the absence of adequate treatment, this is a highly fatal disease. While *B. anthracis* replication can be affected by antibiotics, it is the secreted anthrax toxin that is primarily responsible for the symptoms, signs, and high mortality rates in infected individuals.
L50: Anthrax toxin is a protein complex consisting of lethal factor (LF), edema factor (EF) with protective antigen (PA) constituting the binding moiety. The PA moiety of anthrax toxin binds the anthrax toxin receptors (ATR or CMG2) on host cells to initiate a cascade of molecular events that manifests as clinical disease.
L51: Raxibacumab is a recombinant human immunoglobulin (IgG1λ) monoclonal antibody to *B. anthracis* protective antigen (PA). Raxibacumab blocks the binding of PA to cell surfaces and prevents the anthrax toxins from entering host cells and exerting their downstream toxic effects.
L52: ## 2.2 Tables of Currently Available Treatments for Proposed Indications
L53: Raxibacumab is a first-in-class agent, with no other approved antibody therapies available for the proposed indication of treatment of inhalational anthrax. However, antibiotics approved for the treatment of anthrax disease include penicillin G procaine and antimicrobials of the tetracycline class (doxycycline; tetracycline and minocycline are recommended in situations where penicillin is contraindicated).
L54: In addition, several antimicrobials were approved for the inhalational anthrax (post exposure) in the wake of the US anthrax bioterrorism event in 2001. The evidence for efficacy of these antimicrobials came from the studies in rhesus macaques. These approvals antedated the Animal Rule and were based on subpart H regulations (3).

L68: The original BLA for raxibacumab was submitted to the FDA on May 14, 2009. The application contained a number of proof-of-concept studies in various animal models, safety pharmacology and clinical pharmacology studies in animals and humans, safety studies in healthy human volunteers, and four GLP animal efficacy studies of raxibacumab for the treatment of inhalational anthrax in New Zealand white (NZW) rabbits and cynomolgus macaques in lieu of adequate and well controlled studies in humans.
L69: ## Efficacy Findings
L70: NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaques were selected for the efficacy studies of raxibacumab for treatment of inhalational anthrax. In the original BLA, four treatment studies with raxibacumab were submitted. The two efficacy studies tested raxibacumab versus placebo and two others evaluated the efficacy of raxibacumab plus antimicrobial (two studies each in rabbits and in monkeys). The animals were challenged with aerosolized *B. anthracis* spores at 200x LD50. In rabbit studies, sustained elevation of body temperature above baseline for 2 hours or a positive result on PA toxemia screen assay served as trigger for intervention (average 28 hours postexposure). In monkey studies, intervention commenced at the time of positive PA result (average 42 hours postexposure).
L71: The review revealed that in the population of all treated bacteremic animals raxibacumab at 40 mg/kg IV single dose was superior to placebo in the rabbit and monkey raxibacumab monotherapy studies. In the monkey study, raxibacumab 20 mg/kg was also superior to placebo, but in the rabbit superior efficacy was limited to the 40 mg/kg arm. In the population of all treated animals regardless of bacteremia status prior to treatment both doses of raxibacumab were superior to placebo in monkey and rabbit animal studies.

L76: When given in combination with antimicrobials, the efficacy of the combination was high and superior to placebo, but the efficacy of antimicrobials alone was also high, approaching 100% in both animal models, raising the question whether the animal models adequately represented advanced anthrax disease in humans, where high mortality (45%) was observed despite antimicrobial treatment.

L80: These animal studies were discussed in an AIDAC meeting in October of 2009. Based on the information from the natural history of inhalational anthrax disease in man, in rabbits, and monkeys; the mechanism of action of raxibacumab; and the efficacy of raxibacumab 40 mg/kg IV in the animal studies, FDA and the majority (16/24) of AIDAC committee members concluded that NZW rabbit and cynomolgus macaque models of inhalational anthrax disease are reflective of human disease and the efficacy findings from the therapeutic studies in these models could be extrapolated to humans.
L81: However, several limitations of the efficacy findings in pivotal and combination animal studies and in animal models themselves were discussed.
L82: First, the timing of intervention is likely to differ between animals and humans. In the experimental settings, animals were closely monitored for either an elevation in temperature (rabbits) or a positive plasma PA (rabbits and monkeys), and once detected, a therapeutic intervention was delivered. Humans may have delayed presentation to the healthcare setting or be given alternative diagnoses prior to the definitive diagnosis of anthrax being made. As the effects of delayed administration of raxibacumab after the onset of clinical symptoms has not been studied in the animal models, it is unclear how long raxibacumab administration can be delayed and still provide survival benefit.
L83: Second, the combination efficacy studies demonstrated very high efficacies (nearly 100%) of levofloxacin in NZW rabbits and ciprofloxacin in monkeys. In contrast, during the 2001 anthrax attacks 5 of the 11 people who developed inhalational anthrax died despite best available antimicrobial and supportive treatment. In addition, a question regarding efficacy interaction between raxibacumab and antimicrobial when given together for the treatment of inhalational anthrax remained unanswered. Twelve of twenty four AIDAC committee members pointed out a number of deficiencies in the combination study design that precluded definite conclusions
L84: regarding efficacy interactions, e.g. timing of intervention, antibiotic regimen, and the absence of a raxibacumab alone arm. A majority of the committee members (17/24) recommended additional evaluation of the contribution offered by raxibacumab to the efficacy of antimicrobial alone.
L85: Third, the conditions of an animal experiment do not include any supportive care that human patients with inhalational anthrax will receive in a healthcare or clinical trial setting, including but not limited to mechanical ventilation, fluid resuscitation, pleural fluid drainage, dialysis, etc.
L86: Fourth, due to concerns about the reliability of raxibacumab and antimicrobial PK data generated for the original BLA, FDA was unable to conclude that the proposed human dosing regimen would result in the exposures similar to those seen at the efficacious dose in animal studies. Because of these concerns, it was also unclear that the antimicrobial exposures in the combination animal studies did not exceed human exposures achieved with the approved human dose regimen.
L87: ## Safety Findings
L88: During the BLA review in 2009, an exaggerated inflammatory response in the CNS of the raxibacumab treated non-survivors compared to the placebo non-survivors was found on histopathological examination in the raxibacumab monotherapy animal studies. The duration of bacteremia prior to treatment / prior to death and time to death were similar between the placebo and raxibacumab non-survivors for both the monkey and the rabbit studies. However, within the raxibacumab groups, it appears the animals with CNS pathology lived longer than those without. Non-survivors in the raxibacumab 20 mg/kg dose group had a higher incidence and severity of CNS pathology as compared to the non-survivors the 40 mg/kg group, suggesting an absence of dose/exposure-response relationship for brain histopathology.

L93: These findings were presented at the AIDAC and their implications for humans were discussed. Additional studies to elucidate raxibacumab effect on CNS in survivors and non-survivors were recommended.
L94: ## Animal Studies
L95: The main limitation of the pivotal efficacy studies with respect to the evaluation of the CNS findings was a lack of pathological examination of the survivors to allow comparison to the animals that died. In the monotherapy efficacy studies, surviving rabbits were euthanized and disposed of, while surviving monkeys were observed for the duration of the study and confined to the Biosafety Level 3 (BL3) husbandry for 30 days post exposure, followed by a downgrade to a BL2 husbandry for an additional 60 days and then a release into the colony if in good health to be used in other experiments.
L96: Although survivors were sacrificed in the combination levofloxacin/raxibacumab rabbit study, the high efficacy of the fluoroquinolone in this study limited the number of animals that died from anthrax in the active treatment arms. Only one animal in an active treatment group (levofloxacin alone) died of anthrax. Although it was reassuring that none of the surviving animals in the two treatment arms exhibited CNS pathology attributable to anthrax, all treated animals received a fluoroquinolone in this study.
L97: Similar findings were noted in the combination ciprofloxacin and raxibacumab study in monkeys. No animals in the ciprofloxacin group died during 28 days following exposure. Only one animal in the ciprofloxacin/raxibacumab treatment group died of anthrax disease. None of the surviving animals were sacrificed for microscopic examination.
L98: ## Human volunteers
L99: No serious, fatal or life-threatening reactions attributed to raxibacumab were observed in clinical studies. The most common adverse reactions reported in raxibacumab-treated subjects were headache, upper respiratory infections and rash. In study HGS1021-C1064, 6/27 (22%) volunteers without prior administration of diphenhydramine developed rash and urticaria after infusion of raxibacumab. As a result of this finding, patients are to receive diphenhydramine pretreatment before raxibacumab infusion.
L100: In a safety database of 326 subjects only events that occur with frequency of 1% or greater could be excluded with 95% confidence. As the safety database consisted only of healthy volunteers, any possible study agent/disease interaction could not be assessed. While CNS AE were
L101: reviewed in healthy volunteers, it appears from the animal models that systemic anthrax disease must be present for CNS pathology to be observed. CNS safety review in humans was therefore limited.
L102: Absence of data in the pediatric age range was noted as a limitation of the raxibacumab safety evaluation.
L103: To address the deficiencies identified during review and AIDAC discussion of the original submission the sponsor conducted additional studies that are subject of the BLA resubmission dated June 15, 2012.
L104: ## 2.6 Other Relevant Background Information
L105: Following the anthrax attacks of 2001, the CDC4 recommended the use of two or three antimicrobials in combination in persons with inhalational anthrax based on susceptibility testing with epidemic strains. Limited early information suggested that patients treated intravenously with two or more antimicrobials active against *B. anthracis* had a greater chance of survival. It was also recommended to consider antimicrobial penetration into the central nervous system. CDC recommendations advocate use of ciprofloxacin over doxycycline, plus augmentation with chloramphenicol, rifampin, or penicillin when meningitis is established or suspected.4
L106: ## Raxibacumab for Strategic National Stockpile
L107: In October 2005, an End of Phase 1 meeting was held between the FDA and HGS to discuss the issues related to the licensure and use of raxibacumab under Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) for the post-exposure treatment of anthrax. During this meeting, the Agency indicated that unmet medical need exists for the treatment of anthrax rather than postexposure prophylaxis and expressed the need for studies in healthy volunteers and animal efficacy studies.
L108: In December 2007, agreement was reached on the data necessary to support the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) IND submission to use raxibacumab in the Strategic National Stockpile (SNS), and subsequent additional studies needed in the BLA submission to support licensure.
L109: In January 2009, DSPTP determined that a single dose of raxibacumab 40 mg/kg IV was **acceptable for use under HGS' and the CDC's IND** for the treatment of inhalational anthrax. This decision was based on the review of various preclinical studies (including pivotal efficacy studies in animals as required under the Animal Rule), human safety and PK studies, acceptable product quality assessments, and the Division of Scientific Investigation (DSI) and **Biotechnology Manufacturing Team's inspections**.

L111: ## 3 Ethics and Good Clinical Practices
L112: ## 3.1 Submission Quality and Integrity
L113: The Division of Scientific Investigations (DSI) inspected Human Genome Sciences, as well as two clinical sites that enrolled the majority of subjects in safety studies HGS1021-C1063 and HGS1021-C1064. The studies appeared to have been conducted adequately, and therefore, the data generated were deemed acceptable to support the proposed indication. Please refer to the DSI consults in DARRTS for complete details.
L114: In September 2009, Division of Scientific Investigations (DSI) inspections for the analytical portions of human studies HGS1021-C1063 and HGS1021-C1064 were conducted. During these inspections, multiple issues with the analysis of raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin concentrations were identified. Inspection findings raised concerns regarding the reliability of the pharmacokinetic data submitted in the application and utilized for selection of an effective dose in humans for therapeutic treatment of anthrax. On 14 November 2009, the FDA issued a Complete Response letter to the applicant requesting revisions of the analytical procedures for raxibacumab to address the DSI inspection findings, re-analysis of the PK samples from human studies HGS1021-C1063, HGS 1021-C1064, and HGS1021-C1069, and re-calculation of the PK parameters for raxibacumab from these re-analyses. Upon revalidation of the assay for analysis of serum raxibacumab samples, the analytical sites underwent re-inspection by DSI focusing on the methods and data supporting Clinical Study HGS1021-C1064. Following inspection, the modified raxibacumab assay as used for the reanalysis of Study HGS1021-C1064 was deemed acceptable by DSI inspectors.
L115: On April 23, 2010, the applicant submitted information supporting the revalidated assay for concentrations of raxibacumab in human serum along with PK comparison reports for the original raxibacumab assay (CLI-2879) and the results obtained with the modified assay (CLI-3192) and relevant bioanalytical validation and quantitation reports. Upon review of the submissions of data obtained by both the original and modified bioanalytical methods, the pharmacokinetic data for raxibacumab were considered reliable and sufficient for extrapolation of animal efficacy findings to humans for determination of the efficacious dose in humans for therapeutic treatment of anthrax. Therefore, pharmacokinetic data for raxibacumab obtained by the original bioanalytical method could be used for labeling.
L116: ## 3.2 Compliance with Good Clinical Practices
L117: All animal monotherapy and the raxibacumab/antibiotic combination efficacy studies were conducted in accordance with GLP and the Animal Welfare Act. Human clinical trials for safety data were performed in compliance with GCP and ICH guidelines.

L127: ## 4.3.1 Natural History Studies in NZW rabbits and Cynomolgus Macaque Models of Inhalational Anthrax
L128: In order to be able to develop a therapeutic product for the treatment of inhalational anthrax, it was important to identify and characterize animal models of inhalational anthrax to be used to **evaluate the product's efficacy**. Specifically, as provided in the Animal Rule, it was important to study the natural history of the anthrax infection in the animals, with the goal to understand the pathophysiological mechanism of the toxicity of the substance (*B. anthracis*) and prevention or substantial reduction of disease and/or mortality by the product. After consideration of rodent and larger animal species, the natural history of inhalational anthrax in NZW rabbit and cynomolgus macaque was evaluated with a goal to establish models in each of these species to
L129: be used for the efficacy evaluation of therapeutic products in randomized comparative treatment studies of inhalational anthrax.
L130: NZW rabbit and cynomolgus macaque models of inhalational anthrax have been evaluated in two natural history studies conducted by the Battelle Biomedical Research Center (BBRC) laboratories. These two animal models are proposed to be used for evaluating efficacy of products for treatment of inhalational anthrax under the Animal Rule.
L131: The design was fairly similar between the studies. Animals were exposed to 200\times\text{LD}_{50} of *B. anthracis* spores via head only aerosol. Animals were monitored for clinical signs of the disease, and subjected to laboratory investigations that included hematology and serum chemistry evaluations and daily blood cultures. Following natural death for the disease or euthanasia due to morbundity animals underwent necropsy examination. As for both studies non naïve animals were used, survival up to 25% was observed. Experimental conditions were refined subsequently and only naïve animals were procured for the therapeutic experiments resulting in uniform mortality in the exposed untreated animals in both models.
L132: The table below summarizes the data from the natural history of inhalational anthrax in NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaques in the experiments conducted by BBRC and those published in the literature and compares the findings with historical data on inhalational anthrax in humans.

L138: ## 4.3.3 Nonclinical Study 1103-CG923704 Evaluation of Raxibacumab as Therapeutic Treatment Against Inhalation Anthrax in the New Zealand White Rabbit Model
L139: **INVESTIGATOR:** Daniel Sanford, PhD,
L140: **STUDY CENTER:** Battelle Biomedical Research Center (BBRC)
L141: **STUDY PERIOD:** 7 July 2010 to 19 December 2011
L142: ## **OBJECTIVES:**
L143: ## **Primary:**
L144: - To assess terminal pathology in both non-surviving and surviving rabbits after anthrax exposure and therapeutic treatment with placebo or raxibacumab.
L145: ## **Secondary:**
L146: - To evaluate the efficacy of raxibacumab when administered as a therapeutic treatment against lethality due to inhalation exposure to *B. anthracis* in NZW rabbits
L147: **METHODOLOGY:** Parallel-group, randomized, blinded, single center, GLP-compliant study to evaluate the histopathology in surviving and non-surviving animals after anthrax exposure and therapeutic treatment with placebo or raxibacumab.
L148: **NUMBER OF ANIMALS:** Forty-eight out of 54 screened and quarantined New Zealand White rabbits free of disease and malformations were randomized by gender and body weight into 2 treatment groups (24 animals, ~ 50% male and 50% female each): raxibacumab or placebo. The rest of the animals served as replacements.
L149: **STUDY DRUG:** IV raxibacumab given as a single bolus infusion at 40 mg/kg dose.
L150: Raxibacumab, also known as HGS1021, PA mAb, or ABthrax, is a recombinant, fully human IgG1\lambda mAb that binds *B. anthracis* PA with high affinity and inhibits its biological activity. Raxibacumab is expressed in the NS0 mouse myeloma cell line and secreted into culture media, from which it is purified by a series of chromatography and filtration steps.

L154: **DURATION OF TREATMENT:** Blinded raxibacumab treatment as a single IV bolus dose of 40 mg/kg or matching placebo were given to NZW rabbits at the time of positive plasma PA.
L155: **TREATMENT COMPLIANCE:** Study drug infusion information, including dosage and volume prescribed, and volume administered, was recorded.
L156: **STUDY DESIGN:** Parallel-group, randomized, blinded, single center, GLP-compliant study to evaluate the histopathology in surviving and non-surviving animals after anthrax exposure and therapeutic treatment with placebo or raxibacumab
L157: **Background:** To date the Sponsor has evaluated raxibacumab in several animal species and under various conditions. Efficacy of raxibacumab was evaluated in a proof-of concept rat model of Lethal Toxin infusion in pre-exposure and post-exposure setting. In addition, when used for
L158: pre-exposure prophylaxis raxibacumab showed dose-dependent survival benefit in rabbits and monkeys. Time-related effect on survival was also observed in a post-exposure prophylaxis setting in a rabbit model. Monotherapy studies of raxibacumab administered to rabbits and cynomolgus macaques at the time of diagnosis of inhalational anthrax disease showed a statistically significant survival benefit relative to placebo treatment. The complete response letter for the original BLA identified that the non-survivors that received raxibacumab had a greater rate and severity of central nervous system (CNS) disease than did placebo non-survivors. The reasons for this greater rate and severity of CNS disease as well as the potential relevance to humans were unclear.

L163: ## **Inclusion criteria:**
L164: - Disease and malformation free New Zealand White (NZW) rabbits 50% male and 50% female weighing 2.7-4.3 kg supplied by (b) (4)
- Implanted vascular access ports and telemetry (temperature) transponder
- Quarantine period of 7 days
L165: ## **Exclusion criteria:**
L166: - Malformations
L167: - Clinical signs and symptoms of disease
- Outside approved weight range
- Veterinarian discretion
L168: ## Treatments and Study Groups:
L169: **Table 9: Animal Allocation**
L170: Number of Rabbits Planned	Dose	Route/Frequency	Treatment Point
Group 1 (placebo)	24	Placebo1	IV/single dose	Individual treatment times based on serum PA levels2

L171: 1 Raxibacumab buffer, administered at a dose equivalent in mL/kg volume to Group 2.
L172: 2 Each individual rabbit was to receive raxibacumab or placebo immediately upon its 1st positive PA result via qualitative ECL assay. If an animal was not treated by the 48 hour post-challenge time point (negative for PA by ECL), the animal was to be treated after the results of the 48 hour ECL assay were known regardless of the result
L173: **Study procedures:** The study was conducted under GLP.
L174: - Animals were housed in the individual cages.
- Study animals were randomized by treatment group and gender prior to challenge
- Study animals were randomized to one of two aerosol challenge days and a challenge order
- Aerosol challenge at targeted 200 x LD50 of *B. anthracis* Ames strain spores
- Temperature monitoring was done twice daily for 3 days prior to challenge until 28 days post challenge with the exception of every 6 hours between 18-168 hours post challenge
- Single dose IV study treatments were to be administered immediately upon positive PA result
- Clinical observations were done every 6 hours from 18 hours until 168 hours postexposure and twice daily thereafter
- Animals were euthanized if found moribund on the study or survived until the end of the study on Day 28 postexposure
- Necropsy and histopathology were conducted on all euthanized and all found dead animals in a blinded fashion
- Brains and spleens of all animals were subjected to immunohistochemistry for raxibacumab, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) to detect healed damage in survivors and for endogenous rabbit IgG
- Four brain sections that included cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus/thalamus, basal ganglia and corpus callosum were also subjected to Bielschowsky and Fluoro-Jade C stains to detect neuronal and neurofibrillary degeneration

L179: ## Raxibacumab PK and PA concentrations and TNA
L180: The PK analyses of raxibacumab concentration-time profiles for all raxibacumab-dosed rabbits were conducted using population analysis techniques (mixed effect modeling), with the NONMEM software. Plasma raxibacumab concentration-time data, serum PA concentration-time data, individual raxibacumab PK parameters, and individual PA kinetic parameters were summarized using descriptive statistics. The TNA titers in plasma samples from surviving rabbits were determined using a cell killing assay.
L181: ## Immunogenicity
L182: Plasma samples were assessed for anti-raxibacumab activity using a 2-part ECL-based bridging assay.
L183: ## MIC
L184: Minimal inhibitory concentrations (MICs) of levofloxacin were performed on *B. anthracis* challenge material and on positive cultures from terminal blood samples.
L185: ## CSF
L186: Cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) was collected from all rabbits prior to euthanasia (including survivors euthanized on study day 28) or on animals found dead, whenever possible. CSF was collected for culture, PA and raxibacumab concentration assessments.
L187: ## Endpoints:
L188: **Primary efficacy endpoint** was survival in the ITT study population on Day 28
L189: ## Analysis Populations:
L190: - ITT population is defined as all randomized rabbits that received the study agent
L191: *MO comment: additional sensitivity analyses will be performed by the FDA in bacteremic population (animals that were bacteremic at the treatment onset).*
L192: ## Statistical Plan:
L193: The primary efficacy endpoint was 28-day survival, defined as the proportion of animals that survive to Day 28 after challenge. Based on previous experience (natural history of inhalational anthrax in NZW rabbits and results from the placebo arms in the previous efficacy studies), the sample size of 48 animals allows evaluation of a sufficient number of survivors (approximately 10 survivors). This design also provides 88% power to detect a survival benefit of 42% (10/24) in the raxibacumab-treated group compared to a 4% (1/24) survival rate in the placebo group. Histopathology data will be summarized using descriptive statistics.
L194: The primary analysis of efficacy is to compare the percent of animals alive at study Day 28 post challenge between the placebo control group and the raxibacumab treatment group. The comparison will be performed using a 2-sided likelihood ratio test (or the Fisher's exact test, if any expected cell count in the contingency table is &lt; 5). The secondary efficacy endpoint is animal's survival time from the initiation of spore challenge. Survival time will be compared between the placebo group and the raxibacumab treatment group using a log-rank test. Mortality will be recorded as it occurs to the nearest observation interval.
L195: ## PROTOCOL CHANGES:
L196: The original protocol was submitted and reviewed by the Division on October 10, 2010. Subsequently, the protocol was amended 4 times:
L197: ## Amendment 1 (01 July 2010)
L198: - Prioritizing testing of CSF samples in the following order: culture, PA and raxibacumab concentrations
L199: - Increasing frequency of clinical observations from 12 to every 6 hours between 18-168 hours post challenge
- Clarifications regarding brain tissue collection and staining
L200: ## **Amendment 2 (08 September 2010)**
L201: - Provision was added to euthanize the replacement animals to serve as negative controls for histological evaluation
L202: ## **Amendment 3 (17 January 2011)**
L203: - Unblinding of the treatment assignments will occur at the time of the completion of the in-life portion of the study to the study director, but not to the pathologist to allow analyses of raxibacumab PK and immunogenicity as well as efficacy to proceed while ensuring that the pathology evaluation will proceed in a blinded fashion.
L204: ## **Amendment 4 (27 July 2011)**
L205: - Clarifications were made to the location of the lab for immunohistochemistry, GFAP, raxibacumab and rabbit IgG at BBRC

L208: (b) (4)
L209: Study centers: 1 study center
L210: A total of 54 animals were available for the study. Forty eight were initially selected and randomized, 2 of them were replaced due to health conditions unacceptable for the study. Forty eight animals received spore challenge. All rabbits received the treatment to which they were assigned.
L211: The following flowchart and the tables summarize the composition of the populations for analysis, the primary reasons for exclusion and the demographics of the study population.
L212: **Figure 1: Animal's Disposition**
L213: Two rabbits L35567 and L35572 were randomized, but not challenged, and were replaced by rabbits L35557 and L35569, respectively. Animal L35541 on raxibacumab arm, a survivor, did not have a positive bacteremia result prior to treatment or for the duration of the study. The animal, however, had developed a febrile response. It also had a positive PA screen assay result at 30 hours post challenge, although quantitative PA assay was negative for the duration of the study. In addition, there were no findings on gross necropsy of this animal suggestive of anthrax, while microscopic examination showed minimal inflammatory changes in the lymph nodes and spleen. This animal did not develop a TNA titer at the end of the study.
L214: **MO comment:** It appears that animal L35541 did not develop anthrax disease and did not respond to infection immunologically. The reviewer will conduct efficacy analyses with and without the inclusion on this animal.

L226: ## Clinical Observations
L227: Abnormal clinical signs were first documented in the majority of animals at approximately 48-72 hours post-challenge. The most common abnormal clinical signs reported post-challenge were lethargy, loss of appetite, stool and respiratory abnormalities.
L228: Twenty three of 24 (96%) placebo-treated animals and 8/13 (61.5%) raxibacumab-treated animals were found dead. A single placebo-treated animal L35556 was euthanized due to severe facial and neck swelling with impaired breathing. This animal was toxicemic and bacteremic at the time of death. One raxibacumab treated animal L35562 had impaired hind limb use on Day 2 that became severe enough to warrant euthanasia on Day 3 per the staff veterinarian. This animal in addition to hind limb impairment exhibited loss of appetite, lethargy and respiratory abnormalities at 30-48 hours post exposure. The spore challenge dose of 93 \times \text{LD}_{50} was achieved in this animal; PA screening assay and blood culture became positive at 21 hours, while the treatment was initiated at 25 hours postexposure. At the time of treatment PA level was recorded at 33.3 ng/ml; it continued to rise to a maximum of 922 ng/ml at 10 hours post treatment then declined to 362 ng/ml at the time of euthanasia.
L229: Three additional raxibacumab-treated animals: L35554, L35548 and L35561 were euthanized after ataxia or seizures were noted on Days 4-5 post challenge. They have received spore challenge doses 111-233 \times \text{LD}_{50}. Neurologic symptoms were preceded by lethargy, inappetence, and respiratory abnormalities for 48-72 hours. These animals were toxicemic and bacteremic prior to treatment. PA toxemia in these animals reached peak levels around 10 hours post treatment and declined steadily until prior to death. Animals were persistently bacteremic until prior to death.
L230: **MO comment:** Neurological signs were observed in these animals on Day 4-5 postexposure and approximately 3 days post treatment with raxibacumab. Histopathological examination revealed extensive hemorrhagic, inflammatory, and necrotic changes in the various parts of the brain. CSF PA and raxibacumab concentrations were not determined in these animals as no CSF was collected.
L231: Animal L35568 was euthanized 11 days post-challenge because of inappetence, no stool, and lethargy. This animal was treated with raxibacumab at 28 hours post-challenge after receiving 179 \text{LD}_{50}, had a positive PA assay at 22 hours and was found to be bacteremic at 26.5 hours. It was lethargic and inappetent with increased lacrimation from 36 to 72 hours post challenge. For the next 42 hours his symptoms seemed to have subsided. However, at 114 hours lethargy, lacrimation, and inappetence returned; respiratory abnormalities became evident, and animal met criteria for euthanasia on Day 11 postchallenge. Gross necropsy was negative, and, in contrast to all other animals that died on study, in this animal microscopic findings were not consistent with anthrax infection: minimal hemorrhages in brain and minimal heterophilic inflammation in the mediastinal lymph nodes, but moderate chronic active nephritis, suggestive of other potential pathogens, e.g., *Encephalitozoon cuniculi* (as discussed in the report by the pathologist). Brain cultures and CSF PA assay in this animal were also negative. L35568 had the lowest CSF raxibacumab concentration, negative raxibacumab IHC staining results, and the longest time to
L232: death (263.7 hours) compared with other raxibacumab-treated rabbits that succumbed to anthrax. Upon review of all data collected for this animal, the study pathologist considers it more likely that this rabbit did not die of anthrax.
L233: *MO comment: The reviewer will perform efficacy analyses with and without inclusion of animal L35568.*
L234: Two raxibacumab-treated animals L35581 and L35566 were documented to have bilateral facial edema at a single time point during the study; both survived.
L235: In raxibacumab-treated animals that survived to Day 28, most animals returned to normal by Day 7 with the exception of a few animals that demonstrated some hind limb issues classified as minor. Three animals L35530, L35531 and L35550 were noted to favor a limb following resolution of acute symptoms postexposure (Day 11, 12, and 17 respectively). Abnormal limb use was sporadic and resolved within a few days of onset. For 2 of the animals (L35530 and L35531) these limb issues resolved by Day 13 post challenge while abnormal limb observations for animal L35550 resolved on Day 18 post-challenge. L35550 was examined by veterinarian and noted to have a limb injury.
L236: *MO comment: Pathology reports for the above animals did not detect any gross or microscopic abnormalities in the tissues examined, including brain.*
L237: ## Temperature monitoring
L238: All challenged animals demonstrated increases in body temperature on Days 2 through 5 following exposure to *B. anthracis*. In the majority of animals increased temperature lagged the appearance of PA or bacteremia. Two of 24 raxibacumab treated animals had febrile response prior to treatment initiation. On placebo arm, 3/24 animals had fever at the time of blinded intervention. In total, 34/48 animals developed febrile responses to infection at some point post-challenge: 18/24 on raxibacumab arm and 16/24 on the placebo.
L239: *MO comment: Only 34/48 (71%) animals on the study developed febrile responses to infection and only 5/48 (10%) were febrile prior to treatment, in contrast to the previous rabbit monotherapy study 682, where all animals were febrile at some point post challenge with 65% of them febrile prior to treatment. In addition, average time to fever is almost 24 hours longer in this study compared to study 682.*

L257: ## Toxemia Results
L258: All animals had blood samples collected for PA toxemia at a predetermined schedule throughout the study. Treatment was administered after an animal became positive by qualitative screening ECL PA assay. In addition, the same blood sample was analyzed by a quantitative PA assay. All animals were positive for PA on ECL screening assay. Animal L35560 (raxibacumab arm) was treated based on positive screening assay even though suitability criteria for the assay plate were not met. The study director made a decision to treat the animal as there was a several fold increase in signal as compared to the previous time point. Also, quantitative PA in the same blood sample was positive in this animal.
L259: Overall results between the screen and quantitative PA assays were concordant except for one animal L35541 where PA screening assay was positive while the quantitative PA assay was negative. This animal was never bacteremic, did not develop TNA titers and had normal findings on necropsy.

The duration of the plateau phase in treated non-survivors was longer as compared to placebo controls. The slope of toxemia decrease was much steeper in survivors compared to treated non-survivors.

L288: ## Other Parameters Measured:
L289: ## *MIC*
L290: The *B. anthracis* MIC for levofloxacin was 1 \mug/mL prior to challenge. The terminal MICs ranged from 0.5 to 1.0 \mug/mL for raxibacumab animals and 0.5-2.0 \mug/mL for placebo animals, demonstrating that the original MICs to this antibiotic did not change with raxibacumab treatment.
L291: ## *CSF Culture, PA and Raxibacumab*
L292: CSF was successfully collected from 65% (24/37) of the rabbits that died on study and all (11/11) of the rabbits that survived to day 28 post-challenge.
L293: One hundred percent (19/19) of the placebo-treated animals for which a CSF sample could be collected had positive CSF bacterial culture result. For raxibacumab-treated non-survivors for which a CSF sample could be collected, 80% (4/5) had a positive bacterial culture result whereas none (0/11) of the raxibacumab-treated survivors had a positive bacterial culture result from CSF obtained prior to sacrifice (Day 28). Animal L35568 was the sole raxibacumab treated non-survivor that had negative CSF culture result.
L294: Concentrations of PA in CSF were variable in animals of both treatment groups, ranging from not detectable to &gt; 966 ng/mL. These CSF PA concentrations were 0 -37% of plasma PA concentrations in raxibacumab-treated non-survivors in whom CSF to plasma concentration ratios were calculated. Rabbit L35562 on raxibacumab arm had a CSF PA concentration nearly 7-fold higher than the concurrent plasma PA concentration.

L297: *MO comment.* Raxibacumab treated non-survivors had higher on average levels of CSF PA as compared to placebo non-survivors, indicating more pronounced CNS infection at the time of death.
L298: No animals in the placebo group had measurable raxibacumab in the collected CSF samples. In 4/13 non-survivors from the raxibacumab group, CSF raxibacumab concentrations were measured (due to inability to collect sample from all animals), and ranged from &lt; 1 \mu\text{g/mL} to 545 \mu\text{g/mL} representing 0.2% - 88% of the concurrent plasma raxibacumab concentration. When the highest CSF raxibacumab concentration (545 \mu\text{g/mL} for rabbit L35559) is excluded, less than 2% of plasma circulating raxibacumab reached CSF. For comparison, CSF raxibacumab concentrations for 11 rabbits that survived ranged from not detectable to 0.331 \mu\text{g/mL}. For the only surviving rabbit for whom the CSF to plasma raxibacumab concentration ratio could be determined, the CSF level was &lt;2\% of the concurrent plasma raxibacumab concentration. Overall there was little distribution of raxibacumab into CSF, with the exception of 1 rabbit that died (L35559).
L299: *MO comment.* Interesting to note that animal L35559 with the highest raxibacumab concentration in the CSF did not have any gross or microscopic findings in the CNS despite positive brain immunohistochemistry staining for raxibacumab. It appeared to have died from severe necrotizing mediastinitis.
L300: Three raxibacumab treated survivors L35581, L35566, and L35532 had terminal CSF samples positive for raxibacumab. Two of them (L35566 and L35532) have cleared raxibacumab from plasma prior to study Day 28.
L301: L35581 a survivor with CSF positive for raxibacumab had the following clinical course: after a challenge dose of 197 \times \text{LD}_{50}, this animal was found to be toxicemic and bacteremic at 23 hours post challenge, received treatment at 28 hours post challenge; febrile response in this animal was registered at 47 hours post challenge and lasted 36 hours with no other notable clinical observations; the animal had an uneventful recovery. Gross necropsy was unremarkable; however, on microscopic examination this animal had lymphoid hyperplasia in the spleen and minimal neuronal necrosis in hippocampus identified only based on positivity of Fluoro-Jade staining for acute neuronal degeneration. Positive IHC staining for raxibacumab was only intravascular. This animal was bacteremic until Day 4 post challenge. Detectable PA toxemia was last detected on Day 7 post challenge.
L302: Animal L35566 was found to have minimal hemorrhage of meninges and brain tissue as well as minimal-mild lymphoid hyperplasia of lymph nodes and spleen present on microscopic
L303: examination. This animal was challenged with 151 \times \text{LD}_{50} and developed detectable PA toxemia and bacteremia at 18 and 22 hours post challenge, respectively. This animal was treated at 22 hours and resolved toxemia and bacteremia by Day 7 post challenge.
L304: On histopathologic examination of animal L35532 notable findings related to anthrax included minimal inflammatory changes in spleen and lymph nodes. Brain examination revealed normal findings. Incidental embryonal nephroma was found on kidney examination. This animal was challenged with 130 \times \text{LD}_{50} and developed detectable PA toxemia and bacteremia at 33 and 36 hours post challenge, respectively. This animal was treated at 36 hours and resolved toxemia and bacteremia by Day 7 post challenge.
L305: **MO comment:** Raxibacumab penetration into CSF in three animals above was likely related to increase blood-brain barrier permeability during systemic infection. Animals L35532 and L35566 did not have positive raxibacumab serum concentration at the time of terminal CSF sampling and therefore false positive results due to blood contamination is not possible. Findings of resolving inflammation and hemorrhage in the brain of surviving animals treated with raxibacumab are reassuring as they suggest resolution of meningitis. Direct toxicity of raxibacumab is unlikely, particularly in the absence of positive immunohistochemistry brain staining for raxibacumab in the animals that had detectable levels of raxibacumab in the CSF. It is important to note that in the majority of raxibacumab non-survivors brain immunohistochemistry for raxibacumab was positive, but only 3 animals has concurrent positive CSF samples. There were no raxibacumab-treated non-survivors that had positive CSF raxibacumab in the absence of positive brain immunohistochemistry. This finding indicates that raxibacumab penetration into CSF likely follows meningeal seeding with bacteria. In raxibacumab-treated animals that succumbed to anthrax, low levels of raxibacumab in the CSF were not sufficient to clear the infection, while high levels noted in one non-survivor likely precluded development of significant pathology in the brain.

Thereafter, raxibacumab concentrations were very low or not detected in the rabbits that were positive for anti-raxibacumab antibodies compared with the sustained raxibacumab exposure in rabbits that were anti-raxibacumab antibody negative.

L317: ***MO comment:*** Surviving animals were able to mount an immune response to anthrax in the presence of raxibacumab.
L318: All animals that survived were monitored for 28 days post-challenge. Clinical signs and symptoms of anthrax, including body temperature elevations, resolved following resolution of bacteremia. Animals exhibited normal baseline behavior at the time of study termination. Animals found moribund were euthanized. Complete necropsies were performed on all animals, including those that died and those surviving to terminal sacrifice on Day 28 postexposure.
L319: ## **Pathology, Gross and Microscopic**
L320: Complete necropsies were performed on animals found dead or euthanized, including the animals surviving to terminal sacrifice on Day 28. Gross lesions in the rabbits found dead or sacrificed moribund included discoloration or foci in the appendix and brain, enlargement (with or without discoloration) of bronchial and mediastinal lymph nodes, and fluid in the body cavities and thymus. These gross lesions were considered typical of anthrax in rabbits and correlated histologically with hemorrhage, necrosis, edema, and/or acute inflammation. Lesions of the nervous system were more commonly observed in raxibacumab-treated animals than in placebo-treated animals. Brain inflammation was more common in raxibacumab-treated animals, and localized to the cerebral cortex, hippocampus, ventricular system, cerebellum, and meninges. Neuronal necrosis was also more common in raxibacumab-treated animals, and was more pronounced the cerebral cortex and cerebellum. Cerebral vasculitis was more common in raxibacumab-treated animals. Although hemorrhage was present in the brain of approximately the same number of rabbits in each group, hemorrhage was especially notable in the hippocampus, cerebellum, cerebral cortex and meninges of raxibacumab-treated animals.
L321: In the placebo treatment group lesions in all organs, except the brain, were more commonly observed and generally with greater severity than they were in raxibacumab-treated non-survivors.
L322: Among raxibacumab-treated rabbits surviving to study termination on Study Day 28, several lesions expected in animals recovering from sepsis were identified and included inflammation, increased macrophage numbers, and lymphoid hyperplasia in lymph nodes and spleen, and chronic or chronic-active inflammation in the lungs. Acute hemorrhage in the brain (as an agonal/perimortem change in the absence of other brain lesions), acute renal inflammation and tubulo-interstitial nephritis, hemorrhage and edema in lymph nodes, and splenic hemosiderosis were considered to be incidental findings. All of the microscopic findings in the raxibacumab-treated survivors were graded as minimal to mild, except 1 instance each of hemosiderosis and of hyperplasia in the spleen which were graded as moderate.
L323: **MO comment:** Histopathologic findings of increased inflammatory changes along with elevated bacterial load in the brains of raxibacumab-treated non-survivors relative to non-survivors in the placebo groups were consistent with the findings on microscopic examination from the original monotherapy studies in rabbits and cynomolgus macaques. Taken together with the raxibacumab penetration data and the immunohistochemistry staining patterns for raxibacumab and endogenous rabbit IgG, these findings are most likely indicative of increased permeability of the blood brain barrier in the raxibacumab-treated animals and insufficient levels of the product to eliminate the infection. Exaggerated inflammatory response in these animals relative to placebo remains unexplained with a potential hypothetical mechanism of partial inhibition of lethal toxin immunosuppressive effects within the confined space of the CNS.
L324: However, it is also reassuring that survivors were devoid of significant brain pathology. In addition, it is reassuring to know that raxibacumab penetration into CSF in some survivors, most likely the result of blood brain barrier leak, was not detrimental and resulted in CSF and brain tissue clear of *B. anthracis*.

L345: **MO comment:** There is a significant overlap of time-to-death ranges between raxibacumab-treated and placebo-treated non-survivors. Time to death is also similar between animals with high grade brain lesions and those without. However, within the raxibacumab group of non-survivors, animals with high grade brain lesions had longer mean and median time to death. Although plausible, it does not appear that just the duration of survival alone could account for greater pathologic findings in the brain of animals treated with raxibacumab versus placebo.
L346: ## *Raxibacumab and IgG Immunohistochemistry (IHC), Brain*
L347: Brains sections of survivors and non-survivors as well as of 3 unchallenged negative controls were evaluated for the presence of raxibacumab by IHC staining. These sections were also evaluated for the presence of endogenous rabbit immunoglobulin to aid in interpretation of results of the raxibacumab IHC.
L348: Among unchallenged rabbits, plasma was moderately to strongly positive for endogenous IgG, neuropil ranged from unstained to mild in patches, and choroidal collagen was moderately positive. Cytoplasmic staining was present among occasional members of all cell types observed in the brain (astrocytes, choroid plexus epithelium, endothelial cells, ependymal cells, meninges, neurons, oligodendroglia, and intravascular heterophils) except for microglial cells. Staining was usually greatest in endothelial cells.
L349: Spore-challenged rabbits with inflammation in the brain exhibited greater frequency and intensity of IgG staining than spore-challenged rabbits with no hemorrhage, inflammation, or necrosis in the brain. There was a good concordance of positive IgG staining and presence of inflammation and/or necrosis in brain lesions detected on H&amp;E staining (9/10 animals).
L350: Among non-survivors that had no diagnoses of hemorrhage, inflammation, or necrosis, raxibacumab-treated animals appeared to exhibit slightly more IgG staining in the choroid plexus, endothelium, and neuropil, suggesting greater permeability of the blood-brain barrier than in placebo-treated rabbits. However, staining was greater for placebo-treated animals in meninges and oligodendroglia.
L351: IHC for raxibacumab was positive only in rabbits treated with raxibacumab. The staining pattern was identical to that for endogenous IgG in that plasma was moderately to strongly positive among non-survivors, choroid collagen was frequently more positive than was epithelium, and neuropil exhibited a range of staining from negative (among survivors) to strongly positive in rabbits with abundant lesions. Similarly, cytoplasm was positive occasionally in all cell types. As for endogenous IgG, rabbits with the most severe and widespread brain lesions also had the most intense and widespread staining for raxibacumab in neurons and neuropil and staining was often associated with presence of bacteria and/or inflammation. Among raxibacumab-treated rabbits surviving to Day 28, 3 (L35581, L35530, and L35531) had positive raxibacumab staining of plasma, although in 2 of these (L35530 and L35531) the staining was weak, suggesting the gradual loss of raxibacumab in circulation over time, as is confirmed by the raxibacumab PK results.
L352: Strong correlation between microscopic brain lesions and frequency, location, and intensity of raxibacumab and endogenous rabbit IgG staining of the brain was observed in non-surviving raxibacumab treated animals. An overlapping pattern of endogenous IgG and raxibacumab staining of neurons and neuropil was often observed in regions rich with bacteria, inflammation, and/or necrosis.
L353: **MO comment:** Infection, circulating bacterial toxins, and/or inflammation (including sepsis) has been shown to enhance blood brain barrier (BBB) permeability. The pattern of ICH brain staining revealed a co-localization of raxibacumab and endogenous IgG, suggesting a non-specific leak of plasma across the damaged blood brain barrier during bacterial meningitis in the raxibacumab group. Only one placebo animal (#L35576) with severe meningitis also had positive IgG brain staining, suggesting compromise of the blood brain barrier sufficient for IgG
L354: *and raxibacumab penetration did not generally occur in the placebo group. Surviving animals also may have experienced an alteration in blood brain barrier permeability early in the disease, as greater endogenous IgG positive staining of vascular endothelium, meninges, and neuropil was observed in raxibacumab treated survivors compared to unchallenged controls. However, there was no raxibacumab staining of brain tissue in the surviving animals.*
L355: ## *Other stains*
L356: **Bielschowsky's stain** was used to detect neuritic plaques, i.e, regions where chronic damage to axons or dendrites resulted in aberrant neurite outgrowth. No staining was detected in any study samples, as anthrax-related CNS lesions are typically acute.
L357: Fluoro-Jade C often confirmed acute neuronal degeneration/necrosis in the same regions where acute neuronal necrosis was noted on H&amp;E-stained sections. In a single case of a raxibacumab-treated survivor (L35581), a diagnosis of neuronal degeneration/necrosis was made only on the basis of Fluoro-Jade C without coincident H&amp;E staining.

L372: ## **Efficacy conclusions:**
L373: - Raxibacumab at 40 mg/kg IV bolus dose was superior to placebo in preventing inhalational anthrax induced mortality in ITT population resulting in survival of 45.8% of treated animals as compared to placebo 0% (p=0.0001).
- In the sensitivity analyses of efficacy in the populations of animals bacteremic prior to treatment or toxemic prior to treatment, raxibacumab was superior to placebo in preventing inhalational anthrax induced mortality with survival of 43.5% versus 0% on placebo arm, p=0.0006 (bacteremic animals) and p=0.0002 (toxemic animals).
L374: ## **Safety conclusions:**
L375: - Raxibacumab at 40mg/kg IV offered a statistically significant survival benefit to the NZW rabbits with established systemic inhalational anthrax disease evident by bacteremia and toxemia prior to therapeutic intervention.
- Penetration of raxibacumab into CSF is minimal (&lt;2%) in the absence of meningitis. Low levels of raxibacumab in CSF were present in both survivors and non-survivors in this study. High CSF levels of raxibacumab were associated with absence of pathological changes in the CNS.
- Frequent and more extensive findings of CNS pathology in raxibacumab-treated animals on necropsy as compared to placebo are possibly associated with inability of raxibacumab
L376: achieve adequate levels in CNS to control bacterial spread in raxibacumab treated animals. However, the precise mechanism for exaggerated inflammatory response in the CNS of raxibacumab treated non-survivors remains unclear. This pathology finding should be described in the resultant label of raxibacumab if approved. Studies of lethal toxin suggest that subinhibitory concentrations of raxibacumab within the CNS might have resulted in reversal of lethal toxin-induced immunosuppression and localized findings of immuno-reconstitution.
L377: - Co-localization of endogenous IgG and raxibacumab within the brain of raxibacumab-treated animals together with negative brain tissue cross reactivity studies suggest that direct toxic effect of raxibacumab on CNS is unlikely.
L378: ## 4.3.4 Nonclinical Study 1141-CG920871 Added Benefit of Raxibacumab with Levofloxacin vs. Levofloxacin as Post-exposure Treatment in the New Zealand White Rabbit Inhalational Anthrax Model
L379: **INVESTIGATOR:** Gabriel Meister, PhD
L380: **STUDY CENTER:** Battelle Biomedical Research Center (BBRC)
L381: **STUDY PERIOD:** 10 January 2010 to 15 May 2012
L382: ## **OBJECTIVES:**
L383: Primary objective:
L384: - To evaluate the added benefit against lethality of raxibacumab treatment combined with levofloxacin treatment compared with levofloxacin treatment alone, when administered at a predetermined time-point following inhalational exposure to *B. anthracis* in NZW rabbits.
L385: **METHODOLOGY:** Parallel-group, randomized, blinded, single center study to evaluate efficacy of raxibacumab combined with levofloxacin compared to levofloxacin alone as a therapeutic treatment of inhalational anthrax in NZW rabbits.
L386: **NUMBER OF ANIMALS:** Two cohorts of 90 animals each, shipped on 3 separate days, each shipment group randomized to 1 of 2 challenge days, survivors randomized to treatment or control at 84 hours post exposure. Total enrollment was 209 New Zealand White rabbits (180 required and 29 replacements).
L387: **STUDY DRUG:** IV raxibacumab given as a single bolus infusion at a 40 mg/kg dose. Levofloxacin at 50 mg/kg gavage dose was administered to animals 1 dose at the time of raxibacumab infusion, followed by 2 additional daily doses 24 hours apart.
L388: **Table 30: The Appearance, Formulation, and Dosage Strength of the Study Drug, Study 1141**
L389: Study Drugs	Appearance	Formulation	Dose Unit	Batch numbers
Raxibacumab	Clear liquid	Raxibacumab sterile solution for injection	50mg/ml	71128
Placebo (raxibacumab formulation buffer)	Clear liquid	n/a	n/a	71043
Levaquin Oral Solution	Clear liquid	Oral solution	25mg/ml	AEB2V00
L390: *MO comment: The test article was raxibacumab (Lot #71128). Vials were labeled 1-96 according to the randomization scheme. The levofloxacin dose of 50 mg/kg once daily in NZW rabbits results in exposures (Cmax 8.7 mcg/mL and AUC 66.7 mcg*h/mL) similar to that achieved at human doses of 500-750 mg daily (Cmax 5.1-9.3 mcg/mL and AUC 47.9-101 mcg*h/mL).*
L391: **DURATION OF TREATMENT:** Blinded raxibacumab treatment given as a single IV bolus dose of 40 mg/kg to NZW rabbits at 84 hours post exposure immediately after the first dose of levofloxacin. Levofloxacin was administered by oral gavage for 3 days starting at 84 hours post exposure.
L392: **TREATMENT COMPLIANCE:** Study drug infusion information, including dosage and volume prescribed, and volume administered, was recorded.
L393: **STUDY DESIGN:** Parallel-group, randomized, blinded, single center study to evaluate efficacy of raxibacumab combined with levofloxacin compared to levofloxacin alone as a therapeutic treatment of inhalational anthrax in NZW rabbits at 84 hours post exposure.
L394: **Background:** To date the sponsor has conducted evaluation of raxibacumab in several animal species and under various conditions. Efficacy of raxibacumab was evaluated in a proof-of concept rat model of Lethal Toxin infusion in pre-exposure and post-exposure setting. In addition, when used for pre-exposure prophylaxis raxibacumab showed dose-dependent survival benefit in rabbits and monkeys. Time-related effect on survival was also observed in a post-exposure prophylaxis setting in a rabbit model. Monotherapy studies of raxibacumab administered to rabbits and cynomolgus macaques at the time of diagnosis of inhalational anthrax disease showed a statistically significant survival benefit relative to placebo treatment. Studies evaluating raxibacumab with an antibacterial relative to antibacterial alone in NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaques demonstrated near 100 % survival in both treatment groups when therapeutic intervention was administered at the time of inhalational anthrax disease diagnosis. The complete response letter for the original BLA identified that the timing of intervention resulting in high survival rate with antibacterials as a major deficiency and asked the
L395: sponsor to conduct a combination study where survival with antibacterial alone approaches 50% to evaluate potential added benefit of raxibacumab.
L396: The protocol for this study was reviewed under SPA and an agreement on the study design was reached on October 14, 2010.
L397: Eighty-four hours post challenge was chosen as the timing of intervention based on the data collected by HGS and Battelle on the untreated and levofloxacin-treated animal survival as described in the tables below.

L408: At a regulatory briefing on the applicability of the animal rule to the licensing of anthrax anti-toxin monoclonal antibodies held at CDER on October 10, 2006, a consensus was reached that the efficacy of the monoclonal antibody against anthrax toxin should be demonstrated in two animal species (rabbit and NHP). Both models must show a significant benefit of the monoclonal over placebo. In addition, both models should explore the magnitude of benefit of an antitoxin therapeutic when combined with an antimicrobial over antimicrobial alone.
L409: This submission addresses the evaluation of raxibacumab efficacy in addition to levofloxacin when compared to levofloxacin alone in one of **two proposed recommended animal models** – the NZW rabbit.
L410: The natural history studies in a NZW rabbit model of inhalational anthrax were reviewed prior to the original BLA submission. The natural history of inhalational anthrax disease in NZW rabbits conducted thus far demonstrated reproducible and predictable clinical laboratory profile (body temperature, clinical hematology, PA toxemia, and bacteremia) that correlates with mortality
L411: (see the following table). In addition, a correlation of PA toxemia and temperature elevation of \ge 2^{\circ}\text{F} to onset of bacteremia has been established in the natural history as well as therapeutic efficacy studies in this animal model.

L421: **Study procedures:** The study was conducted under GLP.
L422: - Animals were housed in the individual cages.
- Study animals were randomized by dose group and gender prior to challenge in 6 sets of 30 animals.
- Aerosol challenge at targeted 200 x LD50 of *B. anthracis* Ames strain spores were to occur on Day A, B, C, D, E, F, G, H.
- Clinical observations and temperature monitoring
- Single dose IV study treatment was administered.
- Clinical observations were done every 6 hours from the time of challenge until Day 10 postexposure and twice daily thereafter
- Animals were euthanized if found moribund on the study or survived until the end of the study on Day 35 postexposure
- Necropsy and histopathology were conducted on all euthanized and all dead animals in a blinded fashion

L434: ## Raxibacumab and Levofloxacin PK and PA Concentrations and TNA
L435: The PK analyses of raxibacumab concentration-time profiles for all raxibacumab-dosed rabbits were conducted using population analysis techniques (mixed effect modeling), with the NONMEM software. Plasma raxibacumab and levofloxacin concentration-time data, serum PA concentration-time data, individual raxibacumab and levofloxacin PK parameters, and individual PA kinetic parameters were summarized using descriptive statistics. For the purpose of assessing PA kinetics, the PA concentration-time data was divided into 2 subgroups for analysis: 84 hour non-survivors and 84 hour survivors (treated animals). The TNA titers in plasma samples from surviving rabbits were determined using a cell killing assay.
L436: ## Immunogenicity
L437: Plasma samples were assessed for anti-raxibacumab activity using a 2-part ECL-based bridging assay.
L438: ## Endpoints:
L439: **Primary efficacy endpoint** was survival in the ITT study population on Day 28 after the last dose of levofloxacin treatment (Day 35 post exposure).
L440: ## Analysis Populations:
L441: The ITT population is defined as all randomized rabbits that received the study agent.
L442: **MO comment:** Additional sensitivity analyses will be performed by the FDA in the population of animals that were bacteremic at the treatment onset.
L443: ## Statistical Plan:
L444: The primary efficacy endpoint was 28-day survival, defined as the proportion of animals that survive to Day 28 after the last dose of levofloxacin treatment. Based on previous experience (natural history of inhalational anthrax in NZW rabbits and results from the placebo arms in the previous efficacy studies), about 35% of animals would be expected to survive until 84 hours after spore challenge. It was estimated that 32 animals would be treated in each of the two active treatment groups. This study design had approximately 52% power to detect a 25% absolute improvement in 28-day survival from the raxibacumab/levofloxacin combination group over the levofloxacin group, assuming 40% 28-day survival in the levofloxacin group. The study would
L445: yield a p-value of 0.044 if there were 21 (65.6%) survivors and 13 (40.6%) survivors at Day 28 after the last dose of levofloxacin treatment in the raxibacumab/levofloxacin combination group and the levofloxacin group, respectively. The study was not powered to demonstrate a statistically significant difference at a medically important change in mortality, which would be less than the 25% improvement used for the sample size calculation. The primary efficacy analysis will be performed using 2-sided likelihood ratio test or Fisher's exact test. Adjustment is made for multiple comparisons.
L446: *MO comment: Please refer to the Statistical review by Lan Zeng, Ph. D.*

L483: **MO comment.** The challenge spore dose was within the target of 200 \times LD_{50} for all animals in the study regardless of challenge day, survival to treatment or treatment assignment. Animals on the combination arm received on average 23 \times LD_{50} higher dose than those on levofloxacin alone arm. (two-sided p value of 0.058). There was no relationship between the challenge dose received and survival to study termination, survival to treatment or time to death.
L484: ## Clinical Observations
L485: Abnormal clinical signs were first documented in the majority of animals at approximately 48-72 hours post-challenge. The most common abnormal clinical signs reported were lethargy, loss of appetite, stool abnormalities and respiratory abnormalities. Among animals that succumbed to disease 8/13 (62%) on the levofloxacin + placebo arm and 5/7 (71%) on the levofloxacin + raxibacumab arm were found dead. The rest of the non-survivors were euthanized. Criteria for euthanasia that were observed most often included respiratory distress and unresponsiveness. Among survivors normalization of clinical signs occurred by Day 10-11 post-challenge with the exception of a few animals that demonstrated inappetence and/or minor stool abnormalities. Animal L33741 (raxibacumab arm) had documented muzzle swelling through Day 12, but recovered the following day and survived through Day 35 post-challenge.
L486: ## Temperature monitoring
L487: All challenged animals demonstrated increases in body temperature during the study, most of them on Days 2 through 6 following exposure to *B. anthracis*, similar to observations in previous studies. However, not all animals had temperature elevations high enough to meet fever definition (&gt;2 F above baseline for \ge 2 hours): 50 animals that succumbed to disease prior to
L488: treatment, 8 animals on levofloxacin alone arm, and 7 animals on the combination arm did not meet fever criteria, although these animals were toxicemic and bacteremic either prior to death in the case of untreated animals, or prior to treatment in the case of animals that received treatment. In the majority of treated survivors, body temperature returned to normal levels following the first week after exposure.
