L491: **MO comment.** Although per protocol temperature monitoring was ongoing continuously in all animals on study, temperature data input into the dataset was limited to morning and evening temperatures. Therefore, in this review the fever definition is more restrictive than in reviews for the other rabbit efficacy studies, as 2 consecutive measurements in this study are approximately 12 hours apart as compared to hourly measurements in other studies.
L492: All animals febrile on the study, except for one on the combination arm (L33771) met fever definition criteria prior to treatment. The proportion of animals febrile prior to treatment was not different between the study arms. There were a total of 9 survivors that were persistently febrile for the duration of the study: two on levofloxacin alone arm (L33713 and 34854) and seven on the combination arm (L29365, L33771, L34826, L34833, L34846, L34866, and L34868). These animals were challenged with *B. anthracis* spore doses ranging from 140 to 208xLD50 and were bacteremic and toxicemic at the time of treatment. All of them cleared bacteremia by Day 7 post treatment. Seven of them resolved toxemia by Day 7 post treatment. Animal L34833 cleared toxemia on Day 14.
L493: Animal L29365 was PA negative in Day 3 through Day 14 post treatment samples, then had PA detected at low levels on Day 21 and Day 28 post treatment.
L494: ## Bacteremia Results
L495: All animals except for L34828 (levofloxacin raxibacumab combination arm) were found to be bacteremic prior to randomization and treatment administration. Animal L34828 remained negative for bacteremia following treatment. All but 2 of the animals (L35281 and L33701) that died before 84 hours exhibited positive terminal bacteremia results. Animal L35281 was bacteremic at 24, 36, 48, and 60 hours post spore exposure and succumbed to disease prior to the 72 hours collection time point. Animal L33701 was positive for bacteremia at 36, 48, 60, and 72 hours post exposure and succumbed to disease prior to 84 hours post spore exposure.

L507: *discontinuation are likely to do so because of effects of anthrax toxin rather than bacteremia. Animal model and antimicrobial regimen developmental work was conducted by NIAID. The summary data presented to FDA was assuring since animals that died on the antibiotic arm did so during the course of treatment. Animals on the combination arm cleared bacteremia faster than those on levofloxacin alone arm. The timing of death was similar between the two treatment arms.*

L553: All animals that survived were monitored for 28 days post-treatment. Clinical signs and symptoms of anthrax, including body temperature elevations, resolved following resolution of bacteremia. L554: ## Pathology, Gross and Microscopic
L555: Complete gross necropsies were performed on all animals, including those that died prior to initiation of treatment. Protocol-specified tissues (brain, bronchial lymph nodes, heart, kidney, liver, lungs, mediastinal lymph nodes, and spleen) were sampled and preserved in 10 percent neutral buffered formalin only from treated animals. Animals were examined in a blinded manner: the pathologist was unaware of the treatment assignments. Gross findings in animals died on the study included: discoloration or lesions in the brain, lungs, and large intestines; enlargement of mediastinal lymph nodes; fluid (effusion) in multiple body cavities, mesentery, thymus, and skin; and cystic structures in the lung. These gross lesions were considered typical of anthrax in rabbits and, in animals examined microscopically, were associated with hemorrhage, edema, and acute inflammation.
L556: The only gross lesion present in any of the animals surviving to study termination was a unilateral kidney cyst in a levofloxacin/raxibacumab-treated animal, L33739, which was considered to be a common incidental finding with no relation to anthrax challenge or treatment.
L557: All protocol-predefined tissues from all animals surviving to treatment were examined microscopically for evidence of anthrax, with the exception of the brain from raxibacumab/levofloxacin-treated animal, L34818, and the spleen from raxibacumab/levofloxacin-treated animal, L33747, which were not successfully processed to slides. All microscopic findings were graded semiquantitatively (grades 0-4) according to the following scale: minimal (Grade 1) represented the least detectible lesion; mild (Grade 2) represented an easily discernible lesion; moderate (Grade 3) represented a change affecting a large area of the represented tissue; and marked (Grade 4) represented a lesion that approached maximal.
L558: Microscopic findings consistent with anthrax were present in nearly all animals examined that were found dead or euthanized for moribundity after the initiation of treatment but prior to scheduled Study Day 35 sacrifice in both levofloxacin-treated and raxibacumab/levofloxacin-treated groups. Lesions typical of anthrax in this study included acute inflammation, necrosis, and hemorrhage, and were generally of similar incidence and severity in both treatment groups. Findings in the brain were present in 2 animals in the levofloxacin treatment group and comprised of meningeal and parenchymal hemorrhage and meningeal vascular necrosis (L23083) and parenchymal hemorrhage and necrosis (L34864); there were no brain findings in the raxibacumab/levofloxacin-treated non-survivors. Survivors had the following findings: levofloxacin-treated L34863 had mixed infiltrate in the liver and L34834 had renal tubular
L559: atrophy and cardiac osseous metaplasia; levofloxacin/raxibacumab-treated L35231 had arterial thrombus in the lung, while L35259 had a mixed cellular infiltrate in the liver. The reviewer compared histopathology findings between groups.

L583: ## Efficacy findings:
L584: - Study design achieved survival with levofloxacin alone of 62.9% similar to that observed in inhalational anthrax cases during the 2001 bioterrorism attack (55%).
- Raxibacumab at 40 mg/kg IV bolus dose administered at 84 hours post challenge with levofloxacin 50 mg/kg qd dose for 3 days resulted in improved survival (82.1%) as compared to levofloxacin alone (64.9%) all randomized toxemic animals. The treatment difference of 17.2% did not achieve statistical significance (p=0.0874).
- The difference in efficacy between the treatment groups in the bacteremic population of animals was 16.7% [81.6% versus 64.9% (p=0.0998)] and was similar to the ITT analysis.
L585: ## Safety findings:
L586: - Raxibacumab at 40 mg/kg IV did not interfere with efficacy of levofloxacin. There was a trend of improvement in survival (17% difference, not significant) in the combination arm relative to levofloxacin alone.
- There was no difference between the treatment groups in the timing of clearance of bacteremia or toxemia.
- Animals that succumbed to disease had findings consistent with anthrax in multiple organs. The pattern of organs affected did not differ between the treatment arms.
- Pathological CNS findings were absent in levofloxacin/raxibacumab-treated non-survivors compared to findings of meningitis in 2/13 (15%) of levofloxacin-treated non-survivors.
- Survivors on both arms had incidental findings on microscopic examination unrelated to anthrax.
L587: ## 4.4 Clinical Pharmacology
L588: Please refer to the final Clinical Pharmacology review for this resubmission by Dr. Ryan Owen and the review of the original BLA submission by Dr. Kimberly Bergman. To allow selection of an effective dose in humans for therapeutic treatment of anthrax, the applicant has submitted clinical pharmacology data for raxibacumab in humans and in the two pivotal animal species, rabbits and cynomolgus monkeys. The pharmacokinetics (PK) and safety of raxibacumab administered as the product proposed for licensure has been evaluated in a Phase 1 dose-ranging study (PAM-NH-01), an antibiotic interaction study with ciprofloxacin (HGS1021-C1064), a repeat dose immunogenicity study (HGS1021-C1069) and a Phase 2/3 safety study (HGS1021-C1063). Based on a cross-species comparison of raxibacumab exposure and exposure-response information for raxibacumab dose/concentration, PA concentration and survival, the clinical pharmacology information provided by the applicant is acceptable and supports the use of the 40 mg/kg dose of raxibacumab. The dose and concentration response relationship with the endpoint of survival indicates potential to achieve higher response rates at higher doses. If future trials are conducted, higher doses (e.g. 60 or 80 mg/kg) should be explored along with 40 mg/kg.
L589: ## 4.4.1 Mechanism of Action
L590: *In vitro* studies demonstrated that raxibacumab binds PA in supernatants from Sterne, Ames and Vollum strains of *B. anthracis*. The mechanism of action appears to be by neutralization of free PA. Studies show that PA binds the surface of human and murine macrophages, and the epitope on recombinant PA that binds the cell surface receptor appears to be the same as the one binding raxibacumab (5), thereby suggesting that some structural similarity between the antigen recognition site on raxibacumab and the cell surface receptors binding site for PA exists. Raxibacumab blocks cAMP induction by recombinant ET when PA is preincubated with
L591: 5 Xu L, Frucht DM. *Bacillus anthracis*: a multi-faceted role for anthrax lethal toxin in thwarting host immune defenses. *Internat J. Biochem. Cell Biol* 2007;39:20-4.
L592: raxibacumab prior to addition of EF. Similarly, raxibacumab inhibits killing of murine macrophage (J774-A.1) cells when PA is preincubated with raxibacumab prior to addition of LF.
L593: ## 4.4.2 Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics
L594: The clinical pharmacology characteristics of raxibacumab have been defined in rabbits, monkeys and humans. Raxibacumab dose selection is supported by a cross-species comparison of exposure and exposure-response (E/R) relationships described in in vivo animal models of inhalation anthrax infection. These studies show raxibacumab demonstrates the following clinical pharmacology characteristics:
L595: - Following single intravenous administration of raxibacumab 40 mg/kg in healthy, male and female human subjects, mean raxibacumab steady-state volume of distribution was greater than plasma volume, suggesting some tissue distribution. Clearance values were much smaller than the glomerular filtration rate indicating that there is virtually no renal clearance of raxibacumab. These findings were similar in monkeys and rabbits.
- Humans achieve similar or greater exposures to raxibacumab following a single 40 mg/kg IV dose compared to rabbits and monkeys receiving the same dose. Mean raxibacumab C_{max} in humans following a single 40 mg/kg IV dose was similar to or greater than mean C_{max} values in monkeys and rabbits. Mean raxibacumab AUC_{inf} in humans following a single 40 mg/kg IV dose was 2.4 and 4.6-fold that of the mean AUC_{inf} values in monkeys and rabbits, respectively. Mean total clearance of raxibacumab was substantially slower in humans as compared to rabbits by a factor of approximately 5 and in monkeys by a factor of approximately 3. Thus, half-life of raxibacumab was longer in humans compared to mean half-lives observed in monkeys and rabbits (20.6 \pm 6.5 days versus 10.1 \pm 2.4 days and 4.1 \pm 0.85 days, respectively). Variability in C_{max} was similar across species; %CV values ranged between approximately 13 to 17%. Variability in AUC_{inf} was wider, ranging between 13 and 32% across species.
- Serum raxibacumab concentration-time profiles were similar following administration of raxibacumab alone and with both PO and IV ciprofloxacin. Overall, exposure to ciprofloxacin appears to have no consistent or meaningful impact on raxibacumab PK. Likewise, ciprofloxacin exposure is equivalent when ciprofloxacin is administered alone and with raxibacumab. Thus, there is no significant interaction between raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin.
- The exposure-response data suggest a relationship between raxibacumab dose, concentration, and survival. The dose and dosing regimen selected by the applicant, raxibacumab 40 mg/kg IV single dose, is consistent with the known relationship between dose-concentration-response.
- Dose and concentration response for the endpoint of survival indicates potential to achieve higher response rates at higher doses. If future trials are conducted, higher doses (e.g. 60 or 80 mg/kg) should be explored along with 40 mg/kg.
- Based on in vitro binding kinetics studies, the proposed dose of 40 mg/kg raxibacumab in humans would be expected to maintain levels required for virtually complete binding (99.9%) of PA for 7 days and those required for 99% binding for up to 42 days. Despite
L596: the theoretical importance of targeting virtually complete binding of PA, the duration of time raxibacumab concentrations remain above the threshold of 202 µg/mL (99.9% PA binding) does not appear to impact efficacy in inhalational anthrax models.
L597: - Based on predicted human PK profiles, more than 95% of humans administered a 40 mg/kg IV raxibacumab dose can be expected to achieve serum raxibacumab concentrations that are equimolar to or in excess of the highest observed serum/plasma PA concentration in any animal that died in the therapeutic intervention studies (for 48 and 28 days relative to rabbits and monkeys, respectively). In addition, modeling and simulation indicated that a single 40 mg/kg IV raxibacumab dose in humans is adequate to bind at least 99.7% of serum PA for up to 28 days after administration, in at least 95% of patients who receive raxibacumab.
- In the pivotal animal studies, animals that were treated with raxibacumab and died exhibited a higher incidence and severity of histopathologic findings in the brain versus placebo treated animals. No clear relationship between exposure and CNS pathology can be discerned based on the limited amount of data in animals that died. Overall, the raxibacumab 20 mg/kg dose group had a higher incidence and severity of CNS findings than the 40 mg/kg group in both rabbits and monkeys. Due to the small numbers of animals that exhibited specific pathology findings, no definitive conclusions about exposure-response for bacteria, hemorrhage, inflammation, or necrosis could be made.
- Raxibacumab was non-immunogenic in humans and there were no subjects with a positive anti-raxibacumab antibody response in the human studies following single or repeat (every 14 days or following ≥ 4 months) doses.

L612: ## 6 Review of Efficacy
L613: ## *First Cycle Review Efficacy Summary*
L614: The original BLA for raxibacumab was submitted to the FDA on May 14, 2009. The application contained four GLP animal efficacy studies of raxibacumab for the treatment of inhalational anthrax in New Zealand white (NZW) rabbits and cynomolgus macaques in lieu of adequate and well controlled studies in humans.
L615: NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaques were selected for the efficacy studies of raxibacumab for treatment of inhalational anthrax. In the original BLA, four treatment studies with raxibacumab were submitted. The two efficacy studies tested raxibacumab versus placebo and two others compared the efficacy of raxibacumab plus antimicrobial and antimicrobial alone versus placebo (two studies each in rabbits and in monkeys). The animals were challenged with aerosolized *B. anthracis* spores at 200x LD50. In rabbit studies sustained elevation of body temperature above baseline for 2 hours or a positive result on PA toxemia screen assay served as trigger for intervention (average 28 hours postexposure). In monkey studies intervention commenced at the time of positive PA result (average 42 hours postexposure). The review revealed that raxibacumab at 40 mg/kg IV single dose was superior to placebo in the rabbit and monkey raxibacumab monotherapy studies. In the monkey study, raxibacumab 20 mg/kg was also superior to placebo, but in the rabbit study, superior efficacy was limited to the 40 mg/kg arm.

L620: When given in combination with antimicrobials, the efficacy of the combination was high, but the efficacy of antimicrobials alone was also high. This raised the question whether the animal models adequately represented advanced anthrax disease in humans, where high mortality was observed despite antimicrobial treatment.

L624: NZW rabbit study antimicrobial was 50 mg/kg levofloxacin daily x 3 days
L625: 2 95% CIs are exact confidence intervals
L626: Based on the information from the natural history of inhalational anthrax disease in man, in rabbits, and monkeys; the mechanism of action of raxibacumab; and the efficacy of raxibacumab 40 mg/kg IV in the animal studies, clinical reviewer concluded that NZW rabbit and cynomolgus macaque models of inhalational anthrax disease are reflective of human disease and the efficacy findings from the therapeutic studies in these models could be extrapolated to humans.
L627: However, several limitations of the efficacy findings in pivotal and combination animal studies and in animal models themselves were discussed.
L628: First, the timing of intervention is likely to differ between animals and humans. In the experimental settings, animals were closely monitored for either an elevation in temperature (rabbits) or a positive plasma PA (rabbits and monkeys), and once detected, a therapeutic intervention was delivered. Humans may have delayed presentation to the healthcare setting or be given alternative diagnoses prior to the definitive diagnosis of anthrax being made. As the effects of delayed administration of raxibacumab after the onset of clinical symptoms has not been studied in the animal models, it is unclear how long raxibacumab administration can be delayed and still provide survival benefit.
L629: Second, the combination efficacy studies demonstrated very high efficacies (nearly 100%) of levofloxacin in NZW rabbits and ciprofloxacin in monkeys, respectively. In contrast, during the 2001 anthrax attacks 5 of the 11 people who developed inhalational anthrax died despite best available antimicrobial and supportive treatment. In addition, a question regarding efficacy interaction between raxibacumab and antimicrobial when given together for the treatment of inhalational anthrax remained unanswered. Twelve of twenty four AIDAC committee members pointed out a number of deficiencies in the combination study design that precluded definite
L630: conclusions regarding efficacy interactions, e.g. timing of intervention, antibiotic regimen, and the absence of raxibacumab alone arm. A majority of the committee members (17/24) recommended additional evaluation of the contribution offered by raxibacumab to the efficacy of antimicrobial alone.
L631: Third, the conditions of an animal experiment do not include any supportive care that human patients with inhalational anthrax will receive in a healthcare or clinical trial setting, including but not limited to mechanical ventilation, fluid resuscitation, pleural fluid drainage, dialysis, etc.
L632: Fourth, due to concerns about the reliability of raxibacumab and antimicrobial PK data generated for the original BLA, FDA was unable to conclude that the proposed human dosing regimen would result in the exposures similar to those seen at the efficacious dose in animal studies. Because of these concerns, it was also unclear that the antimicrobial exposures in the combination animal studies did not exceed human exposures achieved with the approved human dose regimen.
L633: ## Resubmission Review Efficacy Summary
L634: Two new animal efficacy studies included in this resubmission of the BLA were conducted to evaluate the added benefit (over antibacterials) of raxibacumab when the treatment intervention is delayed and to provide additional information on the CNS toxicity findings seen in the original BLA submission.
L635: The design of the CNS safety study 1103 in rabbits was similar to the previously-conducted raxibacumab monotherapy study in rabbits, where animals challenged with an aerosolized dose of *B. anthracis* spores (200xLD50) were randomized and treated in a blinded fashion either with raxibacumab 40 mg/kg IV single dose or matching placebo. The primary efficacy endpoint was survival at Day 28 post challenge. Survivors and non-survivors underwent systematic blinded histopathology examination with immunohistochemistry analysis of brain tissue for raxibacumab and endogenous IGG.
L636: The added benefit study 1141 in rabbits evaluated efficacy of the combination levofloxacin and raxibacumab treatment relative to levofloxacin alone. Surviving animals exposed to an aerosolized dose of *B. anthracis* spores (200xLD50) underwent randomization and treatment in a blinded manner at 84 hours post challenge to achieve survival with antimicrobial alone that is reflective of historical survival in humans with inhalational anthrax.
L637: ## 6.1 Indication
L638: (b) (4)
L639: Under the Animal Rule, animal efficacy data was used to support the licensure of raxibacumab for treatment of inhalational anthrax. Efficacy was demonstrated in more than one animal species expected to react with a response predictive for humans and the studies used an endpoint that is clearly related to the desired benefit in humans.
L640: Six animal therapeutic studies of inhalational anthrax were conducted by the applicant: two in cynomolgus macaques and four in New Zealand White rabbits. Among them, three studies evaluated efficacy of raxibacumab as monotherapy against placebo and three others efficacy of raxibacumab administered together with an antimicrobial. Two monotherapy studies and two combination therapy studies in monkey and rabbit animal models of inhalational anthrax have been reviewed by Drs. Susan McCune and Yuliya Yasinskaya during 1st cycle of the BLA review in 2009. This review will focus on studies 1103 and 1141 conducted in the rabbit model of inhalational anthrax and designed to evaluate raxibacumab effect on CNS in surviving and non-surviving animals and added benefit of raxibacumab to antimicrobials as a delayed treatment, respectively. See sections 4.3.3 and 4.3.4 for the complete review of these studies.
L641: ## 6.1.1 Methods
L642: The final reports and accompanying datasets for Studies 1103 and 1141 were reviewed and the findings are described in Section 4.3.3 and 4.3.4, respectively.
L643: ## 6.1.2 Subject Demographics and Disposition
L644: In study 1103 forty-eight experimentally naïve NZW rabbits of both sexes were exposed to a target aerosol of *B. anthracis* spores at 200xLD50 and randomized to receive either raxibacumab alone or placebo at the time of positive PA toxemia. All challenged animals were treated as randomized, twenty-four animals in each treatment group. All but one animal were bacteremic and toxicemic prior to treatment.
L645: In study 1141 one hundred and eighty experimentally naïve NZW rabbits of both sexes were exposed to a target aerosol of *B. anthracis* spores at 200xLD50 and the surviving animals were randomized to receive either levofloxacin alone or a combination of levofloxacin and raxibacumab treatment after an 84 hour delay post challenge. Seventy six challenged animals survived to 84 hours post challenged and were treated as randomized: 37 rabbits with levofloxacin alone and 39 with a combination therapy of levofloxacin + raxibacumab.
L646: ## 6.1.3 Analysis of Primary Endpoint(s)
L647: The primary endpoint was survival at the end of the study: Day 28 for study 1103 and Day 35 for study 1141.
L648: In study 1103 treatment with raxibacumab at 40 mg/kg IV single dose resulted in 45.8% survival compared to 0% survival with placebo, p=0.0002. Similar improvements in survival were seen in the population of animals toxicemic or bacteremic prior to treatment.

L664: ## 6.1.7 Subpopulations

L666: ## 6.1.8 Analysis of Clinical Information Relevant to Dosing Recommendations
L667: A dose-dependent improvement in survival was observed in raxibacumab monotherapy efficacy studies in monkey and rabbit animal models of inhalational anthrax. A tested dose of 40 mg/kg achieved the highest therapeutic efficacy in both animal models. Raxibacumab exposures (C_{max} and AUC) at a 40 mg/kg IV single dose in humans are similar or greater than those achieved at a 40 mg/kg dose in animals.
L668: ## 6.1.9 Discussion of Persistence of Efficacy and/or Tolerance Effects
L669: The survival benefit of raxibacumab as a single IV dose of 40 mg/kg persisted until the end of the therapeutic animal studies 14 to 35 days post exposure. By day 14 animals are able to mount
L670: an immune response as evident by positive Toxin Neutralizing Antibody (TNA) titers. No late deaths had occurred in raxibacumab treated animals.
L671: ## 6.1.10 Additional Efficacy Issues/Analyses
L672: Raxibacumab has limited penetration into CNS and does not prevent or adequately treat anthrax meningitis and should be used in addition to antimicrobials that penetrate the blood-brain barrier. See Section 4.3.3.
L673: ## 7 Review of Safety
L674: ## *Safety Summary*
L675: A total of 326 healthy volunteers received the recommended dose of raxibacumab of 40 mg/kg manufactured by the M11 process (the to-be-marketed product) and were evaluated for safety of raxibacumab. Of these, 303 subjects received a single dose (Study HGS1021-C1064 and Study HGS1021-C1063), 23 subjects received a second dose two weeks after their first dose (Study HGS1021-1063), and 20 subjects from Study HGS1021-C1064 received a 2nd dose more than 4 months after their initial dose (Study HGS1021-C1069). In Study HGS-1021-C1064, 48 subjects who received raxibacumab also received ciprofloxacin as part of this drug interaction study.
L676: Studies HGS1021-C1064, HGS1021-C1063 and HGS1021-C1069 are briefly summarized in the Table 7.2-1 below.

L694: ## 7.1.2 Categorization of Adverse Events
L695: Usual definitions were used in the identification and categorization of adverse events. An adverse event was defined as any unfavorable or unintended sign, symptom, or disease that is temporally associated with the use of a study agent but is not necessarily caused by the study agent. This included worsening (e.g., increase in frequency or severity) of pre-existing conditions. All AEs that were identified from the start of study agent administration on Day 0 through Day 56 (single-dose subjects) or Day 70 (double-dose subjects) were to be recorded on the AE CRF. The record of each AE on the CRF included AE description or diagnosis, start date, end date, whether the AE was ongoing, seriousness, severity, action taken with study agent, relationship to study agent (causality), and outcome. It was required that all data fields on the AE CRF be completed.
L696: The severity of an AE was graded using the modified DMID toxicity tables. For AEs not included in these toxicity tables, the following guidelines applied:
L697: Mild - causing no limitation of usual activities
Moderate - causing some limitation of usual activities
Severe - causing inability to carry out usual activities
Life-threatening - potentially life threatening or disabling
L698: A serious adverse event was defined as any AE resulting in any of the following outcomes:
L699: - Death
- Was life threatening (i.e., was an immediate threat to life)
- Inpatient hospitalization
- Prolongation of an existing hospitalization
- Persistent or significant disability or incapacity
- Congenital anomaly or birth defect
- Medically important
L700: The causality assessment was to be made by the investigator based on information available at the time that the SAE worksheet was completed.
L701: ## 7.1.3 Pooling of Data Across Studies/Clinical Trials to Estimate and Compare Incidence
L702: All single dose exposures were pooled for analysis. This included subjects from studies HGS1021-C1064 and HGS1021-C1063. Double dose subjects were presented both separately (study HGS1021-1063, where subjects received a second dose 2 weeks after their initial dose, and study HGS1021-C1069, where subjects received a second dose more than 4 months after their initial dose) and pooled for analysis.
L703: ## 7.2 Adequacy of Safety Assessments
L704: ## 7.2.1 Overall Exposure at Appropriate Doses/Durations and Demographics of Target Populations
L705: Three hundred twenty-six subjects received a 40 mg/kg IV dose of raxibacumab manufactured with the process intended for licensure. With a safety database of &gt;300 subjects a serious or fatal adverse event of frequency of 1% or greater could be excluded with 95% confidence. Elderly subjects comprised 6.4% of the safety database. Pediatric subjects and pregnant or nursing mothers were not studied.
L706: ## 7.2.2 Explorations for Dose Response
L707: One dose escalation study was performed in the raxibacumab development program. Study PAM-NH-01, which used the M10 formulation of the product, was a phase 1 single-blind, placebo-controlled, single-injection study which evaluated the safety and pharmacokinetics of 3 different single doses of PA mAb [0.3 mg/kg, 1 mg/kg and 3 mg/kg given intramuscularly (IM in **2 different sites – gluteus and vastus lateralis**)] and 5 different single doses of PA mAb [1 mg/kg, 3 mg/kg, 10 mg/kg, 20 mg/kg and 40 mg/kg given intravenously (IV)] in healthy subjects. While this first in man study predominantly used doses well below the putative therapeutic dose and assessed the safety of a developmental product rather than the to-be-marketed scale-up product, it did not find any dose-related AEs. Dose response exploration for the M11 formulation was limited only to subjects who received 2 doses of raxibacumab 14 days apart (Study HGS1021-C1063), but would not include subjects enrolled in Study HGS1021-1069 who received their second dose more than 4 months after the first dose, as washout was complete by this time.

L712: 2 Excluded the 20 subjects who received a 2nd raxibacumab dose in HGS1021-C1069.
L713: 3 Subjects participating in both HGS1021-C1064 and HGS1021-C1069 were counted only once.
L714: The number of subjects reporting at least 1 AE was higher in the single dose group (50.5%) compared to either of the two double-dose groups prior to their 2nd dose (17.4% and 30%). This observation may be related to the small study numbers in the double dose groups. The number of subjects reporting at least 1 AE post 2nd dose was also lower (approximately 40% in both groups), which again could be related to small study numbers, or the absence of a dose-adverse event relationship when a second raxibacumab dose is administered 2 weeks or later following the first dose. Overall, the numbers of SAEs and AEs of severe intensity were infrequently reported.
L715: ## 7.2.3 Special Animal and/or In Vitro Testing
L716: Three relevant nonclinical studies were reviewed in detail by the Pharmacology/Toxicology team and are briefly summarized here:
L717: The initial *ex vivo* tissue cross-reactivity study in human and cynomolgus monkey tissue showed specific cytoplasmic (non-membrane) binding of raxibacumab (M10 manufacturing process) in skeletal muscle and thyroid (both species), endometrium (human only) and breast and prostate (monkey only). These tissues were identified as possible target organs for toxicity.
L718: The second *ex vivo* tissue cross-reactivity study was performed on tissues of NZW rabbits, cynomolgus macaques, and man and tested raxibacumab produced by the to-be-licensed M11 manufacturing process. This study showed no thyroid histopathology or abnormal levels of circulating thyroid hormones. Please refer to **Dr. Terry Miller's summary in Section 4.3 Preclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology** for additional information on these studies.
L719: Regarding safety, three non-clinical studies were reviewed in detail for the purposes of the CDC IND and are briefly summarized here:
L720: The 120-day monkey study evaluated raxibacumab 40 mg/kg given on days 0, 13, and 25, either IM or IV and again at day 69 by IM route. No difference in weight or feeding between the placebo and raxibacumab arms, and no gross pathological changes in the study arms were reported. Local inflammation resulting from trauma at site of IM injection was noted. Some animals had microcysts in the thyroid. Some animals had chronic inflammation in the prostate. These findings were consistent with the tissue cross-reactivity study above. CPK and thyroid hormones were reported to be unremarkable. Although the histological findings were not judged to be significant, these organs were mentioned as possible targets of toxicity. No anti Fab or Fc antibodies were found in these animals. There were no gross or histopathological CNS changes reported.
L721: The rabbit embryo-fetal toxicity study tested raxibacumab 0, 40, 120 mg/kg IV on gestation days 7 and 14. No adverse effects on the fetus or mother were identified, and the NOAEL was determined to be 120 mg/kg, the highest dose tested. Minor skeletal variations were noted, but these were not considered as adverse effects, and were stated to be within the rate for such variations seen in rabbits. It was briefly noted that in this study, 4 animals (2/20 in 40 mg/kg
L722: arm, 2/20 in 120 mg/kg arm) with anti-raxibacumab antibodies had reduced serum raxibacumab levels compared to animals without such antibodies. However, caution should be exercised when interpreting the significance of these findings, as detection of the anti-raxibacumab antibodies is hindered when the raxibacumab concentration exceeds 150 \mu/mL.

L737: The narratives of the nonfatal Serious Adverse events are presented below:
L738: ## **Subject US001-017**
L739: A 52-year-old white female in the raxibacumab double-dose group, developed upper abdominal pain, nausea, and low grade fever 10 days after her 2nd raxibacumab dose (Day 24). The subject was hospitalized and underwent a cholecystectomy on Day 26; the post-operative diagnosis was confirmed to be cholecystitis. Dosing was completed and no action was taken with regard to raxibacumab. The investigator indicated that the cholecystitis (severe) was possibly related to raxibacumab, and most likely caused by progression of concurrent disease as the subject had multiple risk factors for cholelithiasis including female gender, age, obesity (body weight of 111.5 kg), elevated serum glucose and elevated triglycerides.
L740: ## **Subject US001-005**
L741: A 48-year-old black male received his 1st dose of ciprofloxacin (500 mg PO) on Day 0 (31 Jan 2007) and his raxibacumab dose (40 mg/kg IV) on Day 5 per protocol. Relevant medical history which was not disclosed at screening included diagnoses of schizophrenia, depression, and bipolar disorder. There were no concomitant medications taken. The subject completed ciprofloxacin dosing as planned on Day 7. At the Day 47 follow-up visit, the subject reported auditory hallucinations occurring 2 to 3 times per week. He stated that the auditory hallucinations began after receiving raxibacumab; however, he did not report this to the clinical staff at that time. The subject denied suicidal ideation. The subject denied prior history of symptoms before entering the study and denied any history of psychiatric illness for himself or his family. A physical examination was within normal limits with no evidence of agitation, anxiety or depression. The subject left the clinical unit prior to completing further psychiatric evaluation. The subject later returned for evaluation and disclosed a past medical history of depression, bipolar disorder, and schizophrenia dating back to his early 20s. On Day 61, the subject was diagnosed with schizophrenia and prescribed olanzapine. As the subject received all 15 ciprofloxacin doses and the single raxibacumab dose per study schedule prior to disclosing the SAE, no action was taken with regard to study agents. The investigator revised the event term to schizophrenia with a severity grading of life-threatening, and indicated that it was probably not related to raxibacumab or ciprofloxacin. The schizophrenia was ongoing at the end of the study.
L742: Both cases of cholecystitis and schizophrenia were deemed unlikely to be related to raxibacumab based on temporal presentation (long duration between raxibacumab dosing and onset of the AE) and the presence of pre-existing conditions which could account for the SAE.

L754: ## 7.3.5 Submission Specific Primary Safety Concerns
L755: ## *CNS Adverse Events*
L756: Based on the increased CNS findings in animals treated with raxibacumab that died of anthrax in the pivotal efficacy studies, CNS adverse events were examined more closely in the human safety database.
L757: In the nervous system disorders SOC, headache was by far the most frequently reported adverse events. It was reported in 8.8% of single dose subjects, 14% of double dose subjects, and 10% of placebo subjects. The following nervous system disorders adverse events were reported (Table 7.3.5-1).

L761: Headache was reported in similar percentages of placebo and raxibacumab treated subjects (10% and 9.5%, respectively). There were an additional two reports of tension headache in the placebo group.
L762: There were no reports of meningismus across human safety studies. A single raxibacumab treated subject (US004-000030) enrolled in study HGS1021-C1063 reported fever (mild) on day 41 in conjunction with vomiting (mild), both of one day duration with no action taken. Similarly, there was one placebo subject US005-000046 enrolled in Study HGS1021-C1063 with pyrexia and headache reported on Study day 36, **again of one day's duration with no intervention**. It is unlikely that either of these represented cases of meningitis.
L763: ## *Infections/Infestations SOC*
L764: In contrast, within the infections and infestations SOC, upper respiratory tract infection occurred in 11.6% of double dose raxibacumab subjects, compared to 3.9% of single dose raxibacumab subjects and 5.0% of placebo subjects. However, other infections were not reported more frequently in the active treatment groups to suggest a uniform immunomodulatory/suppressive effect of raxibacumab. All AEs in the raxibacumab treated subjects ranged in frequency from 0.2% to 4.9%.
L765: ## *Gastrointestinal SOC*
L766: In the gastrointestinal disorders SOC, rates of abdominal pain, diarrhea, nausea and vomiting were all higher in the placebo group compared to all raxibacumab subjects.
L767: ## *Dermatologic (Skin and subcutaneous tissue) SOC*
L768: Lastly, in the skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders SOC, adverse reactions reported by the raxibacumab-treated subjects ranged from 0.2% to 1.8% in frequency. Pruritis and rash were reported in all raxibacumab subjects at 2.1% and 1.8% respectively, and were comparable to placebo rates (pruritis 0%, rash 1.3%). In Study HGS1021-C1064 evaluating raxibacumab PK in combination with ciprofloxacin, five of the first 25 subjects dosed with raxibacumab developed dermatologic events following administration. Three subjects responded to oral diphenhydramine, and two discontinued the infusion with resolution (one with diphenhydramine and one spontaneous). As a result of these findings, the protocol was amended so that all subsequent subjects received diphenhydramine before raxibacumab infusion. At the completion of HGS1021-C1064 a total of 8/88 (9.1%) subjects reported rash. In comparison, rash occurred in 6/27 (22%) of a subset of subjects who did not receive diphenhydramine premedication. Furthermore, to closely match the anticipated use of raxibacumab in human inhalational anthrax, diphenhydramine pretreatment was also given to the monkeys participating in the inhalational anthrax efficacy studies.
L769: ## 7.4 Supportive Safety Results
L770: ## 7.4.1 Common Adverse Events
L771: The most frequently reported system organ classes (SOC) for AR in the raxibacumab-treated subjects were nervous system disorders (13.2%), infections and infestations (11.3%), and gastrointestinal disorders and skin and subcutaneous tissue disorders (both 9.2%). These were all higher in the raxibacumab-treated subjects compared to placebo.
L772: ## 7.4.2 Laboratory Findings
L773: Laboratory tests with toxicity grade greater than or equal to 3 (severe) were infrequently reported. Overall, the incidence of laboratory abnormalities was comparable between raxibacumab-treated and placebo-treated subjects (only active treatment AR reported here). The incidence was not higher after a second raxibacumab administration than after a single administration. Most lab abnormalities were of low grade (Grade 2 or less), with grade 3 and 4 laboratory abnormalities infrequently reported, isolated and transient.
L774: ## 7.4.3 Vital Signs
L775: Three subjects treated with a single raxibacumab dose in study HGS1021-C1063 had AEs of hypertension, which were judged to be not related to raxibacumab. The hypertension was ongoing at the end of the study for two subjects. Two additional subjects in the raxibacumab
L776: single-dose group had an AE of mild elevated blood pressure, which resolved. The elevated blood pressure for one subject was recorded as possibly related to study agent.
L777: There were two reports of fever in study HGS1021-C1063 which were not related to study agent and resolved on study. One case was likely related to a viral infection, as fever was also reported with vomiting and influenza. The remaining case was reported concurrent with headache. Both AEs lasted two days and resolved without intervention.
L778: Two AEs of mild tachycardia were reported in Study HGS1021-C1063. These AEs resolved with no intervention.
L779: ## 4.4 Electrocardiograms (ECGs)
L780: Electrocardiograms were obtained prior to enrollment in all studies, and subjects with clinically significant abnormalities were excluded from participation. Telemetry monitoring was performed in Study HGS1021-C1064 prior to dosing of raxibacumab, during the infusion, and for 2 hours following the infusion. No significant arrhythmias during this period were noted. There were no protocol-required subsequent electrocardiograms obtained after the day of raxibacumab infusion in any study.
L781: ## 7.4.5 Special Safety Studies/Clinical Trials
L782: Not applicable.
L783: ## 7.4.6 Immunogenicity
L784: ## *Nonclinical Evaluation*
L785: No immunologic response above background levels was detected in healthy cynomolgus macaques treated with raxibacumab in the 120-day study. Antibodies against the Fab and Fc portion of the PA mAb antibody in raxibacumab-treated animals failed to increase above control levels determined from normal sera from 50 untreated monkeys.
L786: The overall incidence of anti-raxibacumab antibody response in pregnant NZW dams above background levels was very low (5/138).
L787: ## Monotherapy Animal Studies:
L788: No immunogenicity assessments were performed in pivotal animal (both rabbits and NHP) efficacy studies.
L789: ## Combination Animal Studies:
L790: Anti-raxibacumab immunogenicity assessments were added to Study 781-G923701 (NZW rabbits) as a protocol amendment to allow for determination of the impact of any observed anti-raxibacumab immunogenicity on plasma raxibacumab levels and survival.
L791: Fifteen of 18 rabbits (83%) in the levofloxacin/raxibacumab group tested positive for anti-raxibacumab antibodies on Day 28. In addition, 6/19 (31.6%) rabbits in the levofloxacin group also tested positive for anti-raxibacumab antibodies on Day 28. HGS accounted for this finding by noting that although the levofloxacin only treatment group did not receive raxibacumab, the levofloxacin-treated rabbits mounted an anti-PA response which may have included antibodies that cross-reacted in the anti-human anti-PA assay. Given the modest incidence of anti-raxibacumab immunogenicity at low titers compared with the raxibacumab-treated animals, this was felt to be a possible explanation. Furthermore, HGS pointed out that the emergence of potential anti-raxibacumab immunogenicity did not negatively impact survival.
L792: ## *Clinical Evaluation*
L793: All four human safety studies looked for the development of an anti-raxibacumab antibody response, including PAM-NH-01 which used the developmental M10 formulation of the product. In Studies HGS1021-C1064, HGS1021-C1063 (second raxibacumab dose 2 weeks following first dose) and HGS1021-C1069 (second dose \ge 4 months following first dose, there were no subjects who had a positive anti-raxibacumab antibody response following single or repeat (every 14 days or following \ge 4 months) doses of raxibacumab.

L801: ## 7.5.4 Drug-Disease Interactions
L802: Clinical trials were conducted in healthy human volunteers.
L803: ## Non-clinical
L804: In both rabbit and monkey raxibacumab monotherapy efficacy studies, raxibacumab-treated non-survivors had more pronounced anthrax meningitis/meningoencephalitis consisting of hemorrhage, necrosis, inflammation and bacteria in the brain compared to placebo non-survivors. A number of hypotheses were considered investigated, although no clear explanation could be
L805: found. Longer survival time in itself did not account for the increased CNS findings observed primarily in raxibacumab-treated non-survivors.

In study 1103, immunohistochemistry staining for raxibacumab and endogenous IgG were performed on the brain tissue. Both raxibacumab and endogenous rabbit IgG-stained neuropil, neurons, and glial cell types were seen in the brains of non-surviving raxibacumab-treated animals. Co-localizing staining patterns suggests non-specific leakage of antibodies across a damaged blood brain barrier. Intense staining of the parabrachial neurons with both raxibacumab and IgG suggested exposure to greater concentrations of circulating immunoglobulins due to their proximity to the ependyma where the BBB is less well-developed. High bacterial load detected in the brains of non-surviving raxibacumab-treated animals suggest a greater proliferation of *B. anthracis* **within the brain compared to other organs**. It's suspected that raxibacumab cannot reach CNS in the early stages of the infection until the circulating toxins and bacteria disrupt endothelial cell tight junctions and compromise the integrity of the BBB. In contrast, high plasma concentrations of raxibacumab immediately after treatment significantly diminished bacterial load in all organs other than brain, with marked reduction in incidence and severity of pathologic findings compared to placebo. An in vitro study described in the literature showed that purified anti-PA antibodies can stimulate phagocytic uptake of spores by macrophages; and inhibit spore germination6. This might explain significant reduction of the bacterial load in organs other than CNS, and high bacterial load in the brains of treated non-survivors. Also, LT-induced immunosuppression may contribute to bacterial invasion and dissemination in all tissues including the brain7. Reversal of LT immunosuppression with raxibacumab treatment in the brain and subsequent immune reconstitution cells may explain the greater CNS inflammatory response in the brains of non-surviving raxibacumab-treated animals compared to placebo. Surviving animals in monotherapy studies lacked CNS pathology.

In 3 combination studies of raxibacumab with antimicrobials in both rabbit and monkey animal models of inhalational anthrax, only a few non-survivors had findings of anthrax meningitis on the microscopic examination, and of these two animals have received antimicrobial alone and one animal was treated with a raxibacumab+antimicrobial combination. Survivors had unremarkable CNS microscopic examination.

No dose/exposure response was found for the CNS findings.

Brain tissue cross-reactivity studies in rabbits, cynomolgus macaques and humans were negative.

In summary the CNS findings in raxibacumab-treated non-survivors do not appear to be a direct toxic effect of raxibacumab and should be taken in the context of:

- reproducible (3 studies, 2 species) survival benefit of raxibacumab monotherapy (35%-69%) as compared to placebo (0%)
- the absence of dose-response with respect to the frequency and severity of the CNS pathology findings
- normal brain tissue cross reactivity studies in both species and humans
L806: 6 Welkos, S., Little, S., Friedlander, A., Fritz, D., and Fellows, P. (2001). The role of antibodies to *Bacillus anthracis* and anthrax toxin components in inhibiting the early stages of infection by anthrax spores. *Microbiology*. 147, 1677-1685.
L807: 7 Sun, C., Fang, H., Xie, T., Auth, R.D., Patel, N., Murray, P.R., Sny, P.J., Frucht, D.M. (2012). Anthrax lethal toxin disrupts intestinal barrier function and causes systemic infections with enteric bacteria. *Plos One*. 7(3); e33583-e33583.
L808: - normal macro and microscopic examination of the brains in raxibacumab-treated survivors
- normal macro and microscopic examination of the brains in raxibacumab/antimicrobial treated survivors and non-survivors
- normal macro and microscopic examination of the brain of the animal with the highest CSF level of raxibacumab
- immunohistochemical co-distribution of raxibacumab and endogenous rabbit IgG within the brains of affected animals suggesting plasma leak across compromised blood-brain barrier. Potential mechanism for CNS finding in raxibacumab treated non-survivors is unknown and is hypothesized to be related to the inadequate levels of raxibacumab in CNS for infection eradication and the reversal of lethal toxin induced immune suppression systemically.

L816: ## 7.6.3 Pediatrics and Assessment of Effects on Growth
L817: As noted previously, there were no studies that included pediatric age human subjects. As exposure of healthy children to raxibacumab is not ethical, the pediatric dosing was based on a pharmacometric bridging approach. Pediatric PK data on clearance and body weight relationship from other monoclonal antibodies (canakinumab, infliximab, pertuzumab and trastuzumab) was analyzed. It was consistently observed that clearance of monoclonal antibodies is strongly related to body weight. Specific dosing in children was derived from simulations matching plasma exposure ranges (AUC and C_{max}) in healthy adults after 40 mg/kg dose. The dose for pediatric patients is based on weight as shown in the table below.
L818: Pediatric Dose	Dose
>50 kg	40 mg/kg
> 15 kg to ≤ 50 kg	60 mg/kg
≤ 15 kg	80 mg/kg
L819: For detailed information regarding the modeled pediatric dose, please see the clinical pharmacology review by Dr. Ryan Owen and pharmacometrics review by Dr. Jingyu Yu. For the discussion of the inclusion of modeled pediatric dose in the raxibacumab labeling please also see consult reviews by Drs. Robert M. Nelson and Michelle D. Roth-Cline, as well as by Dr. Jeanine Best from the Office of Pediatric Therapeutics.
L820: ## 7.6.4 Overdose, Drug Abuse Potential, Withdrawal and Rebound
L821: There is no clinical experience with overdosage of raxibacumab. In toxicity studies in rabbits and cynomolgus monkeys receiving multiple injections of raxibacumab at 3 to 4 times the recommended dose, there was no raxibacumab-related toxicity. In case of overdosage, it is recommended that the patient be monitored for any signs or symptoms of adverse reactions or effects and appropriate symptomatic treatment instituted immediately.
L822: The product abuse and dependence potential of raxibacumab has not been examined in nonclinical or clinical studies but is expected to be negligible.
L823: Withdrawal and rebound are not applicable to raxibacumab as the product is intended for single dose administration.

L833: ## 9.3 Advisory Committee Meeting
L834: An Anti-Infective Advisory Committee Meeting was held on November 2, 2012. Questions posed to the committee, vote tally, and the discussion are summarized below.
L835: ## *Questions to the Committee:*
L836: Considering the information described for raxibacumab in the rabbit and monkey animal model studies and safety trials in healthy human volunteers:
L837: - **VOTE:** Do the results from the therapeutic studies of raxibacumab with and without antimicrobials in two animal models of inhalational anthrax provide substantial evidence that raxibacumab (40 mg/kg IV single dose in adults) is reasonably likely to produce clinical benefit for the treatment of humans with inhalational anthrax?
L838: **YES: 16 NO: 1 ABSTAIN: 1**
L839: **Committee Discussion:** The majority of the committee agreed that the results from the therapeutic studies of raxibacumab with and without antimicrobials in two animal models of inhalational anthrax provided substantial evidence that raxibacumab (40 mg/kg IV single dose in adults) is reasonably likely to produce clinical benefit for the treatment of humans with inhalational anthrax. The committee agreed that the results of the animal studies were statistically significant when comparing raxibacumab monotherapy to placebo. Although the results of the combination studies (raxibacumab + antibiotic vs. antibiotic alone) were not statistically different (p-value 0.0874), the committee agreed that these results were of clinical significance. The committee members stated that 0.05 is an arbitrary cut-off and that this drug has a 92% chance of having added benefit. Given the lack of an antagonistic effect on antibiotics and the lethality of anthrax disease, the majority of the committee agreed that this drug had clinical value especially for patients infected with multi-drug resistant anthrax and patients with multiple antibiotic allergies. The committee member who voted "no" stated that if this product was approved, providers will think that this drug has added benefit,
L840: *despite not demonstrating statistically significant evidence of this. This committee member further added that in the case of an emergency, this product would still be available via an Emergency Use Authorization (EUA) or treatment IND despite not being approved by the FDA. Please see the transcript for details of the committee discussion.*
L841: a. **DISCUSSION:** If yes, do you have any recommendations regarding labeling of the product, or if not, what additional studies are needed?
L842: **Committee Discussion:** The committee recommended several additions to the labeling if this product were to be approved. These additions include 1) clear guidance and protocols on which patients should receive this product; 2) guidance on the logistical use of this product during a large-scale emergency event; and 3) labeling emphasizing that this product will not protect against central nervous system infections such as meningitis due to its inability to penetrate the blood-brain barrier. The committee suggested additional trials be conducted to study the following: 1) potential interactions with anthrax vaccinations; 2) shorter infusion times or more concentrated infusions; 3) dosing in obese patients or those with large amounts of edema/fluid retention (dosing based on actual body weight vs. ideal body weight); 4) efficacy of doses greater than 40 mg/kg and 5) effective dosing during different stages of disease progression. Please see the transcript for details of the committee discussion.
L843: 2. **VOTE:** Do the results from raxibacumab safety trials in healthy volunteers and studies in animals support an acceptable risk benefit profile given the benefits of the therapy discussed in Question 1?
L844: **YES:** 18 **NO:** 0 **ABSTAIN:** 0
L845: **Committee Discussion:** The committee unanimously agreed that the results from the raxibacumab safety trials in healthy volunteers and studies in animals support an acceptable risk benefit profile given the benefits of the therapy discussed in question #1. The committee agreed that the deficiencies in the previous BLA submission have been sufficiently addressed and the lack of dose response regarding the central nervous system events suggest that this product is safe and does not contribute to the death of patients. L847: **Committee Discussion:** The committee stated that labeling should reinforce the fact that the safety of this drug was evaluated in healthy humans rather than patients with inhalational anthrax. Additionally, the committee recommended further studies to evaluate the following: 1) safety of doses greater than 40 mg/kg; 2) higher concentration and shorter infusion times; and 3) effect of raxibacumab on pre-exposure or
L848: *postexposure vaccination. Please see the transcript for details of the committee discussion.*

L851: **Committee Discussion:** The majority of the committee agreed with the proposed dosing of 40 mg/kg for adults. However, some of the committee members stated that this dose may not be the maximum effective dose. Therefore, the committee recommended additional studies to evaluate the efficacy and safety of doses higher than 40 mg/kg. The committee suggested that these additional studies would also provide information about the safety and efficacy of the proposed weight-based dosing in pediatric patients that is higher than proposed for adults. When using the proposed pediatric dosing, the committee noted that pediatric patients who have weights that approach 15 kg or 50 kg will receive doses larger than patients with weights greater than these values while acknowledging that the simplicity of pediatric dosing is an important factor under emergency. In addition, the committee suggested evaluating alternative body surface area (BSA) or lean body weight (LBW) based dosing for pediatric patients. Please see the transcript for details of the committee discussion.

L893: ## Office Director Decisional Memo
L894: Date	11/14/2009
From	Edward M. Cox, MD, MPH
Subject	Office Director Decisional Memo
BLA #	125349
Applicant Name	Human Genome Sciences, Inc. (HGS)
Date of Receipt	May 14, 2009
PDUFA Goal Date	November 14, 2009
Proposed Proprietary Name / Established (USAN) Name	none
raxibacumab
Dosage Forms / Strength	Injection for intravenous use, 50 mg/mL
Proposed Indication	Treatment of patients with inhalational anthrax due to B. anthracis
Action:	Complete Response
L895: Raxibacumab is a fully humanized monoclonal antibody that binds to the protective antigen of *B. anthracis*. HGS is developing raxibacumab as a treatment for patients with inhalational anthrax. Inhalational anthrax is a life threatening condition with a high mortality rate once disease has developed even with antibacterial drug treatment. The currently approved drug therapies labeled for the treatment of patients with *B. anthracis* are penicillin G potassium, penicillin G sodium, and penicillin G procaine, and the tetracyclines. For the indication of post-exposure prophylaxis of inhalational anthrax the previously listed antibacterial drugs and also ciprofloxacin and levofloxacin are approved.
L896: During the bioterrorism-related anthrax cases in 2001, there were 11 cases of inhalational anthrax, 5 of which were fatal.1 *B. anthracis* produces toxins that contribute to much of the pathophysiology of the disease. In inhalational anthrax disease, it is hypothesized that targeting not only the bacteria with antibacterial drugs, but also targeting the toxins produced by *B. anthracis* may be a means to improve survival rates in patients with anthrax disease. Another potential role for therapies acting via a mechanism different than that of an antibacterial drug is for treatment of patients with strains of *B. anthracis* that are resistant to antibacterial drugs.
L897: Protective antigen (PA) binds to the cell surface and forms a heptameric complex that facilitates the entry of lethal and edema toxin into the cell cytosol. Protective antigen also combines with lethal factor and edema factor to form lethal toxin (LT) and edema toxin (ET), respectively. The intended role of an antibody directed against protective antigen is to interrupt the pathophysiologic role of protective antigen in this process.
L898: The review team has reviewed the issues in detail in their respective disciplines. For a detailed discussion of the discipline specific reviews, the reader is referred to the individual discipline
L899: 1 Jernigan DB, Raghunathan PL, Bell BP, et al. Investigation of bioterrorism-related anthrax, United States, 2001: epidemiologic findings. Emerg Infect Dis. 2002 Oct;8(10):1019-28.
L900: specific reviews, the Cross-Discipline/Medical Team Leader Review, and the Division Director Review. This memorandum will focus on selected issues from the application including the animal studies and the information that they provide regarding effectiveness in humans with inhalational anthrax disease.
L901: The evaluation from the Product Quality standpoint for raxibacumab finds that, in general, the manufacturing is well controlled. There was, however, a deficiency from the Product Quality microbiology perspective that the endotoxin for the product needed to be re-assessed and
L902: (b) (4) There were also a number of recommendations for further work on validation procedures and updating testing protocols.
L903: The pharmacology/toxicology review notes no significant adverse nonclinical findings and also notes the finding of binding of raxibacumab to thyroid in human and non-human primate ex-vivo tissue. The review also notes the limitations of the performance of the assay to evaluate immunogenicity in the animal studies that raises questions about conclusions that can be drawn from animal studies to evaluate immunogenicity. The recommendation from Pharmacology/Toxicology regarding Pregnancy Category is Category B. Given the findings from the inspections of the bioanalytic methods from the human pharmacokinetic studies, this raises questions about the analytic results from the toxicokinetic samples from Study 6962-140 and Study 6962-173. Therefore HGS will be asked to re-assay the samples from these studies.
L904: The Microbiologist's review describes the in vitro and animal model studies done with raxibacumab. Of note from the studies evaluating the binding of raxibacumab to free PA or PA bound on the cell surface, it appears that raxibacumab binds to free PA, but not to PA bound to cellular receptors suggesting the binding site for raxibacumab may not be available after PA has bound to its cellular receptor. In contrast, the rabbit anti-PA polyclonal anti-sera used in these experiments bound to PA after it was bound to the cell surface receptor.
L905: The applicant's proposed dose in humans is a single dose of 40 mg/kg administered intravenously over 2 hours and 15 minutes after diphenhydramine pre-medication. The findings from the inspections of the analytic methods and procedures for the human pharmacokinetic studies raise important concerns about the quality and reliability of human pharmacokinetic data in this application. The issues with the reliability of the pharmacokinetic data will need to be resolved, as they serve as the means to link raxibacumab human pharmacokinetic exposure to animal pharmacokinetic exposure for dose selection. Further evaluation of the available information, procedures, and samples will be needed to determine whether re-analyses from these studies can be relied upon or whether additional studies will be needed to address this deficiency.
L906: ## *Animal Studies Evaluating Activity and Effectiveness*
L907: For a complete discussion of the animal studies evaluating activity and effectiveness the reader is referred to the Microbiology, Statistical, and Medical Officer Reviews. The sections that follow provide an overview of the findings from these studies.
L908: The activity of raxibacumab was evaluated in rat toxin models. The studies evaluated the effect of raxibacumab (an earlier formulation) on survival of rats administered LT. The
L909: studies showed that intravenous administration of raxibacumab administered prior to or for a limited time after an infusion of lethal toxin was able to improve survival compared to placebo. The studies provide proof of concept for the role of raxibacumab in interrupting the lethality of LT in the rat models that were studied.
L910: In a rabbit study (Experiment #1 in the table below) of 12 rabbits in each of 5 groups, rabbits received either placebo or 40 mg/kg of raxibacumab at 0, 12, 24, 36 hours post exposure/ challenge with aerosolized *B. anthracis* 100 LD50. Administration of raxibacumab at 0 or 12 hours post exposure resulted in 12 of 12 animals surviving; survival rates declined at later time points.
L911: A second rabbit study (experiment #2) evaluated different doses of raxibacumab administered either 24 or 36 hours post exposure. Survival rates for doses of raxibacumab administered 24 hours after challenge were between 3/12 animals and 5/12 animals for the doses between 5 mg/kg and 40 mg/kg. At 36 hours, at a dose of 20 mg/kg 0/12 animals survived. Bacteremia status was not assessed in this study.

L915: These studies show activity of raxibacumab, based upon differences in survival rates in animal models when given prior to or soon after exposure to aerosol challenge with *B. anthracis* spores.
L916: Studies in cynomolgus monkeys and New Zealand white (NZW) rabbits were performed evaluating the effect of raxibacumab monotherapy at 20 mg/kg and 40 mg/kg following aerosol exposure to *B. anthracis* spores. Animals were exposed to aerosolized *B. anthracis* spores and followed for development of PA in serum (monkeys) or PA in serum along with elevated temperature (rabbits) at which time raxibacumab was administered intravenously. The dose groups were placebo, 20 mg/kg, and 40 mg/kg. Survival rates at the 40 mg/kg dose in cynomolgus monkeys was 9/13 (69%) compared to 0/10 (0%) for placebo recipients. For NZW rabbits the survival rates in the 40 mg/kg group was 6/17 (35%) compared to 0/13 (0%) for the placebo group. The differences in survival rates for the raxibacumab 40 mg/kg dose groups were significantly better than placebo with p-values less than 0.05. The studies show an effect of raxibacumab in increasing survival in cynomolgus monkeys and rabbits with inhalational anthrax in these animal studies.
