L926: In the antimicrobial drug alone group survival was 13/13 in monkeys and 19/20 in rabbits. The very high survival rates for antibacterial drug therapy alone in these studies do not allow for any added benefit of raxibacumab to be shown above what the antimicrobial agent alone provides. During the bioterrorism event of 2001 in humans presenting with established anthrax disease antimicrobial therapy alone achieved an approximately 50% survival rate. Given the high survival rate in the animal studies with antimicrobial agent alone, it appears that intervention may be too early and that the animal models do not adequately model the human disease state where use is anticipated. One important goal of adjunctive anti-toxin therapy is to improve on the survival achieved with antibacterial drug alone. These studies lack capacity to determine if raxibacumab will provide added benefit to antimicrobial therapy alone.
L927: ## *Studies Evaluating Safety*
L928: ## *Animal*
L929: In animal toxicology studies, there was no evidence of CNS toxicity in monkeys dosed with 120 mg/kg raxibacumab. A finding noted in the animal models of infection was that non-surviving animals that received raxibacumab that died of anthrax had a greater rate and severity of CNS disease than animals that received placebo. The reasons for this greater rate and severity of CNS disease are not clear and the potential relevance to humans is not clear. In the rabbit combination study where animals received antimicrobial alone or antimicrobial plus raxibacumab, animals were sacrificed and examined for CNS lesions. There were no brain lesions seen in the surviving animals that received raxibacumab plus levofloxacin, or that received levofloxacin alone. Additional study will be needed to further understand this finding.
L930: ## *Human*
L931: The safety of raxibacumab 40 mg/kg IV was evaluated in 326 normal volunteers, and compared to adverse events reported in 80 normal volunteers who received placebo. Rash was
L932: seen initially in 6/25 (24%) of volunteers. Then diphenhydramine pre-treatment was initiated for all and the observed rash rate decreased to 2/61 (3%). Diphenhydramine pretreatment will be recommended, and was used in the monkey efficacy study. Other adverse effects include infusion site pain and headache. Headaches were reported in 9.5% of raxibacumab volunteers (31/326) and 10% of placebo volunteers (8/80).
L933: ## *Division of Scientific Investigations (DSI) Inspections*
L934: Inspections of the bioanalytical assay methods and conduct of the clinical trials found deficiencies in the testing done (bioanalytic methods) to measure levels of raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin in the human pharmacokinetic studies. This information is of critical importance because it is the means by which exposure in the animals where the efficacy of raxibacumab is evaluated is linked to the exposure in humans to arrive at an appropriate human dose.
L935: Additional information about the testing methods, the assay, use of the appropriate number of QC samples to calibrate the concentration curve and re-analysis of samples will be requested from HGS as a possible mean to address the noted deficiencies. If this additional information and re-analysis cannot address deficiencies, new studies may be needed. Given the findings from the human PKL studies additional information on the bioanalytical assay method used in the animal efficacy studies and two animal toxicology studies will also be needed. The animal studies (Study 724-G005829 and Study 682-G005758) were inspected in 2008 and found to be acceptable.
L936: ## *Anti-Infective Drugs Advisory Committee*
L937: The application for raxibacumab was presented to the Anti-Infective Drugs Advisory Committee on October 27th, 2009. The Committee was made aware of the questions on the reliability of the human PK data based upon inspectional findings, that the data should be disregarded, and that no question on approval/licensure would be asked of the Committee. The concerns regarding the human pharmacokinetic data were also posted publicly in advance of the meeting in an addendum to the FDA briefing material.
L938: The Committee was asked if the animal studies predict efficacy in humans. The vote on this question was Yes 16; No 7; Abstain 1. During the discussion of this question, a reason cited among those that voted "No" was that the time of intervention for the animal models appeared to be early in disease, noting the 95-100% survival rates with antimicrobial drug alone. On the question of whether raxibacumab will not interfere with antibacterial drug, the Committee voted, Yes 10; No 11; Abstain 3. Some expressed concerns that the ciprofloxacin dose was too high and therefore the study was not a sensitive test to detect interference with antibacterial drugs. On the question of whether a study should be done to look for added benefit of raxibacumab plus antibacterial over antibacterial alone, the Committee voted Yes 17; No 5; Abstain 1. During the discussion of this question some Committee members commented that the study could be done post-approval and some noted the study could be done in rabbits only. The Committee also expressed interest in additional work to understand the CNS findings seen with raxibacumab in animal effectiveness studies and additional safety data in the very young (the idea of doing juvenile animal studies was briefly mentioned) and elderly.
L939: ## *Discussion*
L940: Based upon the available information in the application, the application cannot be approved at in its present form. The deficiencies that need to be addressed are enumerated in the Complete Response Letter. As noted, the inspectional issues regarding the bioanalytical methods will need to adequately addressed, re-analyses performed, and if the re-analyses are not able to adequately address the noted deficiencies, new studies may be needed.
L941: The demonstration of effectiveness for a therapy for anthrax disease is based upon findings from animal studies because studies for this life threatening illness cannot be performed in humans. The animal rule can be relied upon when the results of adequate and well-controlled animal studies establish that the biologic product is reasonably likely to produce clinical benefit in humans. As noted in the Complete Response letter, in the animal efficacy studies that evaluated antimicrobial drug alone, antimicrobial drug plus raxibacumab, or placebo, the survival rates were 100% in cynomolgus monkeys and 95% in New Zealand white rabbits with antimicrobial drug alone. The high survival rate implies that the timing of intervention was too early to adequately model established anthrax disease in humans. In patients presenting with inhalational anthrax disease in 2001 and treated with antimicrobial therapy, the survival rate was approximately 50%. The animal model should reflect the human disease state for which the product under study in intended. The animal models and the 100% survival rate in cynomolgus monkeys and the 95% survival rates in New Zealand white rabbits with antimicrobial drug alone do not allow for the contribution of the monoclonal antibody to be assessed. In addition, the anticipated use of raxibacumab in humans would typically be in combination with antimicrobial therapy. The available data do not provide sufficient information to adequately predict response in humans with inhalational anthrax in the manner in which the product is likely to be used. Although the product was superior to placebo when used as monotherapy, this finding does not reflect how the product would typically be used. In addition, the findings in the combination studies where it appears that the intervention may have been given too early, raises questions about the how the time of intervention in the monotherapy studies relates to the point at which treatment would typically be initiated in humans with anthrax disease.
L942: There is a range of opinions across the review team on the adequacy of the data from the animal effectiveness studies. These issue included questions of whether there was an adequate degree of similarity to the human condition and the manner therapy would be used in that setting. I have also discussed the topic of the available data and their adequacy to predict response in humans with OND Office Directors. In the Complete Response letter, I am asking for an additional study to evaluate the effect of raxibacumab in an animal model that better models the condition and the manner in which the product is likely to be used in humans.
L943: A study should be performed in an animal model of inhalational anthrax in which there is a level of mortality in the antimicrobial alone arm to allow a demonstration of added benefit of raxibacumab when used in combination with an antimicrobial drug, for example, by showing that the outcome in the antimicrobial plus raxibacumab arm is higher than the outcome in the antimicrobial alone arm. In order to perform such a study, additional animal model developmental work will be needed.
L944: Another finding of note is the increased rate and severity of CNS findings in non-surviving animals that received raxibacumab compared to those that received placebo. The reasons for this greater rate and severity of CNS disease are not clear and the potential relevance to humans is not clear. There appears to be a drug/disease interaction, a disease manifestation more likely to occur in the setting of raxibacumab therapy, or potentially a toxic effect. This finding should be further evaluated by performing a study to further characterize the effect of raxibacumab on the CNS in an animal model of inhalational anthrax and characterize the clinical course and histological appearance of the CNS in animals that survive and animals that die of anthrax.
L945: As noted in the Completer Response letter, the bacterial endotoxin specification for the raxibacumab product should be re-assessed and (b) (4). In the Complete Response letter we have also provided other recommendations regarding additional product quality and clinical issues.
L946: ## *Deficiencies from the Complete Response Letter*
L947: The section from the Complete Response Letter enumerating deficiencies is provided below.
L948: ## **SAFETY AND EFFICACY**
L949: - In the animal efficacy studies that evaluated antimicrobial drug alone, antimicrobial drug plus raxibacumab, or placebo, the survival rates were 100% in cynomolgus monkeys and 95% in New Zealand White (NZW) rabbits with antimicrobial drug alone. The high survival rate implies that the timing of intervention was too early to adequately model established anthrax disease in humans. In patients presenting with inhalational anthrax disease in 2001 and treated with antimicrobial therapy, the survival rate was approximately 50%. The animal model should reflect the human disease state for which the product under study is intended. The animal models and the 100% survival rate in cynomolgus monkeys and the 95% survival rates in NZW rabbits with antimicrobial drug alone do not allow for the contribution of the monoclonal antibody to be assessed. In addition, the anticipated use in humans would be using raxibacumab in combination with antimicrobial therapy. The available data do not provide sufficient information to adequately predict response in humans with inhalational anthrax in the manner in which the product is likely to be used.
L950: To address this deficiency, we recommend that you conduct a study in an animal model of inhalational anthrax to demonstrate the added benefit of raxibacumab when used with an antimicrobial drug, for example, by showing that the outcome in the antimicrobial plus raxibacumab arm is higher than the outcome in the antimicrobial alone arm. We recognize that additional animal model developmental work will be needed to perform such a study and recommend that you discuss the proposed study with the division.
L951: - In animal studies, non-survivors that received raxibacumab and died of anthrax had a greater rate and severity of central nervous system (CNS) disease than animals that
L952: received placebo. The reasons for this greater rate and severity of CNS disease are not clear and the potential relevance to humans is not clear.
L953: To address this deficiency, we recommend that you conduct a study to evaluate the effect of raxibacumab on the CNS in an animal model of inhalational anthrax and characterize the clinical course and histological appearance of the CNS in animals that survive and animals that die of anthrax.
L954: ## CLINICAL PHARMACOLOGY
L955: - During the inspection of the bioanalytical sites responsible for analysis of serum raxibacumab and plasma ciprofloxacin concentrations in humans, the Division of Scientific Investigations (DSI) noted several deficiencies in the analytical procedures used for each of these products. Therefore, before we can rely on the pharmacokinetic data generated for raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin in humans, you will need to do the following:

Revise the analytical procedures for raxibacumab to address these DSI findings, re-assay the pharmacokinetic samples obtained from human studies HGS1021-C1063, HGS1021-C1064, and HGS1021-C1069, and re-calculate the pharmacokinetic parameters for raxibacumab from these re-analyses. Depending on the outcome of these re-analyses, additional pharmacokinetic studies may be required.

- Revise the analytical procedure for ciprofloxacin to address the DSI findings, re-assay the plasma pharmacokinetic samples obtained from human study HGS1021-C1064, and re-calculate the pharmacokinetic parameters for ciprofloxacin from this re-analysis in humans. Depending on the outcome of this re-analysis, additional pharmacokinetic studies may be required.

- The DSI findings noted above also bring into question whether we can rely on the pharmacokinetic data generated for raxibacumab from the animal efficacy studies in NZW rabbits and cynomolgus monkeys because these bioanalytical procedures are similar to those used for the human studies. Depending on the outcome of the re-analysis of raxibacumab in humans, re-assay of the pharmacokinetic samples from animal studies 682-G005758 and 724-G005829 and re-calculation of pharmacokinetic parameters for raxibacumab from these re-analyses in rabbits and monkeys may be required.

- The DSI findings noted above also bring into question whether we can rely on the pharmacokinetic data generated for ciprofloxacin from the combination animal efficacy study in cynomolgus monkeys because the bioanalytical procedure is similar to that used for the human studies. Depending on the outcome of the re-analysis of ciprofloxacin in humans, re-assay of the ciprofloxacin pharmacokinetic samples from animal study 789-G923702 in monkeys and re-calculation of pharmacokinetic parameters for ciprofloxacin from this re-analysis may be required.

L992: Raxibacumab as a single dose of 40 mg/kg infused intravenously over 2 hours 15 minutes following diphenhydramine pre-treatment is the regimen proposed by HGS for the treatment of inhalational anthrax. Human safety data on 326 normal volunteers, and four animal efficacy studies along with a broad range of nonclinical studies were submitted to support approval of the product under the Animal Rule.

L1020: ## 2 BACKGROUND
L1021: ## 2.1 Raxibacumab and Anthrax
L1022: Raxibacumab is a fully-humanized IgG1\lambda monoclonal antibody that binds domain 4 of protective antigen (PA) of *Bacillus anthracis*. *B. anthracis* is a Gram-positive bacterium found in nature, historically associated with disease in the agricultural setting and later in industrial settings (ragpickers or woolsorters disease)3. Disease can be acquired by the cutaneous, gastrointestinal or inhalational route of entry. Cutaneous anthrax is generally characterized by a local eschar, and responds well to antimicrobial treatment. Gastrointestinal and inhalational anthrax are generally associated with bacteremia, toxemia, and even with antimicrobial treatment are often fatal. *B. anthracis* is considered a CDC Category A potential agent for bioterrorism. Natural disease was very rare in the 20th century, with the exception of two aerosolized exposures. In 1979, accidental release of *B. anthracis* spores from a factory in Sverdlovsk, Russia led to 66 deaths due to inhalational anthrax (IA)4, and in 2001 *B. anthracis* was disseminated through the US mail resulting in 22 cases of anthrax, including 11 cases of cutaneous anthrax and 11 cases of inhalational anthrax (IA). Mortality in the US IA cases was 45% (5/11). In addition to the 11 cases reported in 2001, 2 IA cases were reported in 2006 (Pennsylvania, Scotland) and one IA case in 2008 (London). Overall survival for these cases was 7/14 (50%) in these patients.5
L1023: *B. anthracis* carries two plasmids. The pX01 plasmid encodes for the protective antigen (PA), edema factor (EF) and lethal factor (LF). Plasmid pX02 encodes for the encapsulation B protein. The gene encoding for protective antigen is designated pagA and the gene encoding for capsular protein B is designated capB. EF is a calmodulin-dependent adenylate cyclase that increases cAMP and is responsible for edema. LF is a metalloprotease that cleaves the amino termini of the mitogen-activated protein kinase kinases (MAPKK) 1 and 2, thus inactivating them, and disrupting cellular processes. Based on research conducted by Dr. David Frucht, LT inhibits lymphocyte activation and proliferation, thereby preventing an inflammatory response to the bacterium – this is one proposed mechanism of action to account for the minimal inflammatory response seen in the placebo treated animals in the raxibacumab monotherapy studies described in the Efficacy section.
L1024: 3 Brachman PS. Inhalational anthrax. *Ann NY Acad Sci* 1980; 353:83-93.
L1025: 4 Abramova FA et al. Pathology of inhalational anthrax in 42 cases from the Sverdlovsk outbreak in 1979. *Proc Natl Acad Sci USA* 1993; 90:2291-4.
L1026: 5 http://www.cdc.gov/mmwr/preview/mmwrhtml/mm5510a4.htm (2006 NYC/PA)
L1027: http://www.eurosurveillance.org/ViewArticle.aspx?ArticleId=3025 (2006 Scotland)
L1028: Anaraki et al. Investigations And Control Measures Following A Case Of Inhalational Anthrax In East London In A Drum Maker and Drummer, October 2008. EUROSURVEILLANCE 13(51);1-3. 18 December 2008
(information kindly provided by Dr. Susan McCune, OCTEC)

L1033: ## 3. REVIEW SUMMARY
L1034: A brief summary of the various discipline reviews is presented below, for complete information on these issues, the primary and secondary reviews should be consulted.
L1035: ## 3.1 Product Manufacture and Quality Assessment
L1036: Raxibacumab is expressed in a mouse myeloma cell line (NS0), and the secreted raxibacumab monoclonal antibody is recovered from the cell culture production medium and purified using a series of chromatographic and filtration steps. The clinical product is a single-use liquid product stored at 2-8°C, and it is protected from light until use. Each vial contains 50 mg/mL raxibacumab in 0.13 mg/mL citric acid, 2.8 mg/mL sodium citrate, 10 mg/mL sucrose, 18 mg/mL glycine, and 0.2 mg/mL polysorbate 80, pH 6.5.
L1037: Raxibacumab is supplied at a concentration of 50 mg/mL in a 50 mL sterile single use vial, containing 35.1 mL of liquid formulation per vial. It must be stored between 2°C and 8°C, and is not stable in light. The developmental version of the product was made by the “M10” manufacturing process, key human and animal efficacy studies conducted with the to-be-licensed “M11” process.
L1038: 6 Submission SN 0080, September 19, 2008
L1039: ## 3.1.1 Inspection of Manufacturing Facility and CMC issues
L1040: The HGS production facility was initially inspected in July 2007, at which time the product was considered acceptable for shipment to the SNS. Initial recommendations from plant inspection was that results should not preclude approval, but recommended one PMR and 6 PMCs addressing process validation and more information about endotoxin limits and detection. However, once deficiencies in other areas were identified, based on the review from Patricia Hughes (November 3, 2009) the originally-proposed PMCs and PMR should now be included as deficiencies in the CR letter; these deal with validation of buffers, bioburden control, endotoxin control, limits, container closure, and statibility testing, and endotoxin levels.
L1041: *Comment: Following discussion during the wrap up meeting, DMPQ recommended the bacterial endotoxin specifications in the final product should be listed as a deficiency, and the other items are listed separately as requested studies.*
L1042: In addition, although not part of the HGS application or requirement for approval, an inspection of the Strategic National Stockpile (SNS) has been requested of CDC and is pending.
L1043: ## 3.2 Pharmacology Toxicology
L1044: Preclinical reviews showed specific binding in skeletal muscle and thyroid (both species), endometrium (human only) and breast and prostate (monkey only). These was no binding reported in brain tissue, an observation that is important in context of the evidence of increased brain inflammation, hemorrhage, edema, bacteria and necrosis seen in rabbits and monkeys who had anthrax infection and were treated with raxibacumab.
L1045: *Comment: Based on these results, the toxicology reviewers considered raxibacumab relatively safe, and mentioned the possible target organs for toxicity. Of note, there were no gross or histopathological changes reported in the CNS of the monkeys in the toxicity study.*
L1046: ## 3.3 Microbiology
L1047: Raxibacumab binds protective antigen (PA) produced by the Ames, Sterne, and Vollum strains. Therefore, it is expected that raxibacumab prevents the binding of PA to cells, and interferes with the ability of PA to form heptamers on the cell surface, creating a pore through which EF and LF can access the interior of the cell, resulting in cell damage. In efficacy studies, diagnosis relied on a positive blood culture because there were some concerns about the qualitative electroluminescence assay for PA.
L1048: ## 3.3.1 Mechanism of Action of Raxibacumab
L1049: Raxibacumab binds to domain 4 of protective antigen (PA) with high affinity and inhibits binding of PA to anthrax toxin receptors ATR1 and CMG2 on cells. Because domain 4 is also the portion of PA that binds to cells, the domain is not available once PA is already bound to cell surface, therefore raxibacumab only binds free PA. Whether it binds PA on spore surface is unknown, however PA is expressed on the surface of spores.
L1050: The schematic that summarizes the sequence of events how PA binds to the cell surface, is cleaved, forms a heptamer pore and allows LF and EF to enter, forming LT and EF, and acting on MAPPKs and cAMP, to disrupt signal transduction and cause edema, respectively, is presented below.
L1051: Figure from Dr. Frucht's presentation at the October 27, 2009 Advisory Committee meeting
L1052: ## 3.3.2 Mechanism of Action of Raxibacumab vs. Antimicrobials
L1053: The mechanism of action of raxibacumab differs from small molecule antimicrobials:
L1054: - Raxibacumab targets a secreted toxin that causes immunosuppression and directly damages host tissues.
- Ciprofloxacin and Levofloxacin (approved for anthrax post-exposure prophylaxis) inhibit DNA gyrase and topoisomerase IV activity and are bactericidal.
- Doxycycline (approved for anthrax treatment) inhibits protein synthesis and is bacteriostatic.
- Penicillin (approved for anthrax treatment) inhibits cell wall synthesis and is bactericidal.
L1055: ## 3.4 Clinical Pharmacology
L1056: The proposed dose for treatment was 40 mg/kg, and while HGS' study results supported the dose, the Division of Scientific Investigation determined that there were problems with the results of the bioanalytical assay inspection (Review dated October 7, 2009) and therefore HGS was asked to revise their procedures, correct the deficiencies, and re-assay sample to address these findings. Depending on the results, additional studies may be needed.
L1057: When the DSI inspection deficiencies were brought to the attention of the review team, there was discussion of cancelling the October 27 2009 AC meeting, but after discussion with OND and CDER the decision was made that the AC should continue, and animal efficacy models discussed. An update to the AC briefing document was issued summarizing the situation and explaining that the FDA presentations and questions would cover the efficacy and safety of the animal results, and principles of determining a human dose based on animal studies, but that FDA would not present PK data, or ask a question regarding licensure. HGS stated they were confident in their PK data and presented the information at the AC.
L1058: The principles of determining an effective human dose are:
L1059: - Determine a regimen in animals that is safe and effective in the species chosen for the indication studied.
- Determine the corresponding pharmacokinetic exposure (AUC, C_{max}).
- Determine a dosing regimen in humans that will give similar or greater exposure to that observed in the animal.
L1060: The inability to discuss the PK data limited the FDA's ability to explain the doses of ciprofloxacin administered to monkeys and levofloxacin given to rabbits in the two combination studies: monkey study 789-G923702 and rabbit study 781-G923701. In her review, Dr Bergman concludes that levofloxacin dosing in rabbits at 50mg/kg by gavage q24h and that ciprofloxacin dosing in monkeys of 75mg bid by gavage were appropriately humanized before these studies were started.
L1061: The regimen in monkeys: intragastric ciprofloxacin at a dose of 75 mg or intragastric placebo (sterile water for injection), according to treatment group assignment. This was followed by intragastric ciprofloxacin or placebo doses administered every 12 hours (q12h) for a total of six doses (three days of treatment). The recommended oral ciprofloxacin dose in humans for post-exposure of inhalational anthrax is 500 mg q12h for 60 days. An oral dose of 500 mg ciprofloxacin in humans yields a C_{max} of 2.4 \mug/mL. In the current study, the mean ciprofloxacin C_{max} values following the first intragastric dose of 75 mg in monkeys with and without raxibacumab co-administration were 1.12 and 0.675 \mug/mL, respectively. Thus, the ciprofloxacin dose of 75 mg in monkeys was not equivalent to the human oral dose of 500 mg approved for post-exposure inhalational anthrax. Ciprofloxacin administered at the labeled oral dose of 500 mg in humans is expected to achieve higher exposures than those observed in this study conducted in monkeys with inhalational anthrax.
L1062: The regimen in rabbits: intragastric levofloxacin 50 mg/kg or placebo (sterile water for injection), according to treatment group assignment. Intragastric 50 mg/kg levofloxacin or placebo doses were then administered every 24 hours (qd) for a total of 3 doses (3 days of treatment). The recommended oral levofloxacin dose in humans for post-exposure of inhalational anthrax is 500 mg q24h for 60 days. An oral dose of 500 mg levofloxacin in humans yields a C_{max} of 5.1 \mug/mL. In the current study, mean levofloxacin C_{max} values following intragastric dosing of 50 mg/kg rabbits with and without raxibacumab co-administration were slightly lower than the human C_{max} with a 500 mg oral dose (mean C_{max} range in rabbits was approximately 3.94 to 4.98 \mug/mL). Thus, levofloxacin administered at the labeled oral dose of 500 mg in humans is expected to achieve slightly higher exposures than those observed in this study conducted in rabbits with inhalational anthrax.
L1063: ## 3.4 Division of Scientific Investigation (DSI) findings
L1064: Initially the inspections of efficacy studies (monkey Study 724-G005829, rabbit Study 682-G005758) were acceptable in 2008; brain lesions were identified and promptly brought to the attention of DSPTP.
L1065: During the August and September 2009 inspection of the [REDACTED] facilities where human studies C1201-1064 and C1201-1063, minor deviations were found but these were judged to have negligible impact on the results. Drs Thompson and Purohit-Sheth determined that studies C1063 and C1064 were acceptable (NAI letter September 14, 2009).
L1066: The bioanalytical assays done at HGS for human study C1201-1064 and C1201-1063 and at [REDACTED] (b) (4) for ciprofloxacin in humans raised issues about the acceptability of the results and reliability of human clinical pharmacology data. These findings were brought to the attention of the review team around October 20, and resulted in an update being issued to the AC members and a revision to the FDA presentations at the AC meeting, as well as omission of any discussion of clinical pharmacology issues (See also 3.4 Clinical Pharmacology).

L1087: ## 3.7 Animal Rule7
L1088: Because inhalational anthrax is exceedingly rare, is not acquired naturally, and is highly fatal, intentional exposure would be unethical. Therefore, efficacy data on raxibacumab was obtained from animal models of infection, and HGS requested approval of the BLA under Subpart H of the regulations 21 CFR 601.90, *Approval of Biological Products When Human Efficacy Studies Are Not Ethical or Feasible*. This rule applies when adequate and well-controlled studies in humans cannot be ethically conducted and field efficacy studies are not feasible. In such circumstances, products intended to reduce or prevent serious or life-threatening conditions may be approved for marketing based on evidence of effectiveness derived from appropriate studies in animals and additional supporting data.
L1089: To obtain guidance whether approval should be based on the demonstration of superiority of monoclonal antibody over placebo or whether animal efficacy studies should also show the contribution of monoclonal over antimicrobial to survival, this issue was presented at a Regulatory Briefing in October 2006. Following presentations and discussions, the senior leadership group recommended that statistical superiority must be shown of the monoclonal over placebo, and studies evaluating the monoclonal and antimicrobials should be requested. However, recognizing the challenge to conducting these studies, the group did not recommend that approval be withheld if an additive effect of each component could not be demonstrated. Furthermore, it was noted that the two products have different mechanisms of actions.
L1090: The animal rule further provides four elements that must be met for animal studies of efficacy to support approval under this rule. HGS conducted the four efficacy studies summarized above, and demonstrated that raxibacumab is superior to placebo in two species, but did not demonstrate that the monoclonal offered an added benefit over antimicrobials in the two studies where this was tested. However, the information provided by HGS in the preclinical, natural history, and efficacy studies can be used to address the elements below. In addition, before DSI inspections identified deficiencies in the bioanalytical assay, HGS had provided PK data to address the fourth element.
L1091: *(1) There is a reasonably well-understood pathophysiological mechanism of the toxicity of the substance and its prevention or substantial reduction by the product;*
L1092: 7 Animal Rule published May 31, 2002, titled Evidence Needed to Demonstrate Effectiveness of New Drugs When Human Efficacy Studies Are Not Ethical or Feasible, Biologics 21 CFR 601.90 (Subpart H), Drugs 21 CFR 314.600 (Subpart I)
L1093: Studies evaluating PA and raxibacumab were conducted, and the information is summarized in section 3.3 Microbiology, showing that raxibacumab blocks the binding of PA to the cell surface receptors, thereby blocking the cascade by which LT and ET are formed and interfere with normal cellular function, leading to edema and death.
L1094: In rat lethal toxin infusion model, raxibacumab prevented mortality compared to no treatment, supporting the direct toxic effect of LT in the rat model, and demonstrating that raxibacumab prevented mortality due to LT.
L1095: (2) *The effect is demonstrated in more than one animal species expected to react with a response predictive for humans, unless the effect is demonstrated in a single animal species that represents a sufficiently well-characterized animal model for predicting the response in humans;*
L1096: Efficacy studies were done in rabbits and monkeys, both of which appear to share similarities in disease pathogenesis and outcome compared to humans. In these animal models two doses were tested. In both species the 40 mg/kg was superior to placebo; in the monkey the 20 mg/kg dose was also superior to placebo.
L1097: (3) *The animal study endpoint is clearly related to the desired benefit in humans, generally the enhancement of survival or prevention of major morbidity; and*
L1098: In both humans and animals, the desired benefit is survival, and this endpoint was evaluated in all four animal studies.
L1099: (4) *The data or information on the pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics of the product or other relevant data or information, in animals and humans, allows selection of an effective dose in humans.*
L1100: The 40 mg/kg dose presented by HGS was also considered to be the appropriate dose in humans, however, the DSI inspection findings have put further discussion of the PK data on hold.
L1101: The four elements do not specifically address the need to show a benefit over existing therapy, however, the preamble to the animal rule states:
L1102: “We have decided to eliminate the requirement that ‘products would be expected to provide meaningful therapeutic benefits to patients over existing treatments,’ as well as the limitation that the toxic agent be ‘without a proven treatment’ (proposed §§ 314.600 and 601.60). Recent events involving the multiple exposures to anthrax in our population, and deaths resulting from those infections, have indicated a need for a wide range of therapeutic options that, in some instances, might be inappropriately limited by requiring new products to have a therapeutic benefit over existing treatments, or to be used only in the absence of a proven treatment. Availability of a variety of drug and biological products is important because, for example, patient recipients may be allergic to one product and require another, may be intolerant of a product because of side effects, or may respond more favorably to one product than another. We also believe that a wider variety of therapeutic choices will limit potential problems with availability, accessibility, and distribution of products. We have modified the final rule to address these concerns and help ensure the availability of more than one therapeutic option.”
L1103: The language in the preamble portion of the rule has been interpreted differently by reviewers for raxibacumab. One interpretation (shared by this reviewer) is that under the animal rule, demonstration of superiority can serve as basis of approval without the need to demonstrate an added benefit – a study to demonstrate such a benefit, however, should be requested as a post-marketing commitment. During development, FDA did ask HGS to conduct a study examining raxibacumab plus antimicrobials, but the treatment model yielded 95% to 100% survival following antimicrobials, and further animal development is needed to more closely parallel the outcome seen during 2001 (55% survival). On the other hand, the preamble can be interpreted to mean that if the studies are designed so that the “standard treatment” arm becomes the de facto “placebo” arm, then efficacy of the monoclonal would be demonstrated by showing that it is superior to the de facto “placebo” arm. Although the antimicrobial and raxibacumab arm did not show a benefit over antimicrobials, one piece of information was gained from this study. In the rabbit study, all animals were necropsied and brains examined – there were **no brain lesions** seen in any of the raxibacumab plus antimicrobial treated animals, providing initial evidence that suggests that raxibacumab in the setting on anthrax may not be toxic to the brain, albeit in this study it was used in combination with antimicrobials.
L1104: The animal rule also requires that products approved require
L1105: - **Postmarketing studies**such as field studies, to verify and describe the biological product's clinical benefit and to assess its safety when used as indicated when such studies are feasible and ethical
L1106: A protocol has been requested and will be submitted by HGS
L1107: - **Approval of product with restrictions to ensure safe use**e.g., certain facilities, practitioners, procedures, recordkeeping
L1108: This is an intravenous product intended for the treatment of a potentially fatal disease, and there are no safety issues that would preclude making the product immediately available, therefore, no restrictions are anticipated at this time.
L1109: - **Information to be provided to patient recipients**Labeling that explains the product was approved based on animal efficacy studies
- Indication, directions for use, safety information, other relevant information
- Must be available to patient prior to administration, if possible
L1110: Patients labeling information was proposed in the original labeling and will be addressed during the resubmission.

However, put in context of the entire study and pathophysiology, one also needs to consider that there was a significant benefit in terms of survival in the monotherapy studies:
L1114: - Survival was 0% 25% and 35% in rabbits at 0, 20, and 40 mg/kg of raxibacumab
- Survival was 0% 44% and 69% in monkeys at 0, 20, and 40 mg/kg of raxibacumab

L1121: Referring to the table of histologic findings, the animals in the placebo group are likely to have died because of systemic effects (lung, cardiac) while animals that were treated were beginning to show a systemic response (less pathology systemically) but perhaps because of the inability of raxibacumab to gain access to brain tissue, bacteria continued to proliferate in this protected site, and there is evidence of an inflammatory response to the bacteria. Fundamentally, however, the mortality in these animals was attributable to anthrax, with probably variable progression of disease in different organs, depending probably on treatment and dose. The idea that raxibacumab may be toxic to the brain has been raised, and may be considered, however, the explanation that LT blocks T cell and B cell proliferation, and PML activation, and this effect is then blocked by raxibacumab once it binds PA, may be an alternative explanation for this finding. As noted, the apparent dose effect (severity of brain lesions is lower in the 40 mg/kg arm than 20 mg/kg arm), also would suggest an efficacy component to this finding.
L1122: In the monkey/ciprofloxacin study, only the animals that died were evaluated grossly and histologically. The placebo animals has low grade bacteria present in CNS, no ciprofloxacin treated
L1123: monkey died. Two animals died in the ciprofloxacin/raxibacumab arm. The one that died of gavage accident had no brain lesions, while the one that died of anthrax had CNS lesions consistent with anthrax.
L1124: In the rabbit/levofloxacin study, placebo treated animals had low grade bacteria in the CNS, one levofloxacin treated rabbit that died of anthrax and had brain lesions, the levofloxacin treated rabbits that lived had no CNS abnormalities. One levofloxacin /raxibacumab treated rabbit died of a gavage accident after having bacteremia and starting treatment, but had no brain findings. The rabbits that survived had no pathological findings in the brain on autopsy.
L1125: *Comment: Therefore, preliminary evidence from rabbits and one monkey suggest that animals that survive treatment with raxibacumab plus antimicrobial do not develop CNS lesions.*
L1126: *Given that bacterial meningitis is generally a symptomatic, rapidly progressive condition in the absence of appropriate treatment, the likelihood is that surviving animals have normal brain histology. HGS reported that there were no abnormal behaviors in the monkeys that survived and were observed for up to 3 months before being returned to the colony.*
L1127: The reason for the brain lesions is unknown and has not been further investigated at this stage of development. Monoclonal antibodies generally are not known to penetrate the CNS, and it is not even clear whether they can penetrate the CNS when there is meningitis. In the case of raxibacumab, CNS levels have not been measured in either infected animals or as part of routine toxicology studies in normal animals. However, given that there was no evidence of inflammation, hemorrhage or edema in the toxicology studies, the effect is probably not independent to raxibacumab but in some way represents a disease/drug interaction. Tissues taken at necropsy were not stained to see whether raxibacumab penetrated the CNS.
L1128: ## 3.8.3 Hypotheses regarding the CNS lesions include:
L1129: ## (1) Increased Duration of Survival
L1130: Increased duration of survival in the animals that have CNS findings: various analyses of time to death in animals that died was done and showed no statistical differences among the arms. Numerically, however, the animals that had the more severe CNS lesions lived 4 days, while those without severe lesions lived less than 3 days, but only one placebo monkey and no placebo rabbits fell into this category. Therefore, this hypothesis would need to be further studied.

L1144: *Comment: In his consult, Dr. Walton suggests one hypothesis that anthrax may be a rapidly progressive disease and significant progression of CNS involvement may be seen within a few hours, terminally. To that end, it is intriguing that the median duration of survival is the shortest in the placebo arm (3.3 days, 2.7 days) where animals had on average less severe lesions, and longest in the 20 mg/kg arm (3.9 days and 3.0 days) where animals had on average most severe lesions, and intermediate in the 40 mg/kg group (3.7 day and 2.9 days) also consistent with the findings. On the other hand the mean values do not show a similar patter. Given all these are post-hoc analyses, they should be viewed with caution.*
L1145: ## (2) LT causes Immunosuppression
L1146: The other hypothesis was offered by Dr. Frucht based on his research and is related to the immunosuppressive activity of LT (LT inhibits proliferation and function of T cells, B cells and PMLs), and effective treatment may play a part in reversing this inhibition (e.g., monoclonal, antimicrobials).
L1147: Also noteworthy, however, is that LT is considered to cause circulatory shock by direct effects on endothelial cells, vascular “leakiness,” and cause cardiac toxicity (by endothelial necrosis, mitochondrial and myofilament degeneration). This may be relevant to the mechanism of death in the placebo animals which had more systemic anthrax present and less severe anthrax lesions in the brain.
L1148: ## 3.8.4 PA and disease
L1149: PA levels detectable in animal correlated with survival or death. Surviving animals had an early rise followed by decline over 7-9 days peak and then drop, while animals that died had a rise-plateau-rise as PA levels continued to escalate as show in the figure below.
L1150: HGS slide CC-47 presented at the AC meeting
L1151: ## (3) Toxicity of Raxibacumab
L1152: The question was raised whether the CNS findings represent toxicity due to raxibacumab. This is not supported by the preclinical and human safety data in uninfected subjects. Raxibacumab did not bind or show toxicity in brain tissue. No CNS events in humans were noted -- the incidence of headaches was similar between raxibacumab and placebo arms, the one patient with schizophrenia had a pre-existing diagnosis. The likely explanation would seem to be related to a drug/disease interaction, but further data are needed.
L1153: ## (4) Other Mechanisms
L1154: The role of cytokines, chemokines, antigen/antibody complexes may be considered, although no data to confirm or refute this is available. CSF analysis or immunohistochemical staining of brain tissue for raxibacumab was not performed.
L1155: ## (5) Consult from DNP
L1156: DNP met with DSPTP for an informative discussion of the studies and commented that the precise mechanism of the brain lesions is not clear, but monoclonals are considered unable to penetrate the CNS.8 Whether there is some drug disease interaction that changes the blood brain barrier characteristics and allows more bacteria and raxibacumab to penetrate, and somehow influences the severe inflammation and edema, is not known. As noted in the DNP consult, in the absence of information, it is not possible to determine whether the brain findings are relevant. DNP recommended that animal studies be repeated, all animals examined to see whether survivors had similar lesions, and histochemical staining of brain tissue be requested to evaluate distribution of raxibacumab.
L1157: ## (6) Consult from Dr Walton
L1158: 8 See consult reviews by Barbara Wilcox and Eric Bastings, and Louis Freed 8/18/09
L1159: Dr. Walton reviewed the information from preclinical, animal efficacy, and human studies and noted that a direct toxicity due to the antibody was unlikely given the brain cross-reactivity studies were negative, suggested that the meninges in such studies be examined if this had not already been done. Absence of cross-reactivity makes direct toxicity very unlikely. The most likely drug disease interaction is insufficient treatment effect due to raxibacumab access to the brain, and did note that the survival benefit should not be dismissed because of the CNS findings.
L1160: *Comment: Although the mechanism of brain findings in treated animals is not elucidated, CNS lesions were not seen in rabbits that survive treatment with antimicrobial and raxibacumab, or antimicrobial alone. Although there was concern articulated by some reviewers that surviving animals may have brain lesions, this is probably unlikely but not proven; survivors who received only raxibacumab have not been sacrificed and brain examined histologically.*
L1161: ## 3.9 Raxibacumab Treatment Doses and Timing
L1162: Although survival was significantly higher with 40 mg/kg raxibacumab compared to placebo in rabbits (35% vs 0%) and in monkeys (69% vs. 0%), the question came up whether survival could be increased if ever higher doses of raxibacumab were tested. One reason for this suggestion was because the lesions seen in the brains were more frequent and severe in the lower dose of 20 mg/kg than the higher dose of 40 mg/kg. This pattern suggests a dose response seen, and raises the question whether a dose of 60 mg/kg or 80 mg/kg may be even more effective. The animal toxicology monkey study found a dose of 120 mg/kg safe for further testing; however, doses above 40 mg/kg have not been tested in humans and therefore would need to be tested. Whether these higher doses would be safe in humans is not known, however, given that this is a fully humanized antibody infused intravenously, it is possible that toxicity would be similar to what was seen at 40 mg/kg (e.g., rash), although it is also possible that infusion time would need to be prolonged beyond the 2 hours 15 minutes used in human volunteer studies to minimize any infusion related adverse events.
L1163: Raxibacumab was also evaluated in post exposure prophylaxis studies which showed that there was a dose response (40 mg/kg most effective compared to lower doses) and a timing effect (raxibacumab 40 mg/kg given pre exposure or within 12 hours of exposure resulted in 100% survival) whereas delay of raxibacumab in rabbits of 24 and 36 hours resulted in about 45% survival.
L1164: HGS slide CC-66 presented at the AC meeting
L1165: HGS slide CC-69 presented at the AC meeting
L1166: Interestingly, the delay also correlated with the appearance of bacteremia and temperature elevations, which are considered evidence that the animal is infected (i.e., the spores present in lungs have germinated and become vegetative cells which have gained access to blood stream and are capable of producing and releasing PA, EF, LF).

L1181: TNA titers indicative of immunity developed. L1209: ## 5. DISCUSSION:
L1210: ## 5.1 Clinical Considerations in Treatment
L1211: ## 5.1.1 *Infections where antimicrobial and antitoxin therapy is used*
L1212: Given that the mechanism of action of antimicrobial and antitoxin is different, the likelihood they would interfere with each other is unlikely. Small molecule antimicrobials and antitoxin are used is in the treatment of a number of diseases:
L1213: - **Tetanus (*Clostridium tetani*):** antibiotics (e.g., metronidazole, penicillin), tetanus immunoglobulin (TIG) and tetanus toxoid
- **Botulinum (*Clostridium botulinum*):** botulinum antitoxin, antibiotics (e.g., penicillin, metronidazole)
- **Diphtheria (*Corynebacterium diphtheriae*):** antibiotics (e.g., erythromycin, penicillin), diphtheria antitoxin
L1214: The effectiveness of these agents is stated to be greatest if administered early in the course of disease.9 10 Supportive measures are also needed.
L1215: ## 5.1.2 *Supportive measures in anthrax treatment*
L1216: In animal studies, no supportive treatment was given in addition to treatment with raxibacumab and antimicrobials. In humans, however, patients were admitted to intensive care unit and supported as necessary and received multiple simultaneous interventions including BP and respiratory support, fluid drainage, dialysis, and other measures.
L1217: In the publication by Jernigan,11 patients had pleural effusion, often requiring chest tube placement for removal of fluid. In the absence of such measures, it is possible that death could occur early due
L1218: 9 http://www.medicinenet.com/diphtheria/page3.htm
L1219: 10 Rob Roy MacGregor. *Corynebacterium diphtheriae* (Chapter 193) in Principles and Practice of Infectious Diseases. Mandell, Douglas and Bennett, Churchill Livingstone 2000, fifth edition.
L1220: to for example due to the direct toxin mediated damage to the host, before the bacteria could be killed and toxin neutralized. In contrast, in humans, with supportive care in addition to antimicrobials, patients survived following hospitalizations ranging up to 3 weeks (Case 2).
L1221: ## 5.1.3 *Animal Efficacy Studies*
L1222: Superiority of raxibacumab over placebo has been demonstrated. The rates were 35% in rabbits and 69% in monkeys. Evaluation of higher doses should be undertaken to see whether survival rate may increase.
L1223: Combination studies were conducted but the success rates of antimicrobials were 95-100%, exceeding the 55% seen in patients during the events of 2001. Additional model development is needed before repeat combination studies. Work at the NIAID to date has led to preliminary models with survival rate in the 10-20% based on antimicrobial administration in rabbits at 96 hours, and rates around 25% in monkeys based on administration of partially protective ciprofloxacin doses. The practical considerations that impact the design and conduct of these studies, and need to be kept in mind when designing these studies, are:
L1224: - BL4, BL3 laboratory
- Working with biologic agent
- Animal use, care, &amp; handling issues
- Extensive real time diagnostics needed to guide initiation of therapy for **Treatment studies**
- Individualized intervention (24/7 monitoring)
- Duration of intervention and follow-up
- Animal availability (NHP but in rabbits sensitive to veterinary source, animal age, etc)
- Number of animals that can be studied in a cohort12 monkeys per group
- 26 rabbits per group

L1245: ## Executive Summary
L1246: On the basis of recommendations from the FDA's Division of Scientific Investigations' audit, the Division of Special Pathogen and Transplant Products will take a Complete Response action on BLA 125,349 (raxibacumab) on November 13, 2009.
L1247: The primary basis for this decision is the result of deficiencies in the analytical procedures used to collect pharmacokinetic data for raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin. A critical element of the Animal Rule which must be addressed for product approval is that "data or information on the kinetics and pharmacodynamics of the product or other relevant data or information, in animals and humans, allows selection of an effective dose in humans". The inability to substantiate the reliability of the pharmacokinetic data generated for raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin in humans to provide the necessary link between the animal models and humans by the action date resulted in the Division's decision to take a Complete Response action.
L1248: A Complete Response (CR) action will be taken by FDA on the goal date of November 13, 2009 for BLA 125,349 (raxibacumab) as a result of analytical deficiencies identified by the FDA Division of Scientific Investigations' audit of the clinical investigation sites for this application.
L1249: This addendum to the full Clinical review of raxibacumab summarizes the key clinical points and recommendations from the expert panel discussion at the Raxibacumab Anti-infective Drug Committee Advisory Committee meeting, and from the Division of Scientific Investigations' audit, the latter of which resulted in the CR action.
L1250: Please refer to the Divisional Director's review and the issued CR letter for additional details. Please refer to the OC/DMPQ review for details regarding the compliance/manufacturing deficiencies.
L1251: ## 1. Advisory Committee Recommendations - Clinical
L1252: At the Anti-infective Drug Committee Advisory Committee convened on October 27, 2009 to discuss the data on raxibacumab's efficacy in animal models and its safety in animals and human volunteers, the panel recommended additional information be obtained to evaluate added benefit or possible antagonism of raxibacumab on antimicrobials in animal models. It was agreed that the unanticipated high efficacy of antibiotics alone in the combination studies limited the determination of any added benefit of raxibacumab in studies submitted in the BLA. It was further discussed that such information was necessary because of anticipated conditions of use in the setting of a bioterrorism event, namely that antimicrobials are likely to be administered in the first-line treatment of inhalational anthrax unless contraindicated and therefore the effects of
L1253: combination use should be evaluated. Given that an animal model of approximately 50% decreased antibiotic efficacy to replicate the antibiotic efficacy observed in humans in the 2001 US attacks has not been developed, and questions remain regarding feasibility of a study demonstrating statistically significant added benefit of antitoxin treatment to a 50% efficacy antibiotic alone model (number of animals per arm ranging from 40 up to &gt;300 depending on the effect of raxibacumab), details of the design and conduct of such study will require additional discussions. The Applicant should be required to submit a protocol of the added benefit study pending the establishment of an appropriate animal model for evaluation of added benefit.
L1254: The Applicant will also be required to conduct two additional clinical studies. The first study will be to investigate the effect of raxibacumab on the central nervous system. Similar to the added benefit study, details of the design and conduct of this study will require additional discussion between FDA and the Applicant. Second, to fulfill a requirement of the Animal Rule, the Applicant will also be asked to submit the field study protocol for review. While a study synopsis was submitted to FDA on November 5, 2009, a protocol for such a study will be requested as a Complete Response issue.
L1255: ## 2. Division of Scientific Investigations' audit
L1256: In October 2009, the Division of Special Pathogen and Transplant Products (DSPTP) was made aware of the results of the Division of Scientific Investigations (DSI) audit of the clinical and analytical portions of studies HGS1021-C1063 and HGS1021-C1064. Upon inspection of the bioanalytical sites responsible for analysis of serum raxibacumab and plasma ciprofloxacin concentrations in humans, DSI reported several deficiencies in the analytical procedures used for both drugs. These findings raised concern about the reliability of the pharmacokinetic data generated for raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin in humans.
L1257: Upon review of these findings, the Clinical Pharmacology team has recommended the following:
L1258: - Adequate revision of the analytical procedures to address these inspection findings.
- Re-assay of the pharmacokinetic samples from human studies HGS1021-C1063, HGS1021-C1064, and HGS1021-C1069 using the revised procedures.
- Re-calculation of the pharmacokinetic parameters.
L1259: Similarly, the plasma pharmacokinetic samples obtained from HGS1021-C1064 and the cynomolgus monkey study 789-G923702 for determining ciprofloxacin concentrations should be re-assayed using a revised analytical method that
L1260: adequately addresses the DSI findings. The pharmacokinetic parameters for ciprofloxacin should be re-calculated.
L1261: Lastly, as the pharmacokinetic data generated from the animal efficacy studies in New Zealand White rabbits and cynomolgus macaque monkeys used the same bioanalytical procedures as that for the human studies, FDA has also recommended repeat assay of the pharmacokinetic samples from animal studies 682-G005758 and 724-G005829 using the revised procedures followed by re-calculation of the pharmacokinetic parameters for raxibacumab.

L1270: ## 1. Introduction
L1271: Inhalational anthrax due to *Bacillus anthracis* is a disease characterized by bacillary replication in mediastinal lymph nodes leading to septicemia with accumulation and dissemination of bacterial toxins to various organs. In the absence of adequate treatment, it is a highly fatal disease. Several drugs in the penicillin and tetracycline class are approved for the treatment of anthrax due to *B. anthracis* and include penicillin G procaine, penicillin G potassium, and penicillin G sodium as well as doxycycline, doxycycline calcium, and doxycycline hyclate. Tetracycline, demeclocycline hydrochloride and minocycline hydrochloride are recommended in situations when penicillin is contraindicated.
L1272: Antimicrobial treatment is directed at eradicating the bacterium. Antimicrobials, however, have no direct activity against the toxins of *B. anthracis*: lethal toxin (LT) and edema toxin (ET), the key pathogenic factors in anthrax disease responsible for the signs, symptoms, and high rates of mortality in infected individuals. These toxins are not preformed, but rather are assembled on the cell membrane of the host target cells after *B. anthracis* elaborates individual components of these toxins: protective antigen (PA), the binding moiety (1), lethal factor (LF), and edema factor (EF). The PA moiety of anthrax toxins binds the anthrax toxin receptors (ATR or CMG2) on host cells to initiate a cascade of molecular events that manifest as clinical disease. There are currently no approved therapies against anthrax toxins.
L1273: Raxibacumab is a first in class recombinant humanized (IgG1λ) monoclonal antibody to *Bacillus anthracis* protective antigen (PA). Raxibacumab blocks the binding of PA to cell surfaces and prevents the anthrax toxins from entering host target cells and inducing their cytotoxic effects.
L1274: The proposed indication is treatment of inhalational anthrax, and the proposed treatment regimen for raxibacumab is 40 mg/kg administered as a single 2 hour 15 minutes IV infusion. Because of infusion reactions seen during drug development, pretreatment with diphenhydramine is recommended.
L1275: Early in the development program the Applicant requested Fast Track designation for raxibacumab, which was granted on August 15, 2003 for the investigation of raxibacumab for “*post-exposure prophylaxis and adjunctive therapy of inhalation anthrax disease, and for lessening the severity of inhalational anthrax disease, including disease caused by antibiotic resistant organisms*”. Although the study reports were being submitted to the IND prior to BLA filing, no formal rolling BLA submission was pursued by the Applicant.
L1276: The Applicant also requested Orphan Drug designation for raxibacumab; the request was granted on November 12, 2003 for “*the treatment of anthrax*”.
L1277: As inhalational anthrax is an extremely rare naturally-occurring disease in humans and intentional research exposure would be unethical, efficacy data on raxibacumab was obtained from animal models of anthrax infection, with the approval sought under Subpart H of the
L1278: 1 Inglesby TV, O'Toole T, Henderson DA et al. Anthrax as a biological weapon, 2002 : Updated recommendations for management. JAMA 2002 ;287(17) :2236-52.
L1279: regulations 21 CFR 601 (“Approval of biological products when human efficacy studies are not ethical or feasible”). The Animal Rule, published in 2002 by the FDA (“New Drug and Biological Drug Products: Evidence Needed to Demonstrate Effectiveness of New Drugs When Human Efficacy Studies Are Not Ethical or Feasible”) provides a regulatory mechanism to accept efficacy from animal models when adequate and well-controlled studies in humans cannot be ethically conducted and field efficacy studies are not feasible. To obtain further guidance on whether approval should be based on the demonstration of superiority of monoclonal antitoxin over placebo, or whether animal efficacy studies should also show the contribution of monoclonal to antimicrobial efficacy in survival, the issue was presented at a Regulatory Briefing meeting in October 2006. The group recommended that statistical superiority of the monoclonal over placebo must be demonstrated, and studies evaluating the monoclonal and antimicrobials should be requested. However, recognizing the challenge in conducting these studies, the group did not recommend withholding approval if an additive effect of raxibacumab to antimicrobial efficacy could not be demonstrated. Furthermore, it was noted that the two products, i.e. antimicrobials and raxibacumab have different mechanisms of actions.
L1280: The Applicant's development program included studies showing that raxibacumab binds PA of *Bacillus anthracis* (Ames, Sterne, and Vollum strains tested) with high affinity and inhibits PA binding to the anthrax toxin receptor (ATR), on host cells; thereby, protecting the cells from anthrax toxin-mediated injury. Proof-of-concept studies with raxibacumab demonstrated a survival advantage in the rat lethal toxin infusion model, and in several pre-exposure and post-exposure prophylaxis animal model studies. The raxibacumab development program also included identification and characterization of the natural history of anthrax disease in animal models of infection (New Zealand White rabbits, cynomologus macaques), and these animal models were used to evaluate the efficacy of raxibacumab in the treatment of inhalational anthrax. Four key animal studies were conducted. These included 2 studies of raxibacumab monotherapy compared to placebo in the treatment of inhalational anthrax (rabbits, monkeys) and 2 studies of raxibacumab plus antimicrobials (levofloxacin in rabbits, ciprofloxacin in monkeys) in the treatment of inhalational anthrax.
L1281: Efficacy studies were conducted in animal models of anthrax infection because naturally-occurring inhalational anthrax infection in humans is rare to nonexistent and intentional exposure of healthy human volunteers to aerosolized *B. anthracis* spores for research purposes is unethical. In pivotal animal studies of raxibacumab monotherapy, raxibacumab conferred a statistically significant survival benefit over placebo in both monkey and rabbit animal models of inhalational anthrax. When raxibacumab was studied in combination with either levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin and compared to antimicrobial alone, there was no statistically significant difference between active treatment groups. These latter studies were not powered to detect added benefit of raxibacumab over antimicrobials alone. In addition, the animal models themselves were limited by the high (&gt;90%) efficacy of antimicrobial monotherapy.
L1282: Raxibacumab safety was evaluated in a panel of preclinical studies and in 326 normal volunteers that received proposed 40mg/kg therapeutic dose of raxibacumab. Upon histological examination of tissues from the non-survivor animals in pivotal animal studies it was noted that, although, all animals had evidence of anthrax disease in organs examined, the pattern of histopathologic changes was different between placebo and raxibacumab treated animals. While in placebo animals moderate to marked bacteria,
L1283: hemorrhage, inflammation, and necrosis were more frequently observed in the visceral organs including lungs, mediastinum, spleen and liver, in raxibacumab treated non-survivors the most prominent pathology findings were primarily localized to the brain. Such difference in the frequency and the severity of the pathologic findings in the brain between placebo and raxibacumab treated non-survivors across both animal species could not be fully explained by the duration of survival or duration of bacteremia prior to death. Direct CNS toxicity of raxibacumab appears to be unlikely in lieu of negative tissue cross-reactivity studies and favorable safety profile of raxibacumab in animal toxicology studies and in healthy human volunteers. While drug-disease interaction could not be excluded, in the context of survival benefit offered by raxibacumab and the knowledge that hemorrhagic meningitis is a pathognomonic feature of systemic anthrax disease reported in up to 66% of historical clinical cases, 50-60% in NHP and in 30% of rabbit animal models described in the scientific literature the clinical significance of this finding remains unclear.
L1284: Initial human safety studies showed that raxibacumab was associated with the development of infusion reactions (primarily rash); therefore, subsequent studies in human subjects and monkey efficacy studies included diphenhydramine pretreatment, and premedication with diphenhydramine is recommended in the proposed labeling. Immunogenicity was evaluated for this intravenous product and the results suggest a low risk for immunogenicity.
L1285: ## 2. Background
L1286: Because inhalational anthrax is a rare naturally occurring disease (occupational exposure has been eradicated, intentional exposure is not ethical), efficacy of new products for the treatment of inhalational anthrax need to be derived from animal model of infection studies. In January 2009, the Agency published a draft *Guidance for Industry: Animal Models – Essential Elements to Address Efficacy Under the Animal Rule*,2 which provides information on the development of animal models to study efficacy, including the critical characteristics of an animal model that need to be addressed under the Animal Rule. For example, these elements include the characteristics of the agent that causes the disease (in this case *Bacillus anthracis*), the host susceptibility and response to the agent, the natural history of the disease in humans and comparability in animal models, the trigger and timing of intervention, the characteristics of the medical intervention, and study design considerations.
L1287: All animal studies subject to this rule must be conducted in accordance with preexisting requirements under the good laboratory practices.
L1288: Safety evaluation of products is not addressed in the Animal Rule. Biological products (e.g., monoclonals) evaluated for effectiveness under subpart H of part 601 for are expected to be evaluated for safety under preexisting requirements for establishing the safety of new biological products. The agency believes that the safety of most of these products can be studied in human volunteers similar to the people who would be exposed to the product. Information on the safety of the product, immunogenicity, as well as potential drug interactions (e.g., raxibacumab and antimicrobial) would be expected. FDA recognizes that some safety data, such as data on possible adverse interactions between the toxic substance itself and the new product, may not be available.
L1289: 2 http://www.fda.gov/Drugs/GuidanceComplianceRegulatoryInformation/Guidances/ucm065014.htm
L1290: The Animal Rule3 states that a biologic (e.g, raxibacumab) can be approved on the basis of adequate and well-controlled animal studies when the results of those animal studies establish that the biological product is reasonably likely to produce clinical benefit in humans. In assessing the sufficiency of animal data, the agency may take into account other data, including human data, available to the agency. FDA will rely on the evidence from studies in animals to provide substantial evidence of the effectiveness of these products only when:
L1291: - There is a reasonably well-understood pathophysiological mechanism of the toxicity of the substance and its prevention or substantial reduction by the product;
- The effect is demonstrated in more than one animal species expected to react with a response predictive for humans, unless the effect is demonstrated in a single animal species that represents a sufficiently well-characterized animal model for predicting the response in humans;
- The animal study endpoint is clearly related to the desired benefit in humans, generally the enhancement of survival or prevention of major morbidity; and
- The data or information on the kinetics and pharmacodynamics of the product or other relevant data or information, in animals and humans, allows selection of an effective dose in humans.
L1292: Therefore, data from appropriate studies to address each of the above bullet points have to be provided to support the conclusion that the product is effective.
L1293: In addition, approval under this subpart is subject to three requirements:
L1294: - Postmarketing studies. The applicant must conduct postmarketing studies, such as field studies, to verify and describe the biological product's clinical benefit and to assess its safety when used as indicated when such studies are feasible and ethical. A commitment to conduct such studies is typically included in the letter to the applicant that their biological licensing application (BLA) is "approved." Such postmarketing studies would not be feasible until an exigency arises. When such studies are feasible, the applicant must conduct such studies with due diligence. Applicants must include as part of their application a plan or approach to postmarketing study commitments in the event such studies become ethical and feasible.
- Approval with restrictions to ensure safe use. If FDA concludes that a biological product shown to be effective under this subpart can be safely used only if distribution or use is restricted, FDA will require such postmarketing restrictions as are needed to ensure safe use of the biological product, commensurate with the specific safety concerns presented by the biological product, such as:Distribution restricted to certain facilities or health care practitioners with special training or experience;
- Distribution conditioned on the performance of specified medical procedures, including medical follow-up; and
L1295: 3 Request For Comments: 62 FR 40996 (July 31, 1997); Proposed Rule: 64 FR 53960 (Oct 5, 1999); Final Rule: 67 FR 37988 (May 31, 2002); Regulations: 21 CFR § 314.600-650 (New Drugs), § 601.90-95 (Biologics)
L1296: - Distribution conditioned on specified recordkeeping requirements.
- **Information to be provided to patient recipients.** For biological products or specific indications approved under this subpart, applicants must prepare, as part of their proposed labeling, labeling to be provided to patient recipients. The patient labeling must explain that, for ethical or feasibility reasons, the biological product's approval was based on efficacy studies conducted in animals alone and must give the biological product's indication(s), directions for use (dosage and administration), contraindications, a description of any reasonably foreseeable risks, adverse reactions, anticipated benefits, drug interactions, and any other relevant information required by FDA at the time of approval. The patient labeling must be available with the product to be provided to patients prior to administration or dispensing of the biological product for the use approved under this subpart, if possible.
L1297: FDA may withdraw approval if:
L1298: - A postmarketing clinical study fails to verify clinical benefit;
- The applicant fails to perform the postmarketing study with due diligence;
- Use after marketing demonstrates that postmarketing restrictions are inadequate to ensure safe use of the drug product;
- The applicant fails to adhere to the postmarketing restrictions applied at the time of approval under this subpart;
- The promotional materials are false or misleading; or
- Other evidence demonstrates that the drug product is not shown to be safe or effective under its conditions of use.

The product is free from endogenous or adventitious infectious agents sufficient to meet the parameters recommended by FDA. The conditions used in manufacturing have been sufficiently validated, and a consistent product is produced from the multiple production runs presented.

Raxibacumab however is nearly completely degraded by [REDACTED](b) (4) of storage at room temperature with light exposure [REDACTED](b) (4).
