L1307: ## 4. Nonclinical Pharmacology/Toxicology
L1308: Drs. Terry Miller, Tracy McGill, and Ying Mu reviewed the nonclinical toxicity studies in this application. The following are their findings:
L1309: There were no significant toxicologic observations in either of the submitted toxicity studies of raxibacumab in healthy animals. The NOAEL values obtained in both animal studies were the high doses tested; i.e., 40 mg/kg in healthy cynomolgus macaques and 120 mg/kg (3 times the clinical dose) in an embryo-fetal development study in pregnant New Zealand White rabbits. Based on comparisons of AUC in monkey and human, there is an approximately 2-fold safety margin; based on comparisons of C_{max}, there is a less than 2-fold safety margin. Based on comparisons of C_{max} in rabbits and humans (AUCs were not generated in the rabbits), there is a 2- to 4-fold safety margin.
L1310: Tissue cross-reactivity studies with raxibacumab show significant cytoplasmic cross-reactive binding only to the thyroid of both non-human primates and human donor tissues; however the significance of these findings remains unknown.
L1311: NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaques that succumbed to inhalation anthrax disease after treatment with raxibacumab alone or in combination with antibiotics showed enhanced CNS bacterial infiltration, inflammation, and meningitis compared to placebo. In the absence of any similar findings in healthy animals or in human volunteers, the clinical significance of these findings and their responsible mechanism(s) are unknown.
L1312: Results of the dose-ranging placebo controlled animal studies appear to confirm a “superior” treatment benefit of intravenous raxibacumab over placebo alone in preventing anthrax-induced lethality. Although the CNS findings are concerning and should be further investigated, the benefits of raxibacumab treatment in combination with antibiotics most likely will exceed any risk of potential adverse CNS effects that may develop in the clinic.
L1313: *Due to the DSI identified deficiencies in the bioanalytical assay measuring raxibacumab concentrations at HGS serum samples from the monkey and embryo-fetal toxicology study need to be re-analyzed after revising the bioanalytical procedures to correct the deficiencies identified.*
L1314: ## 5. Clinical Pharmacology/Biopharmaceutics
L1315: Kimberly Bergman, Pharm. D. performed Clinical Pharmacology review of this application. Analyses of raxibacumab pharmacokinetic data allowed for the selection of the therapeutic raxibacumab dose in humans based on the comparable PK parameters (Cmax, AUC) between the efficacious 40mg/kg single raxibacumab dose in animals and the 40mg/kg single raxibacumab dose tested in human volunteers.
L1316: Ms. Bergman documents the following in her review of the data submitted by the Applicant:
L1317: The clinical pharmacology characteristics of raxibacumab have been defined in rabbits, monkeys and humans. Raxibacumab dose selection is supported by a cross-species comparison of exposure and exposure-response (E/R) relationships described in *in vivo* animal models of inhalation anthrax infection. These studies show raxibacumab demonstrates the following clinical pharmacology characteristics:
L1318: - Following single intravenous administration of raxibacumab 40 mg/kg in healthy, male and female human subjects, mean raxibacumab steady-state volume of distribution was greater than plasma volume, suggesting some tissue distribution. Clearance values were much smaller than the glomerular filtration rate indicating that there is virtually no renal clearance of raxibacumab. These findings were similar in monkeys and rabbits.
- Humans achieve similar to or greater exposure to raxibacumab following a single 40 mg/kg IV dose compared to rabbits and monkeys receiving the same dose. Mean raxibacumab Cmax in humans following a single 40 mg/kg IV dose was similar to or greater than mean Cmax values in monkeys and rabbits. Mean raxibacumab AUCinf
L1319: in humans following a single 40 mg/kg IV dose was 2.4 and 4.6-fold that of the mean AUCinf values in monkeys and rabbits, respectively. Mean total clearance of raxibacumab was substantially slower in humans as compared to rabbits by a factor of approximately 5 and in monkeys by a factor of approximately 3. Thus, half-life of raxibacumab was longer in humans compared to mean half-lives observed in monkeys and rabbits (20.6 \pm 6.5 days versus 10.1 \pm 2.4 days and 4.1 \pm 0.85 days, respectively). Variability in Cmax was similar across species; %CV values ranged between approximately 13 to 17%. Variability in AUCinf was wider, ranging between 13 and 32% across species.

- Serum raxibacumab concentration-time profiles were similar following administration of raxibacumab alone and with both PO and IV ciprofloxacin. Overall, exposure to ciprofloxacin appears to have no consistent or meaningful impact on raxibacumab PK. Likewise, ciprofloxacin exposure is equivalent when ciprofloxacin is administered alone and with raxibacumab. Thus, there is no significant interaction between raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin.
- The exposure-response data suggest a relationship between raxibacumab dose, concentration, and survival. The dose and dosing regimen selected by the applicant, raxibacumab 40 mg/kg IV single dose, is consistent with the known relationship between dose-concentration-response.
- Dose and concentration response for the endpoint of survival indicates potential to achieve higher response rates at higher doses. If future trials are conducted, higher doses (e.g. 60 or 80 mg/kg) should be explored along with 40 mg/kg.
- Based on *in vitro* binding kinetics studies, the proposed dose of 40 mg/kg raxibacumab in humans would be expected to maintain levels required for virtually complete binding (99.9%) of PA for 7 days and those required for 99% binding for up to 42 days. Despite the theoretical importance of targeting virtually complete binding of PA, the duration of time raxibacumab concentrations remain above the threshold of 202 µg/mL (99.9% PA binding) does not appear to impact efficacy in inhalational anthrax models.
- Based on predicted human PK profiles, more than 95% of humans administered a 40 mg/kg IV raxibacumab dose can be expected to achieve serum raxibacumab concentrations that are equimolar to or in excess of the highest observed serum/plasma PA concentration in any animal that died in the therapeutic intervention studies (for 48 and 28 days relative to rabbits and monkeys, respectively). In addition, modeling and simulation indicated that a single 40 mg/kg IV raxibacumab dose in humans is adequate to bind at least 99.7% of serum PA for up to 28 days after administration, in at least 95% of patients who receive raxibacumab.
- In the pivotal animal studies, animals that were treated with raxibacumab and died exhibited a higher incidence and severity of histopathologic findings in the brain versus placebo treated animals. No clear relationship between exposure and CNS pathology can be discerned based on the limited amount of data in animals that died. Overall, the raxibacumab 20 mg/kg dose group had a higher incidence and severity of CNS findings than the 40 mg/kg group in both rabbits and monkeys. Due to the small numbers of animals that exhibited specific pathology findings, no definitive conclusions about exposure-response for bacteria, hemorrhage, inflammation, or necrosis could be made.
L1320: - Raxibacumab was non-immunogenic in humans and there were no subjects with a positive anti-raxibacumab antibody response in the human studies following single or repeat (every 14 days or following \ge 4 months) doses.
L1321: Also, Ms. Bergman finds that ciprofloxacin administered at the labeled oral dose of 500 mg in humans is expected to achieve higher exposures (C_{max}) than those observed in combination ciprofloxacin/raxibacumab study conducted in monkeys with inhalational anthrax. Levofloxacin administered at the labeled oral dose of 500 mg in humans is expected to achieve slightly higher exposures (C_{max}) than those observed in this study conducted in rabbits with inhalational anthrax.
L1322: Clinical pharmacology conclusions described above hinge on the assurance that pharmacological data is reliable, i.e. collected and processed according to GLP standards. *However, the reliability of clinical pharmacokinetic data came under question as a result of the issues identified during DSI inspections of the bioanalytical sites at HGS and [REDACTED] (b) (4) The inspectional issues identified included incomplete data and documentation, questions regarding some of the quality control samples, questions regarding several SOPs, among others. The assays under question measured raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin concentrations in clinical study C-1064. Raxibacumab pharmacokinetic data from this study is crucial and was used for the above human raxibacumab exposure analyses for the determination of the appropriate human therapeutic dose when compared to the exposures at the 40mg/kg efficacious dose from the animal models of anthrax. Ciprofloxacin PK data was necessary to document the absence of PK/PD drug interaction between raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin. Thus, the following deficiencies are to be included in the Complete Response Action letter and to be addressed by the Applicant prior to approval of this application:*
L1323: - *Following adequate revision of the analytical procedures to address these inspection findings, the pharmacokinetic samples from human studies HGS1021-C1063, HGS1021-C1064, and HGS1021-C1069 should be re-assayed using the revised procedures. Pharmacokinetic parameters for raxibacumab from these re-analyses should be re-calculated in humans following re-assay of the samples. Depending on the outcome of these re-analyses, additional pharmacokinetic studies may be required.*
- *The plasma pharmacokinetic samples obtained from the human study HGS1021-C1064 and the plasma samples obtained from the cynomolgus monkey study 789-G923702 should be re-assayed for ciprofloxacin concentrations using a revised analytical method that adequately addresses the DSI findings for the ciprofloxacin assay. Pharmacokinetic parameters for ciprofloxacin from these re-analyses should be re-calculated in both humans and monkeys following re-assay of the samples. Depending on the outcome of these re-analyses, additional pharmacokinetic studies may be required.*
- *Because of the outstanding issues with the assay of raxibacumab in human serum, we have now become concerned about the reliability of the pharmacokinetic data that was generated from the animal efficacy studies in New Zealand White rabbits and cynomolgus monkeys, which used similar bioanalytical procedures as that for*
L1324: *the human studies. Therefore, the pharmacokinetic samples from animal studies 682-G005758 and 724-G005829 should also be re-assayed using the revised procedures. Pharmacokinetic parameters for raxibacumab from these re-analyses should be re-calculated in rabbits and monkeys following re-assay of the samples. Depending on the outcome of these re-analyses, additional pharmacokinetic studies may be required.*
L1325: ## 6. Clinical Microbiology
L1326: Drs. Maureen Davidson and Lynnette Berkeley reviewed the natural history studies of inhalational anthrax in cynomolgus macaques and NZW rabbits, *in vitro* PA binding studies, performance of PA detection and Toxin Neutralization assays as well as the provided an insight on the animal efficacy studies.
L1327: These reviewers concluded that *in vitro* studies show that raxibacumab can bind PA in culture supernatants from Ames, Sterne and Vollum strains of *B. anthracis*. Raxibacumab binds free but not cell surface bound PA.
L1328: Studies in rabbits and monkeys show that raxibacumab is effective in improving survival. The survival rate decreases as the time to treatment is increased.
L1329: In animal efficacy studies in rabbits and monkeys, detection of PA was used as a trigger for intervention. Due to the limitation of the detection of PA by ECL assay, the cure rates should be based on presence or absence of bacteremia alone. Results show that 40 mg/kg raxibacumab is effective in improving survival in monkeys. Efficacy in rabbits showed a similar trend like the monkeys, however, the difference between the treated and untreated animals was less.
L1330: Raxibacumab appears to decrease the numbers of bacteria present in tissues other than the brain. Greater proportion of lesions (necrosis, hemorrhages, suppurative inflammation, and meningitis) was reported in the brain of raxibacumab treated animals compared to placebo. It is unclear whether an increase in lesions in the brain in animals treated with raxibacumab is due to longer survival time in treated animals compared to placebo, longer duration of bacteremia prior to therapeutic intervention, activation of inflammatory responses to treatment with raxibacumab or due the presence of bacteria, toxins or raxibacumab in the brain. Necropsies of animals that survived were not done in the studies except rabbits treated with levofloxacin or levofloxacin + raxibacumab.
L1331: The reviewers were reassured that no serious safety concerns were observed in the nonclinical pharmacology/toxicology studies. The data from healthy subjects in the clinical safety studies showed that adverse reactions frequently observed included headaches, cough, arthralgia, and paresthesias. Blood levels of IL-2, IL-4, IL-5, IL-8, IL-10, IL-12, IL-13, and histamine were slightly higher on average after the raxibacumab infusion in blood samples from first 25 subjects dosed with raxibacumab from to-be-licensed raxibacumab (M11process), but did not correlate with any clinically significant outcomes. However, the presence of infection such as that with *B. anthracis* can potentially damage the blood-brain barrier, activate immune cells,
L1332: and induce innate and acquired immune responses. Additionally, the possibility of raxibacumab or toxins crossing the blood brain barrier and inducing inflammatory responses in the brain, either alone or in combination with *B. anthracis*, cannot be ruled out.
L1333: *The recommendation was made in the future animal studies to perform necropsy of all surviving animals in addition to non-survivors in order to understand the differences in inflammatory responses between the animals that survive and those that die. Additionally, immunohistochemical staining of brain tissue sections to evaluate whether the cause of CNS lesions might be due to the presence of raxibacumab, bacteria, or both, could be helpful.*
L1334: ## 7. Clinical/Statistical-Efficacy
L1335: Efficacy of raxibacumab as treatment of inhalational anthrax was evaluated in 2 animal models of inhalational anthrax: NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaques, selected based on the results of their respective natural history studies. Four treatment studies with raxibacumab were conducted. The initial two efficacy studies tested raxibacumab versus placebo; one study was conducted in rabbits and the other one in monkeys. Both of these studies demonstrated that the 40 mg/kg IV raxibacumab dose was superior to placebo.
L1336: The subsequent two studies evaluated the efficacy of raxibacumab plus antimicrobial (a fluoroquinolone) versus antimicrobial alone in the treatment of anthrax; a placebo arm was included in these studies as well. As designed the main purpose of these studies was to see whether there may be any antagonism when the two components are used together. However, it was also of interest whether raxibacumab made a contribution to the efficacy of the combination (raxibacumab and antimicrobial) and whether the efficacy of the combination was higher than the efficacy of antimicrobial alone. In these studies, unexpectedly, the efficacy of the antimicrobial (levofloxacin in rabbit and ciprofloxacin in monkey) was 95-100%, and similarly, high rates of efficacy were also seen in the raxibacumab plus antimicrobial combination arm. Given the high efficacy of the antimicrobial in these studies, it was not possible to demonstrate a contribution of raxibacumab to the efficacy of the regimen, raising the question about the need for an animal model that more closely approximates the 55% survival seen in 2001 in the patients with inhalational anthrax.
L1337: ## Analyses populations:
L1338: In The FDA reviews the analysis populations for the four efficacy studies were defined as follows:
L1339: *Intention-to-treat (ITT):* all animals that were randomized and challenged with *B. anthracis*.
L1340: The ITT analysis was to be based on the treatment group planned at randomization rather than the actual treatment the animals received. Animals that were spore-challenged, but died before receiving placebo or active treatment, were to be included in this population as treatment failures.
L1341: *FDA Primary:* all animals that were bacteremic (defined as a positive blood culture) at the time of therapeutic intervention, and according to the actual treatment administered. FDA used this as its primary analysis population because both PA assays quantitative ELISA and ECL trigger for intervention exhibited high intra and inter animal variability as well as a
L1342: significant operator-dependency. The FDA primary analysis using only animals that were bacteremic at the time of treatment was specified in order to clearly differentiate the animals that received raxibacumab for treatment as opposed to post-exposure prophylaxis.
L1343: As treated: all treated animals according to the actual treatment administered.
L1344: Toxemic at treatment: the ITT population according to the detection of toxemia at treatment, defined as the detection of PA by quantitative ECL.
L1345: Excluding non-anthrax death: the above analysis populations, excluding animal(s) that died from non-anthrax causes.
L1346: ## 7.1 Raxibacumab versus Placebo
L1347: The efficacy of raxibacumab monotherapy was compared to placebo in the treatment of inhalational anthrax in two pivotal animal studies (Cynomolgus macaque and New Zealand White rabbit).
L1348: ## 7.1.1 Cynomolgus Macaque
L1349: Study 724-G005829: “Evaluation of Raxibacumab Efficacy as Therapeutic Treatment Against Inhalation Anthrax in the Cynomolgus Macaque”
L1350: ## Objectives
L1351: - To evaluate the efficacy of raxibacumab when administered as a therapeutic treatment against lethality upon appearance of clinical symptoms due to inhalation exposure to *B. anthracis* in cynomolgus macaques.
- Although not pre-specified as primary or secondary study objectives in the protocol, additional objectives of this study were to determine the pharmacokinetics (PK) of raxibacumab following a single IV raxibacumab dose and the kinetics of *B. anthracis* PA in monkeys with inhalation anthrax.
L1352: ## Study Design
L1353: This was a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled efficacy study designed to evaluate single IV doses of raxibacumab vs. placebo as therapeutic treatment against lethality in cynomolgus macaques with symptomatic inhalation anthrax. This study also evaluated the kinetics of *B. anthracis* PA and the PK of IV raxibacumab in symptomatic monkeys.
L1354: ## Methods
L1355: Forty naïve cynomolgus macaques were randomized into two separate groups of 14 monkeys and one group of 12 monkeys (each group 50% male, 50% female) for treatment as delineated in the table 7.1.1-1 below:
L1356: Table 7.1.1-1 Treatment Groups

L1359: (Adapted from HGS' BLA submission, p.21)
L1360: The study was conducted at Battelle Biomedical Research Center (BBRC), West Jefferson, OH. Monkeys were randomized to 1 of 3 aerosol challenge days and a challenge order per day. On Study Day 0, monkeys were challenged with a targeted 200 x lethal dose (LD50) (1.24 x 107 spores) dose of *B. anthracis* spores (Ames strain) via a nebulizer in a head-only inhalation exposure chamber.
L1361: After aerosolization the animals were observed twice daily throughout the study, with observations performed every six hours from 24 through 192 hours post challenge. Body temperature was monitored hourly throughout the course of the study. Beginning at 24 hours through up to 54 hours post spore challenge, blood samples for culture and PA were taken every six hours up to the time of treatment.
L1362: When an animal was found positive for PA in serum via the ECL screening assay or at 54 hours post challenge, a single bolus IV injection of either 40 or 20 mg/kg raxibacumab, or 1 mL/kg raxibacumab buffer (dependent upon that animal's treatment assignment) was administered. Just prior to treatment intervention (\pm 5 minutes), monkeys were administered a single 1 mg/kg dose of diphenhydramine (or equivalent) intramuscularly (IM) to parallel the treatment paradigm for humans in Phase 2/3 studies. Staff members administering the study agent were blinded to study arm assignments and study drug preparation.
L1363: Death or euthanasia was recorded at the time observed and a complete necropsy was performed. Blood samples were collected during the study for hematology and CRP, as well as for bacteremia by culture and PCR, serum PA levels, anti-PA and TNA levels, and serum raxibacumab levels. Blood was collected 3 days prior to spore challenge, just prior to spore challenge, and 5 minutes, 12 and 24 hours, and 3, 5, 8, 14, and 28 days following treatment intervention. A terminal blood sample was also collected if possible.
L1364: ## Demographics and Anthrax Exposure
L1365: The treatment groups were comparable with respect to sex, weight, and age at randomization. The anthrax spore challenge by treatment group is shown in the table 7.1.1-2 below:

L1370: The spore challenge dose was lower on average in the 40 mg/kg raxibacumab group than in the other two treatment groups. There were statistically significant differences in mean spore exposure levels among the three treatment groups (F test, p=0.0255). The difference in inhaled spores between the 40 mg/kg raxibacumab group and the placebo group was statistically significant even after the conservative Bonferroni multiplicity adjustment. However, there did not appear to be a relationship between challenge day, challenge dose, and survival.
L1371: The time to treatment for animals that were bacteremic at the time of treatment was no significantly different between the groups.
L1372: ## Statistical Methods
L1373: According to the HGS protocol, the primary efficacy analysis was to be subject to multiple comparison adjustment using a step-down sequential testing procedure.
L1374: The primary efficacy analysis was performed using a 2-sided likelihood test and was to be subject to multiple comparison adjustment using a step-down sequential testing procedure. First the 40 mg/kg raxibacumab group was compared with placebo. If this was statistically significant then the 20 mg/kg raxibacumab group was compared with placebo for statistical significance. Sensitivity analyses were to be performed for the as-treated population, HGS' modified ITT population, the FDA primary population, and the group of all animals that were randomized including any that were randomized but not challenged with spores.

L1389: ## 7.1.2 New Zealand White Rabbit
L1390: ## Title of Study: 682-G005758: Evaluation of Raxibacumab Efficacy as Therapeutic Treatment Against Inhalation Anthrax in the Rabbit Model
L1391: ## Objectives
L1392: - To evaluate the efficacy of raxibacumab when administered as a therapeutic treatment against lethality upon appearance of clinical symptoms due to inhalation exposure to *B. anthracis* in New Zealand White (NZW) rabbits.
- To determine the PK of raxibacumab following a single IV raxibacumab dose and the kinetics of *B. anthracis* PA in rabbits with inhalation anthrax.
L1393: ## Study Design, and Methods
L1394: This study was designed as an open-label, single center, randomized, placebo controlled dose-ranging study of raxibacumab given as a single IV bolus at either 20 or 40mg/kg dose or placebo to NZW rabbits to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy of a single IV dose of raxibacumab in anthrax spore inhalation challenged rabbits experiencing the symptoms of inhalation anthrax. The study was conducted at BBRC. The primary objective was to evaluate raxibacumab efficacy as therapeutic treatment against inhalation anthrax induced lethality in a NZW rabbit model of established inhalational anthrax. Survival in the bacteremic population was the primary analytic endpoint in the FDA analysis, as had been discussed with HGS, whose protocol prespecified primary analysis in the ITT population. Assuming raxibacumab efficacy of 50%, with three cohorts of 18 animals per group, the study provides 80% power at overall significance level of 0.05 to detect an absolute difference of 45% or more in 14 day survival in one of the raxibacumab treatment groups (20 or 40 mg/kg). Animals received the following interventions when disease was identified (trigger) by bacteremia, or either PA toxemia and temperature elevation of \ge 2^\circ\text{F}. The latter criteria correlate with bacteremia development in the natural history study in NZW rabbits.
L1395: Table 7.1.2-1 illustrates the treatment groups. Raxibacumab was administered as a bolus infusion. The animal's disposition is illustrated in Figure 7.1.2-1.
L1396: **Table 7.1.2-1 Treatment Groups**
L1397: Group	# of Animals	Raxibacumab Treatment
Dose (mg/kg)	Dose Schedule and Route	Treatment Point Post-Challenge
1 (Control Group)	18	Raxibacumab buffera	Single IV	Individual times will be based on serum PA levels or body temperatureb
2	18	20 Raxibacumab	Single IV	Individual times will be based on serum PA levels or body temperatureb

L1398: a Dose equivalent in ml/kg volume to Group 3.
L1399: b Each individual rabbit in groups 1-3 will receive assigned treatment immediately upon either its first positive PA result, or its first two consecutive time points of a body temperature 2 or more degrees F higher than the baseline average (whichever occurs first).
L1400: Study animals were randomized by dose group and gender, and aerosol challenged with the *B. anthracis* Ames strain at 200 x LD50 at Day 0. Temperature was measured every hour from 12h to 72h post-challenge. Blood samples were collected for detection of PA (ECL and ELISA), culture, PCR for *B. anthracis*, and CBC/CRP every 4 hours from 12h to 72h post-challenge. Intervention was to occur based on the trigger for intervention: positive PA toxemia by ECL or a 2° F sustained temperature increase over baseline. Clinical observations were recorded every 12h and animals were euthanized at day 14 or if found moribund. Necropsy and histopathology were conducted on all euthanized for moribundity and all dead animals.

L1411: *An issue of weak statistical significance (p value of 0.0237) between 40mg/kg raxibacumab arm and placebo was raised by statistical reviewer Dr. Hongling Zhou. Specifically, it was pointed out that the result of statistically significant difference between raxibacumab at 40mg/kg arm and placebo is predicated on inclusion of a single animal (L08147) in the FDA primary analysis population (see animal disposition Figure 7.1.2-1 above). However, this medical reviewer argues to retain the animal in the FDA primary analysis population (animals bacteremic prior to study treatment administration) to be consistent with current standards of clinical practice (even a single positive blood culture for B. anthracis along with the elevated body temperature is reflective of bacteremia, i.e. a documented systemic bacterial illness). In addition, this finding of statistical significance is seen in the most conservative approach in selecting the primary analysis population for efficacy as a population of animals bacteremic by culture prior to study treatment and assigning the study group to an animal made according to the actual treatment received. In addition, as stated above, the finding of statistically significant difference for 40mg/kg raxibacumab holds true in the sensitivity analyses of the ITT, mITT population (both FDA and Sponsor's) as well as in the analyses of efficacy in toxemic animals.*

L1416: The animals that succumbed to disease or were sacrificed due to moribundity were necropsized. L1417: ## 7.2 *Efficacy of Raxibacumab and Antimicrobial in Animal Models of Inhalational Anthrax*
L1418: In addition to conducting studies of raxibacumab versus placebo in monkeys and rabbits, HGS also conducted studies to test the efficacy of raxibacumab in combination with antimicrobial therapy in monkeys and in rabbits. These studies were performed to simulate anticipated conditions of use in clinical practice, when antimicrobial treatment will be administered to anthrax patients along with raxibacumab.
L1419: The analysis populations for these studies were defined in the same way as for the raxibacumab versus placebo studies. The study design and outcome for each study are summarized below.
L1420: ## 7.2.1 Cynomolgus Macaque
L1421: ## Study 789-G923702: “Evaluation of the Efficacy of Raxibacumab in Combination with Ciprofloxacin for Therapeutic Treatment in the Cynomolgus Macaque Inhalation Anthrax Model”
L1422: ## Objectives
L1423: - To evaluate the efficacy of raxibacumab when administered as a therapeutic agent in combination with ciprofloxacin against lethality due to inhalation exposure of *B. anthracis* in cynomolgus macaques.
- To determine the PK of intragastric (IG) ciprofloxacin doses and of an IV raxibacumab dose when co-administered, as well as the kinetics of *B. anthracis* protective antigen (PA), in monkeys with inhalation anthrax.
L1424: ## Study Design
L1425: This was a parallel-group, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled study to evaluate the efficacy of raxibacumab in combination with ciprofloxacin as a therapeutic treatment in the cynomolgus macaque inhalation anthrax model. PA kinetics and raxibacumab and ciprofloxacin PK were also examined.
L1426: ## Methods
L1427: Forty (50% male, 50% female) juvenile (&lt; 5 years of age) cynomolgus macaques (*Macaca fascicularis*) weighing between 2.0 to 6.0 kg at randomization were randomized into 3 treatment groups (see table 7.2.1-1 below), and randomly assigned to 1 of 3 aerosol challenge days and a challenge order.
L1428: **Table 7.2.1-1 Treatment Groups**
L1429: Group	N	Ciprofloxacin/Control	Raxibacumab/Control	Treatment Point
Group 1
(Control)	12	Sterile water IG	Raxibacumab buffer IV
(1mL/kg)	Individual treatment times were based on serum PA levels as detected by ECL
Group 2
(Ciprofloxacin)	14	75 mg IG every 12h for 6 doses	Raxibacumab buffer IV
(1mL/kg)

L1430: (Adapted from HGS' BLA submission, p.29)
L1431: The study was conducted at BBRC. On Day 0, monkeys were aerosol challenged with a targeted 200 x LD50 [1.24 x 107 spores] dose of aerosolized *B. anthracis* spores (Ames strain).
L1432: Monkeys were observed every 6 hours beginning 24 hours through 192 hours (8 days) post median challenge time for clinical signs including, but not limited to, anorexia, lethargy, respiratory distress, moribundity, activity (recumbent, weak, or unresponsive), seizures, and
L1433: other abnormal clinical observations, afterwards they were observed twice daily, or more often at any sign of distress.
L1434: Treatment with study agent was triggered by detection of serum PA via the ECL screening assay or at 54 hours post-challenge. Ciprofloxacin (75 mg) or control material (sterile water for injection, WFI) was administered IG for 6 doses: initially once the criterion for treatment was met and then every (Q) 12 hours (\pm 1 hour) for 5 doses. In addition, a single IV bolus dose of raxibacumab (40 mg/kg) or raxibacumab buffer (1 mL/kg) was administered immediately after administration of the first ciprofloxacin dose. Within five minutes prior to treatment each monkey received a single 1 mg/kg intramuscular (IM) dose of diphenhydramine to parallel the treatment paradigm for humans in Phase 2/3 studies. Staff members administering study agents were blinded to study agent preparation to preclude introduction of bias into the study following treatment.
L1435: Monkeys surviving the post-challenge could be returned to HGS (if required) or donated following observation for an additional 60 days under BL-2 laboratory conditions for recrudescence. Gross necropsy and histopathology were performed on all monkeys that were found dead or were euthanized. Blood samples were collected for hematology and CRP, as well as to measure bacteremia by culture, serum PA levels, anti-PA and TNA levels, serum raxibacumab levels and ciprofloxacin levels.
L1436: ## Statistical Analysis
L1437: All statistical tests were to be 2-sided and performed at a significance level of 0.05.
L1438: ## Demographics and Anthrax Exposure
L1439: The treatment groups were comparable with respect to sex, weight, age at randomization, and anthrax spore challenge.

L1454: ## 7.2.2 New Zealand White Rabbit
L1455: ## Study 781-G923701: “Evaluating the efficacy of raxibacumab in combination with levofloxacin for treatment in the New Zealand White Rabbit inhalational anthrax model”
L1456: ## Objectives
L1457: - To evaluate the efficacy of raxibacumab when administered in combination with levofloxacin as a therapeutic treatment against lethality due to inhalation exposure to *B. anthracis* in NZW rabbits.
- To determine the PK of intragastric (IG) levofloxacin doses and of an IV raxibacumab dose when co-administered, as well as the kinetics of *B. anthracis* protective antigen (PA), in rabbits with inhalation anthrax.
L1458: ## Study Design
L1459: This was a parallel-group, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled GLP study to evaluate the efficacy of raxibacumab in combination with levofloxacin for therapeutic treatment in the NZW rabbit inhalational anthrax model. PA kinetics and raxibacumab and levofloxacin PK were also examined.
L1460: ## Methods
L1461: Fifty-two rabbits New Zealand White rabbits (*Oryctolagus cuniculus*) (b) (4) weighing 2.97 to 4.02 kg at randomization, were randomized into one group of 12 rabbits and two groups of 20 rabbits (each group approximately 50% male, 50% female) and assigned to 1 of 3 aerosol challenge days and a challenge order. The eight remaining rabbits were to serve as replacements.
L1462: Rabbits were to be aerosol challenged on Day 0 with a targeted 200x the median lethal dose (LD50) (1.24 x 107 spores) of *B. anthracis* (Ames strain) spores. Treatment was administered based on a positive plasma PA result via ECL screening assay or two consecutive timepoints of a body temperature 2 or more °F higher than the baseline average temperature, whichever was noted first. Beyond 36 hours postchallenge until 72 hours postchallenge, only temperature was used as a trigger for treatment. If an animal had not been treated by 72 hours postchallenge (negative for PA and did not meet the temperature criteria), the animal was to be treated after its last hourly temperature assessment.
L1463: The following three treatment groups were evaluated:
L1464: - Group 1 (X): Individual rabbits received sterile WFI (2 mL/kg) IG upon trigger symptom detection, immediately followed by a single IV dose of raxibacumab buffer (1 mL/kg), and then one dose of sterile WFI (2 mL/kg) at 24 and 48 hours after trigger symptom detection.
- Group 2 (Y): Individual rabbits received levofloxacin (50 mg/kg) IG upon trigger symptom detection, immediately followed by a single IV dose of raxibacumab buffer (1 mL/kg), and then one dose of levofloxacin (50 mg/kg) at 24 and 48 hours after trigger symptom detection.
L1465: - Group 3 (Z): Individual rabbits received levofloxacin (50 mg/kg) IG upon trigger symptom detection, immediately followed by a single IV dose of raxibacumab (40 mg/kg), and then one dose of levofloxacin (50 mg/kg) at 24 and 48 hours after trigger symptom detection.
L1466: ## Demographics and Anthrax Exposure
L1467: The treatment groups were comparable with regard to sex, weight, and age at randomization. The extent of anthrax exposure was similar between groups, with no statistically significant difference in mean spore dose among the three treatment groups. The mean inhaled spore dose exceeded the targeted dose of 200x LD50 in all groups.
L1468: ## Efficacy Results
L1469: ## *Primary Endpoint*
L1470: The primary efficacy endpoint was survival at Day 28, defined as the percent of animals alive at Day 28. In the FDA primary analysis, the 28-day survival rates were 0%, 95.0%, and 94.1% in the placebo, levofloxacin, and levofloxacin/raxibacumab combination groups, respectively (Table 7.2.2-1). There was no difference (p=0.947) in survival rates between the levofloxacin and levofloxacin/raxibacumab combination groups (-0.88%, 95% CI [-23.9%, 19.6%]).
L1471: None of the 12 rabbits in the placebo group survived. There was one death in the levofloxacin group and one death in the levofloxacin/raxibacumab group. The one non-survivor in the levofloxacin group was discovered moribund and was euthanized 11 days post challenge. The one non-survivor in the levofloxacin/raxibacumab group (K99246) was bacteremic and toxicemic at 20h post challenge and at the time of treatment administration; blood cultures were negative at the time of death and histopathology findings were consistent with aspiration pneumonia. There were no meningeal findings on histopathology of this animal. This animal was considered to have died as the result of a dosing accident (inadvertent intratracheal gavage of levofloxacin).

L1482: ## 8. Safety
L1483: ## 8.1 *Histopathology findings from animal efficacy studies*
L1484: Upon histological examination of tissues from the non-survivor animals in pivotal animal studies it was noted that, although, all animals had evidence of anthrax disease in organs examined, the pattern of histopathologic changes was different between placebo and raxibacumab treated animals. There was greater incidence and/or severity of CNS lesions in raxibacumab-treated non-survivors as compared to placebo non-survivors.
L1485: Histopathologic examination revealed that more bacteria (intra-, peri-vascular areas, subarachnoid space, choroid plexus), fibrinoneutrophilic inflammation, hemorrhage, fibrinoid or neuropil necrosis were present in the brains of raxibacumab-treated non-survivors.
L1486: A consistent method was applied to compare histopathology findings between the study groups and between the studies with focus on “high grade” lesions defined as presence of either bacteria hemorrhage, or inflammation of &gt;2 or any evidence of necrosis.

L1498: The difference in the frequency and the severity of the pathologic findings in the brain between placebo and raxibacumab treated non-survivors across both animal species could not be fully explained by the duration of survival from challenge or duration of bacteremia prior to death due to limited number of non-survivor animals in the active treatment arms and also due to a considerable overlap in the time to death or duration of bacteremia prior to death between placebo animals with low level CNS pathology and raxibacumab treated non-survivors with high level CNS pathology.
L1499: Additional hypotheses on the mechanism of the CNS findings in the raxibacumab-treated non-survivors should be considered further:
L1500: - Increased permeability of blood-brain barrier in a setting of severe systemic disease that allows raxibacumab penetration into CNS and potential binding to the toxin damaged brain tissue with ensuing inflammatory response. This could potentially be evaluated by systematic collection and examination of histopathology data from survivors and non-survivors and immunohistochemistry of the brain/meninges.
- Inhibition of inflammatory response by lethal toxin in a setting of acute systemic anthrax disease does not allow for recruitment and activation of inflammatory cells into CNS. In the presence of raxibacumab action of lethal toxin will be blocked and host inflammatory response is restored. *Ex vivo* studies of neutrophil activation from raxibacumab treated and untreated exposed animals could potentially be performed.
- Additional drug-disease interaction hypotheses included: immune-complex disease (unlikely as kidney damage was more pronounced in the placebo animals), and cytokine, chemokine storm, complement activation in the presence of raxibacumab during ongoing anthrax infection.
L1501: *Direct CNS toxicity of raxibacumab appears to be unlikely in lieu of negative tissue cross-reactivity studies and favorable safety profile of raxibacumab in animal toxicology studies and in studies of healthy human volunteers. While drug-disease interaction could not be excluded, in the context of survival benefit offered by raxibacumab and the knowledge that hemorrhagic meningitis is a pathognomonic feature of systemic anthrax disease reported in up to 66% of historical clinical cases, 50-60% in NHP and in 30% of rabbit animal models described in the scientific literature the clinical significance of this finding remains unclear.*
L1502: Consults on the significance and potential mechanisms of the above histopathology findings were requested from the DNP and Marc Walton, M.D. former Director of ODE
L1503: VI. The findings and conclusions were similar to that of the primary reviewers of this BLA.
L1504: *Additional studies were recommended to investigate the relationship of raxibacumab to the CNS findings in treated non-survivors and the significance of such findings for the survivors and include the following:*
L1505: - *Evaluate neurological function/behavior in survivor and non-survivor animals in further efficacy studies recommended*
- *Conduct necropsy on all survivor and non-survivor animals and histopathology examination of tissues, particularly the brain and meninges*
- *Report the findings on raxibacumab binding to the meninges from previously conducted tissue cross reactivity studies, if available, or conduct a new cross reactivity study on rabbit, monkey, and human meningeal tissue.*
- *Perform an immunohistochemical staining of the brains of raxibacumab treated animals to evaluate whether raxibacumab is present in CSF and brain, if feasible.*
L1506: ## 8.2 Human Safety Findings
L1507: The safety database consisted of 326 healthy subjects treated with the recommended dose of raxibacumab of 40 mg/kg manufactured by the M11 process (the version intended for licensure), with 303 subjects receiving a single dose (studies HGS1021-C1064 and HGS1021-C1063), 23 subjects receiving a 2nd dose 2 weeks after their first dose (study HGS1021-1063), and 20 subjects from study HGS1021-C1064 who received a 2nd dose more than 4 months after their initial dose (study HGS1021-C1069). In Study HGS1021-C1064, 48 subjects who received raxibacumab also received ciprofloxacin as part of this drug interaction study.
L1508: The M11 formulation of raxibacumab is safe for use in the adult population at the intended single IV dose of 40 mg/kg when administered after diphenhydramine pre-medication. There was only 1 death in a subject who received placebo from injuries sustained in a motor vehicle accident. In addition to this death, there were 2 additional SAEs reported, 1 case of cholecystitis and 1 case of schizophrenia, both of which were likely related to underlying conditions. There were 4 subjects (1.2%) who discontinued raxibacumab during infusion because of AEs. Two of these were cases of urticaria in subjects who did not receive premedication with diphenhydramine. AEs of severe intensity were infrequently reported (1.9%). The most frequently reported AE was headache; other commonly reported AEs included upper respiratory tract infection and rash.
L1509: As the safety database consisted of healthy volunteers, a study agent/disease interaction could not be directly assessed. While CNS AEs were reviewed, it appears from the animal models that systemic anthrax disease must be present for CNS pathology to be observed. A review for CNS safety in humans was therefore limited. Other limitations with respect to safety include the exclusion of pediatric subjects and pregnant patients from the safety database. While subjects greater than 65 years of age were enrolled in the study, they represented only 6.4% (21 subjects) of the population which is insufficient to make any conclusions as to whether these subjects respond differently to raxibacumab compared to subjects less than 65 years of age. Similarly, non-white subjects represented 28% of the
L1510: safety database. Therefore, it is unclear how generalizable the results of raxibacumab safety assessments are to the above populations.
L1511: ## 9. Advisory Committee Meeting
L1512: Advisory Committee meeting was held on October 27, 2009. The following questions were posed to the committee:
L1513: (1) Does the evidence from the animal models evaluating raxibacumab at 40 mg/kg IV predict response for treatment of humans with inhalational anthrax disease?
L1514: 16 members voted Yes, 7 voted No, 1 abstained
L1515: **Minutes excerpt:** The majority of the Committee Members felt that the criteria for the Animal Rule were met and agreed that that the data from the animal studies could be used to extrapolate to humans. Concerns remain about dosing and the timing of treatment after exposure. Further studies should include special populations, including the pediatric population.
L1516: Members of the Committee that voted 'no' thought that all four elements of the animal rule were not met and extrapolation to humans was not possible, and recommended studies be conducted that more accurately depict the course of disease in humans. Additional studies were requested to determine the benefit of raxibacumab in relation to timing post exposure.
L1517: The member of the Committee that abstained from voting did so because of a personal perception of conflict of interest.
L1518: (2) Does the evidence provided in these studies support the conclusion that raxibacumab will not diminish the anticipated efficacy of antimicrobials in inhalational anthrax?
L1519: 10 members voted Yes, 11 voted No, 3 abstained
L1520: **Minutes excerpt:** Members of the Committee that voted 'yes' agreed that raxibacumab did not appear to diminish the effects of antimicrobials in treatment of inhalational anthrax.
L1521: Members of the Committee that voted 'no' thought that it was difficult to determine the effects of raxibacumab with antibiotics because there was no study with the antibody as the control arm. It could not be seen whether effects were due to the combination therapy or possibly antimicrobial therapy alone. It was noted that high doses of antimicrobial could have masked any detrimental effects of raxibacumab. Studies related to timing of administration, proper dosing of antimicrobials, and use of different antimicrobials were suggested.
L1522: Members of the Committee that abstained from voting did so because the need for more data and because of a personal perception of conflict of interest.
L1523: (3) Given the high efficacy of the antimicrobial arms in the rabbit (95%) and monkey (100%) studies, the added benefit of raxibacumab to antimicrobial could not be determined. Should evidence be requested that raxibacumab makes a contribution to the efficacy over the antimicrobial alone (in rabbit and monkey animal models)?
L1524: 17 members voted Yes, 5 voted No, 1 abstained, 1 not voted
L1525: **Minutes excerpt:** Members of the Committee that voted 'yes' to the question thought that more evidence was needed to conclude that raxibacumab contributed to efficacy over antimicrobial therapy alone. Recommendations included studies where standard or suboptimal doses of antibiotic therapy in humans are used to see contributing effect of raxibacumab, use of timing to mimic course of infection in human, and the use of rabbits instead of primates. It was noted that additional studies should not necessarily be requested from the Sponsor.
L1526: Members of the Committee that voted 'no' to the question thought that raxibacumab possibly contributed to efficacy over antimicrobial therapy, but needed more precise animal studies to determine exact benefit. Additional studies should address when to start treatment and the state of the animal prior to treatment with raxibacumab. It was noted that the animal rule does not require benefit over conventional therapy.
L1527: ## 10. Pediatrics
L1528: Raxibacumab has not been studied in pediatric patients or healthy pediatric subjects. Raxibacumab has been granted Orphan Designation for "the treatment of anthrax". It is exempt from PREA obligations.

L1533: ## 13. Recommendations/Risk Benefit Assessment
L1534: - **Recommended Regulatory Action:**Complete response pending resolution of bioanalytical assays' deficiencies. Under the Animal Rule 21CFR 601.90 the animal efficacy studies did establish raxibacumab efficacy (prevention of anthrax induced lethality) in two animal models of inhalational anthrax disease (NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaques) in the FDA primary population of animals bacteremic prior to raxibacumab administration. The reviewer concludes that requirements 1-3 of the Animal Rule were met in this application:

There is a reasonably well-understood pathophysiological mechanism of the toxicity of the substance and its prevention or substantial reduction by the product;
L1535: Mechanism of action of anthrax toxin is well understood and proximal targets for anthrax toxin toxicity are well established in humans and animals. Raxibacumab binds PA and prevents formation of anthrax toxin and its downstream cytotoxic effects. This is documented in the in vitro binding studies of recombinant PA as well as the PA from antibiotic susceptible *B. anthracis* strains: Ames, Sterne, and Vollum. In proof of concept/mechanism of action rat lethal toxin infusion study administration of raxibacumab improved survival of the animals as compared to placebo.
L1536: 2. The effect is demonstrated in more than one animal species expected to react with a response predictive for humans, unless the effect is demonstrated in a single animal species that represents a sufficiently well-characterized animal model for predicting the response in humans;
L1537: Statistically significant improvement in survival with raxibacumab administered as a 40mg/kg IV single dose as compared to placebo was observed in two animal models of inhalational anthrax disease (NZW rabbits and cynomolgus macaques) in the FDA primary analysis population of animals bacteremic prior to the study treatment intervention. The selected animal models were sufficiently similar to humans with respect to etiology, pathogenesis, route of exposure, and host susceptibility factors. *The course of the disease was shorter in the animal models as compared to historical data on human disease, but the spore challenge dose of approximately 200xLD50 in the animals was highly lethal and represented the worse case scenario (100% mortality in the placebo group). However, the FDA efficacy analyses focused on the animals that were bacteremic prior to study treatment, ensuring that the animals, in fact, had systemic anthrax disease and would reflect the human patient population diagnosed with anthrax disease by culture.*
L1538: There are additional limitations of the efficacy data with respect to predicting response in humans. First, the time of intervention could be different between animals and humans. In the controlled research environment setting, animals were closely monitored for either an elevation in temperature (rabbits) or a positive serum PA (rabbits and cynomolgus macaques), and once detected, a therapeutic intervention was delivered. Humans will likely to have variable time to presentation to the health care setting or be given alternative diagnoses prior to the definitive diagnosis of anthrax being made. *Although animal efficacy data might not be applicable to the whole spectrum of human inhalational anthrax disease at the time of the health care setting presentation, it likely to be applicable to a subset of patients with positive blood cultures at the time of presentation possibly in the prodromal phase of the disease.*
L1539: Second, the combination efficacy studies demonstrated nearly 100% efficacy of levofloxacin in NZW rabbits and ciprofloxacin in cynomolgus macaques, respectively. In contrast, during the 2001 anthrax attacks, 5 of the 11 people who developed inhalational anthrax died despite best available treatment. Both of these factors may affect the degree of certainty in extrapolation of efficacy
L1540: from the animal models to humans. *Although helpful for the healthcare provider to be aware of the window of a successful therapeutic intervention to be characterized in an animal model of delayed treatment (antibiotic efficacy of only 55%) the studies evaluating added benefit of raxibacumab to antimicrobial under these conditions have not been conducted to date and in the preamble to the Final Animal Rule is discussed as not required preapproval.*4
L1541: *Third, in the animal studies therapeutic interventions were limited only to study drugs while in clinical care setting multiple supportive measures will likely be instituted including but not limited to cardio-respiratory support, fluid resuscitation, dialysis, pleural fluid drainage, etc.*
L1542: 3. The animal study endpoint is clearly related to the desired benefit in humans, generally the enhancement of survival or prevention of major morbidity;
L1543: Survival was the primary endpoint measured at 14 days post challenge in rabbit and 28 days post challenge in NHP animal models.
L1544: The results of the safety evaluation of raxibacumab as a 40mg/kg IV single dose in healthy human volunteers were unremarkable, except for mild self limiting infusion related rashes prevented with diphenhydramine premedication. However, this BLA application cannot be approved as PK/PD link (4th requirement under the Animal Rule) between the efficacious dose in animals and proposed efficacious and safe dose in humans cannot be reliably established at this time due to remaining concerns from DSI inspections about the raxibacumab assays from human PK/safety studies C-1064 and C-1063.
L1545: *The following deficiencies should be included in the Complete Response letter and must be addressed by the Applicant prior to approval of this BLA:*
L1546: a. *Following adequate revision of the analytical procedures to address these inspection findings, the pharmacokinetic samples from human studies HGS1021-C1063, HGS1021-C1064, and HGS1021-C1069 should be re-assayed using the revised procedures. Pharmacokinetic parameters for raxibacumab from these re-analyses should be re-calculated in humans following re-assay of the samples. Depending on the outcome of these re-analyses, additional pharmacokinetic studies may be required.*

b. *The plasma pharmacokinetic samples obtained from the human study HGS1021-C1064 and the plasma samples obtained from the cynomolgus monkey study 789-G923702 should be re-assayed for ciprofloxacin concentrations using a revised analytical method that adequately addresses the DSI findings for the ciprofloxacin assay. Pharmacokinetic parameters for ciprofloxacin from these re-analyses should be re-calculated in both humans and monkeys following re-assay of the samples. Depending on the outcome of these re-analyses, additional pharmacokinetic studies may be required.*
L1547: 4 Final Rule 21 CFR Parts 314 and 601 (p. 39790-1)
L1548: c. *Because of the outstanding issues with the assay of raxibacumab in human serum, we have now become concerned about the reliability of the pharmacokinetic data that was generated from the animal efficacy studies in New Zealand White rabbits and cynomolgus monkeys, which used similar bioanalytical procedures as that for the human studies. Therefore, the pharmacokinetic samples from animal studies 682-G005758 and 724-G005829 should also be re-assayed using the revised procedures. Pharmacokinetic parameters for raxibacumab from these re-analyses should be re-calculated in rabbits and monkeys following re-assay of the samples. Depending on the outcome of these re-analyses, additional pharmacokinetic studies may be required.*

d. *Re-assess and (b)(4) the bacterial endotoxin specification for the raxibacumab final drug product. The re-assessment should consider the endotoxin contribution from the saline solution used to dilute raxibacumab drug product prior to administration. The revised specification should provide a safety factor (e.g., 2-4 fold) when the endotoxin limits from both the saline and the drug product are considered.*

- **Risk Benefit Assessment**Raxibacumab is a recombinant humanized monoclonal antibody that binds the protective antigen (PA) of *B. anthracis* and prevents the binding of PA with its receptors. As the PA-receptor interaction is required for disease progression, its inhibition represents a direct antitoxin therapy to complement very limited armamentarium of approved anti-anthrax treatments, i.e. antibiotics5,6,7.
L1549: Current approved treatments of anthrax include antibiotics: penicillin G and tetracyclines1. Antibiotics however have several limitations: the absence of direct activity against anthrax toxin and anthrax spores8, resistance to engineered antibiotic-resistant strains9, and poor patient adherence with the recommended 60 day treatment duration1. Furthermore, the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapy is less than ideal; following the dissemination of anthrax spores through the US Postal Service system in September 2001 where 11 people developed inhalational anthrax, the survival rate was 55% (6/11) despite early intervention with antimicrobial therapy and advanced supportive care10. Benefit of raxibacumab would also be expected in individuals for whom antibiotics are contraindicated or who are non-adherent. Although could not be
L1550: 5 Little SF, Leppla SH, Friedlander AM. Production and characterization of monoclonal antibodies against the lethal factor component of *Bacillus anthracis* lethal toxin. Infect Immun 1990 ;58(6) :1606-13.
L1551: 6 Maynard JA, Maassen CB, Leppla SH et al. Protection against anthrax toxin by recombinant antibody fragments correlates with antigen affinity. Nat Biotechnol 2002 ;20(6) :597-601.
L1552: 7 Kobiler D, Gozes Y, Rosenberg H et al. Efficiency of protection of guinea pigs against infection with *Bacillus anthracis* spores by passive immunization. Infect Immun 2002 ;70(2) :544-60.
L1553: 8 Friedlander AM, Wellkos SL, Pitt ML et al. Postexposure prophylaxis against experimental inhalational anthrax. J Infect Dis 1993 ;167(5) :1239-43.
L1554: 9 Athamna A, Athamna M, Abu-Rashed N et al. Selection of *Bacillus anthracis* isolates resistant to antibiotics. J Antimicrob Chemother 2004 ;54(2) :424-8.
L1555: 10 Inglesby TV et al. Anthrax as a biological weapon, 2002: Updated recommendations for management. JAMA 2002:May 1;287(17):2236-52.
L1556: tested against PA from multi-drug resistant *B. anthracis*, mechanism of action of raxibacumab is different from those of antibiotics and it is potentially could serve as an antitoxin therapy for those patients in whom disease is due to antibiotic-resistant anthrax.
L1557: In a proof-of-concept rat lethal toxin infusion model study conducted by the Applicant, raxibacumab at a concentration of ten-fold the concentration of recombinant PA (rPA) resulted in 100% survival for 24 hours, while isotype antibody treated control rats died within 90 minutes of LT administration. These results support the current thought that secreted *B. anthracis* toxins are responsible for the morbidity and mortality characteristic of anthrax infection despite appropriate antimicrobial therapy.
L1558: In animal studies (rabbit and monkey models of inhalational anthrax), raxibacumab conferred a statistically significant survival benefit over placebo when administered to the animals confirmed to be bacteremic with *B. anthracis*. When raxibacumab was studied in the same animal models (rabbit and monkey) of inhalational anthrax in combination with either levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin and the efficacy of combination was compared to antibiotics alone, there was no statistically significant difference in survival between both active treatment groups. While these supportive studies were not powered to detect added benefit or antagonism between raxibacumab and antibiotics and the animal models themselves are limited by the high efficacy of antibiotics alone, the absence of numerical difference (a single anthrax death in both models: on combination arm in the NHP study and on levofloxacin alone arm in the rabbit study) and the absence of a pharmacokinetic drug-drug interaction are reassuring and the additional benefit conferred with concurrent use of raxibacumab in humans remains a viable possibility and might need to be further explored in animal studies when a suitable animal model of delayed intervention in inhalational anthrax becomes available.
L1559: From a safety perspective, the M11 formulation of raxibacumab is safe for use in the adult population at the intended single IV dose of 40 mg/kg when administered after diphenhydramine pre-medication based on the analysis of a database composed of 326 subjects. There were no deaths in raxibacumab-treated subjects, and only 2 SAEs reported (0.6%) that were likely related to the subjects' underlying conditions. There were 4 subjects (1.2%) who discontinued raxibacumab during infusion because of infusion-related AEs. Two of these were cases of rash in subjects who did not receive premedication with diphenhydramine. AEs of severe intensity were infrequently reported (1.9%). The most frequently reported AE was headache; most cases were mild in severity, did not lead to study agent discontinuation and resolved spontaneously during the study period.
L1560: ## Risks
L1561: While the anthrax animal models have been carefully and extensively tested and characterized, it is still unknown as to how well they predict efficacy in humans for several reasons. First, the time of intervention is likely to be different between animals under study conditions and humans in real life clinical care settings. Animals evaluated in efficacy studies have received therapeutic intervention at the time of trigger positivity (early in the course of the disease) compared to humans who may
L1562: present to the health care setting with variable time of symptom onset, including delayed presentation, or have the appropriate treatment delayed due to alternative diagnoses considered prior to the establishment of definitive diagnosis due non-specific nature of symptoms in the prodromal phase of inhalational anthrax disease. However, there would be patients with inhalational anthrax disease who will present and will be diagnosed with inhalational anthrax and receive treatment in the prodromal phase when blood cultures are positive for *B. anthracis*, similar to the conditions of treatment in the animal studies conducted.
L1563: In addition, antibiotic efficacy observed in the two combination efficacy studies was close to 100%, which is far higher than the rates observed historically during the 2001 anthrax attacks (55% efficacy). *The additional benefit that raxibacumab may offer could not be determined in animal models studied and, therefore, it is difficult to predict the extent of survival improvement what might occur in humans with the addition of raxibacumab. The delayed treatment models in inhalational anthrax are under development. It is unclear when such model will become available. Multiple factors will need to be well characterized and considered in designing added benefit delayed model study, including but not limited to: desired efficacy of antimicrobials to be replicated, humanized dose and regimen of antimicrobial (relevant human exposures for an approved duration achieved in an animal), therapeutic window post challenge or trigger detection for each animal model, statistical power to detect superiority of combination treatment versus antimicrobial alone, ethical issues of allowing large numbers (hundreds) of animals to die prior to treatment initiation in order to mimic 55% human survival with antibiotics in 2001, and feasibility of conducting such a study under BL-3 laboratory conditions. Although, this study will provide additional information on the potential synergy/added benefit of a combination therapy, the Reviewer concludes that it is not required for product approval in accordance with the defined goal of a therapeutic product development in the Final Rule 21 CFR Parts 314 and 601 (p. 39790-1), specifically for a bioterrorism target, where the requirement for products to demonstrate meaningful therapeutic benefit over existing treatments was eliminated, in order to allow for a wide range of products to be available for treatment indications studied under the Animal Rule, i.e. inhalational anthrax where current therapeutic options are limited to only 2 classes of antibiotics. However, a study evaluating added benefit of antitoxin to antimicrobial will be requested as a postmarketing commitment upon application approval, contingent on the development of a delayed treatment (50% antimicrobial efficacy) animal model of treatment of inhalational anthrax.*
L1564: While animal models represent the best studied efficacy evidence to date, the true efficacy of raxibacumab can only be determined under field study conditions.
L1565: *Next, the risk of central nervous system (CNS) toxicity in humans associated with raxibacumab exposure remains unclear. In the pivotal rabbit and NHP efficacy studies, animals treated with raxibacumab and died of anthrax had more CNS pathology compared with placebo animals that died. Survivors were not sacrificed and, therefore, it could not be determined if the same pathophysiologic process occurred in survivors. In the rabbit combination antibiotic study, all animals (survivors and non-survivors), were sacrificed and had their tissues examined microscopically. While all placebo animals had both systemic and CNS findings*
L1566: *consistent with anthrax, only 1 animal in an active treatment group died of anthrax, but did not have CNS findings. None of the rabbits surviving to study termination had lesions attributable to anthrax on histopathologic examination. Similarly, in the combination NHP study, only 1 animal in the ciprofloxacin/raxibacumab group died of anthrax. While this animal did have evidence of hemorrhagic meningitis, the single death limits the degree of analysis that can be performed. However, negative brain tissue cross reactivity and animal toxicology studies as well as unremarkable safety of raxibacumab in healthy volunteers argue against the direct CNS toxicity of raxibacumab. Although drug-disease interaction cannot be ruled out, its' clinical significance has to be assessed in lieu of survival benefit provided by raxibacumab monotherapy and will not likely be easily discernable even with the conduct of the studies recommended by the reviewers and consultants. The studies recommended to be conducted to evaluate potential mechanisms of CNS findings in raxibacumab treated animals include the following:*
L1567: - *Evaluate neurological function/behavior in survivor and non-survivor animals in further efficacy studies recommended*
- *Conduct necropsy on all survivor and non-survivor animals and histopathology examination of tissues, particularly the brain and meninges in further efficacy studies recommended*
- *Report the findings on raxibacumab binding to the meninges from previously conducted tissue cross reactivity studies, if available, or conduct a new cross reactivity study on rabbit, monkey, and human meningeal tissue.*
- *Perform an immunohistochemical staining of the brains of raxibacumab treated animals to evaluate whether raxibacumab is present in CSF and brain, if feasible.*
L1568: There are several limitations of the clinical safety data. First, a safety database of 326 subjects cannot exclude a serious adverse event (SAE) or fatal event occurring at less than 1% frequency. In addition, as the safety database consisted only of healthy volunteers, any possible study agent/disease interaction could not be assessed. Lastly, the exclusion of pediatric subjects and other special populations (pregnant patients, and patients with renal and hepatic dysfunction), and insufficient numbers of subjects aged 65 years and older limit the generalizability of safety results to these populations.

L1592: ## 1 Recommendations/Risk Benefit Assessment
L1593: ## 1.1 Recommendation on Regulatory Action
L1594: Raxibacumab, a monoclonal antibody against protective antigen (PA) of *Bacillus anthracis*, manufactured by the process proposed for licensure (M11) administered as a single intravenous dose of 40 mg/kg dose is safe and effective (b) (4)
L1595: A premedication regimen of diphenhydramine administered within 1 hour prior to the raxibacumab dose is recommended.
L1596: The efficacy recommendation is based on 2 pivotal efficacy studies, studies 682-G005758 (New Zealand White (NZW) rabbit) and 724-G005829 (nonhuman primate, NHP) and 2 supportive efficacy studies of raxibacumab used in combination with antibiotics, studies 781-G923701 (NZW rabbit) and 789-G923702 (NHP).
L1597: The safety recommendation is based on the pooled safety analyses of 326 subjects treated with the recommended dose of raxibacumab of 40 mg/kg manufactured by the M11 process. The database analysis consisted of 303 subjects receiving a single dose (studies HGS1021-C1064 and HGS1021-C1063), 23 subjects receiving a 2nd dose 2 weeks after their first dose (study HGS1021-1063), and 20 subjects from study HGS1021-C1064 who received a 2nd dose more than 4 months after their initial dose (study HGS1021-C1069).
L1598: ## 1.2 Risk Benefit Assessment
L1599: Raxibacumab is a human monoclonal antibody which binds the PA of *B. anthracis* and prevents the binding of PA to its receptors. As this PA-receptor interaction is required for disease progression, its inhibition represents a novel and viable clinical strategy to complement the bactericidal activity of antibiotics (1,2,3).
L1600: The only therapies currently approved for the treatment of anthrax due to *B. anthracis* are tetracycline and penicillin antibiotics:
L1601: 1 Little SF, Leppla SH, Friedlander AM. Production and characterization of monoclonal antibodies against the lethal factor component of *Bacillus anthracis* lethal toxin. Infect Immun 1990 ;58(6):1606-13.
L1602: 2 Maynard JA, Maassen CB, Leppla SH et al. Protection against anthrax toxin by recombinant antibody fragments correlates with antigen affinity. Nat Biotechnol 2002 ;20(6):597-601.
L1603: 3 Kobiler D, Gozes Y, Rosenberg H et al. Efficiency of protection of guinea pigs against infection with *Bacillus anthracis* spores by passive immunization. Infect Immun 2002 ;70(2):544-60.
L1604: Tetracyclines: doxycycline, doxycycline calcium, doxycycline hyclate
Tetracycline, demeclocycline hydrochloride and minocycline hydrochloride are recommended in situations when penicillin is contraindicated
L1605: Penicillins: penicillin G procaine, penicillin G potassium, and penicillin G sodium.
L1606: These agents are approved on the basis on *in vitro* activity against *B. anthracis*.
L1607: Limitations of antibiotics include the absence of activity against anthrax toxin and anthrax spores (4), resistance of engineered strains (5), and poor patient adherence. Furthermore, the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapy is less than ideal; following the dissemination of anthrax spores through the US Postal Service system in September 2001 where 11 people developed inhalational anthrax, the survival rate was 55% (6/11) despite early intervention with antimicrobial therapy and supportive care (6). Benefit would also be expected for individuals for whom antibiotics are contraindicated or who are non-adherent.
L1608: In a proof-of-concept toxin rat model study conducted by the Applicant, raxibacumab at a concentration of ten-fold the concentration of recombinant PA (rPA) was administered up to three weeks prior to challenge with recombinant lethal toxin, rLT (composed of recombinant lethal factor, rLF + rPA) in F344 rats and resulted in 100% survival for 24 hours. In contrast, isotype antibody treated control rats died within 90 minutes of LT administration. These results demonstrate that secreted *B. anthracis* toxin alone in the absence of bacteremia is lethal. These results, in addition to the results of the pivotal efficacy studies of anthrax bacterial disease in cynomolgus monkeys and New Zealand White (NZW) rabbits demonstrate that raxibacumab prevents death in both toxin infusion and bacterial disease models.
L1609: In animal studies, raxibacumab conferred a statistically significant survival benefit over placebo. When raxibacumab was studied in combination with either levofloxacin or ciprofloxacin and compared to antibiotics alone, there was no statistically significant difference between either active treatment group. While these latter studies were not powered to detect added benefit of raxibacumab to antibiotics alone and the animal models themselves are limited by the high efficacy of antibiotics monotherapy, the absence of interaction is reassuring. However, potential additional benefit conferred with concurrent use of raxibacumab and antibiotics in humans remains to be evaluated.
L1610: 4 Friedlander AM, Wellkos SL, Pitt ML et al. Postexposure prophylaxis against experimental inhalational anthrax. J Infect Dis 1993 ;167(5) :1239-43.
L1611: 5 Athamna A, Athamna M, Abu-Rashed N et al. Selection of *Bacillus anthracis* isolates resistant to antibiotics. J Antimicrob Chemother 2004 ;54(2) :424-8.
L1612: 6 Inglesby TV et al. Anthrax as a biological weapon, 2002: Updated recommendations for management. JAMA 2002:May 1;287(17):2236-52.
L1613: From a safety perspective, the M11 formulation of raxibacumab is safe for use in the adult population at the intended single IV dose of 40 mg/kg when administered after diphenhydramine pre-medication. This finding is based on the analysis of a database composed of 326 subjects. There were no deaths in raxibacumab-treated subjects, and only 2 SAEs reported (0.6%) which were likely related to the subjects' underlying conditions. There were 4 subjects (1.2%) who discontinued raxibacumab during infusion because of infusion-related AEs. Two of these were cases of rash in subjects who did not receive premedication with diphenhydramine. AEs of severe intensity were infrequently reported (1.9%). The most frequently reported AE was headache; most cases were mild in severity, did not lead to study agent discontinuation and resolved during the study period.
L1614: ## Risks
L1615: ## *Limitations of animal efficacy findings*
L1616: While the anthrax animal models have been carefully and extensively tested and characterized, it is unknown as to how well they predict efficacy in humans for several reasons. First, the time of intervention is likely to differ between animals and humans. In the clinical trial setting, animals were closely monitored for either an elevation in temperature (rabbits) or a positive serum PA (rabbits and cynomolgus monkeys), and once detected, a therapeutic intervention was delivered. Animals enrolled in clinical studies are therefore likely to have earlier therapeutic intervention compared to humans who may either have delayed presentation to the health care setting, or have alternative diagnoses made prior to the definitive diagnosis of anthrax given the non-specific signs and symptoms in early inhalational anthrax disease. In addition, antibiotic efficacy observed in the two combination efficacy studies was close to 100%, which is far higher than rates seen historically with the 2001 anthrax attacks (55% efficacy). Both of these factors may affect the degree of extrapolation of efficacy from the animal models to humans. Lastly, additional potential benefit of raxibacumab could not be determined with animal models, and therefore it is unclear what will occur in humans. The efficacy of delayed administration of raxibacumab after the onset of clinical symptoms has not been reported in animal models and therefore the therapeutic window for effective raxibacumab delivery is unknown. While animal models still represent the best studied efficacy evidence to date, the true efficacy of raxibacumab can only be determined under field conditions.
L1617: ## *Limitations of animal safety (central nervous system) findings*
L1618: Next, the risk of central nervous system (CNS) toxicity in humans associated with raxibacumab exposure remains unclear. In the pivotal rabbit and NHP efficacy studies, animals treated with raxibacumab and died of anthrax had more CNS pathology compared with placebo animals that died. Survivors were not sacrificed, and therefore it could not be determined if the same pathophysiologic process occurred in survivors. In the rabbit antibiotic combination study, all animals (survivors and non-survivors), were sacrificed and had their tissues examined microscopically. While all placebo
L1619: animals had both systemic and CNS findings consistent with anthrax, only 1 animal in an active treatment group died of anthrax but did not have CNS findings (rabbit K99203 in the levofloxacin group; note rabbit K99246 in the levofloxacin/raxibacumab group died of a gavage accident). None of the rabbits surviving to study termination had lesions attributable to anthrax at sacrifice. Similarly in the combination NHP study, only 1 animal in the ciprofloxacin/raxibacumab group died of anthrax. While this animal did have evidence of hemorrhagic meningitis, the single death limits the degree of analysis that can be performed.
L1620: ## *Limitations of clinical safety findings*
L1621: There are several risks with respect to safety as determined in human subjects. First, a safety database of 326 subjects cannot exclude a serious adverse event (SAE) or fatal event occurring at less than 1% frequency. In addition, as the safety database consisted only of healthy volunteers, any possible study agent/disease interaction could not be directly assessed. Lastly, the exclusion of pediatric subjects and other special populations (pregnant patients, and patients with renal and hepatic dysfunction), and insufficient numbers of subjects aged 65 years and older limit the generalizability of safety results to these populations.
